2048.heroParagraph: 2048 was created by Italian developer Gabriele Cirulli in March 2014 as an open-source clone of the tile-merging game Threes. This build runs on a fixed 4x4 grid and includes a built-in AI: press the Auto-run button and the game's own heuristic solver (which scores boards on tile smoothness, monotonic ordering, and open-cell count) takes over the arrow keys for you.
instructions: Use the arrow keys to slide every tile on the board in that direction at once; two tiles with the same number merge into one tile with double the value the instant they collide, and after every move the game drops a new tile into a random empty cell — 90% of the time a 2, 10% of the time a 4.
The game is won the moment any tile reaches the value 2048, but the board keeps accepting moves afterward if you want to keep merging toward higher tiles once that condition is met.

Press the Auto-run button to hand control to the built-in solver, which picks each move by evaluating board smoothness and monotonicity rather than playing randomly — watching a few of its moves is a fast way to see why keeping your highest tile in a corner matters.

sections.heading: Keep your highest tile cornered
sections.body: Because every arrow-key move slides the entire board in one direction, a high-value tile that is not pinned in a corner gets shuffled around and blocks merges instead of anchoring them. Picking one corner and repeatedly sliding toward it keeps your largest tiles stacked in descending order along that edge.

sections.heading: Watch the 90/10 spawn odds
sections.body: New tiles spawn as a 2 nine times out of ten and a 4 the rest of the time, always in an empty cell. Since you cannot control where the new tile lands, leaving at least one empty row or column gives the spawn room to land without immediately blocking your next planned merge.

sections.heading: Avoid sliding toward your empty side
sections.body: The board only fills up once open cells run out, so repeatedly sliding in the direction that empties tiles away from your corner strategy is what causes most losses — once movesAvailable() returns false because every adjacent tile has a different value, the run ends immediately.

Rooftop Snipers comes from New Eich Games, also behind Getaway Shootout and House of Hazards. Two ragdoll gunmen face off on a narrow rooftop, and one well-placed shot sends the loser flying off the edge. Player 1 jumps with W and fires with E; Player 2 jumps with I and fires with O. Holding the shoot key raises the rifle and lets you adjust the angle before releasing, while a quick tap fires immediately at the current angle. Because the rooftop has hard edges, a hit near the edge ends the round even from a shot that would only stagger someone at center stage, so position matters as much as landing hits.

houseofhazards.heroParagraph: House of Hazards is another New Eich Games title, the same studio behind Getaway Shootout and Rooftop Snipers. Up to four players race around a house completing everyday tasks — drinking coffee, collecting mail — while triggering hazards like flying toast, swinging hammers, and laser traps to sabotage whoever is chasing the same task.
instructions: Player 1 moves with A/D (or the left/right arrow keys) to turn, W (or up) to jump, and S (or down) to crouch; Player 2 uses J and L to turn, I to jump, and K to crouch. A third and fourth player need a gamepad, using the left stick to move and the face buttons to jump and duck.

Tasks around the house — like the coffee machine or the mailbox — are what you are racing to complete, and finishing one before your rivals is how you score, so beelining for the nearest active task usually beats exploring the whole house.

Hazards like the swinging hammer or the toaster's flying toast trigger automatically as players walk near them and will hit whoever is closest regardless of which player caused it, so a hazard that just fired is briefly safer to walk past than one that hasn't triggered yet.

sections.heading: Crouching dodges more than jumping does
sections.body: Several hazards, like swinging hammers and thrown objects, pass at head height, which means crouching (S for Player 1, K for Player 2) clears them when jumping would put you directly in the hazard's path. Reflexively jumping at every hazard is a common mistake — check whether the hazard is low or high before reacting.

sections.heading: Hazards reset on a timer, not on demand
sections.body: A hazard that just triggered needs a moment before it can fire again, so the instant after a hammer swings or toast launches is the safest window to walk past that specific spot. Waiting out an active hazard's reset is usually faster than detouring around it.

sections.heading: Race the task, not the other player
sections.body: Since completing your assigned task is what scores points, chasing down an opponent to block them costs time you could spend finishing your own task, especially in 1-player mode against computer opponents that path directly to their goal without hesitation.

drivemad.name: Drive Mad
drivemad.title: Drive Mad Unblocked - Play Free Online | Schplay
drivemad.metaDescription: Play Drive Mad unblocked at Schplay across 100 physics-driving levels. Two buttons — accelerate and brake — control a ragdoll-suspension vehicle that tips forward on the gas and backward on the brake, over icy slopes, ramps, and bouncing bridges.
drivemad.metaKeywords: Drive Mad, drive mad unblocked, physics driving game, ragdoll car, obstacle course driving, schplay drive mad
drivemad.heroParagraph: Drive Mad is a physics driving game built around just two controls — accelerate and brake — spread across roughly 100 browser levels. The car's suspension behaves like a ragdoll: accelerating tips the body forward, braking tips it backward, and both actions have visible, sometimes exaggerated consequences on the vehicle's balance.
instructions: Hold the accelerate key to move forward and tip the car's weight forward, and hold the brake key to slow down and tip the weight backward — there is no steering input, so every obstacle is solved through throttle and brake timing alone, not lateral movement.

The first ten to fifteen levels are built to teach this balance-and-timing rhythm on relatively forgiving terrain; difficulty ramps up sharply afterward, so a technique that works on an early icy slope may fail on a later level that changes the vehicle entirely.

Surfaces change how the car behaves from level to level: wooden bridges bounce under the car's weight, ramps launch it higher than a flat surface would, and some levels reverse which key accelerates versus brakes, so read each new level's terrain before committing to a throttle rhythm that worked on the last one.

sections.heading: Balance is the whole game, not steering
sections.body: With only accelerate and brake as inputs, tipping the car too far forward or backward is what causes most crashes, not misjudging distance. Tapping the throttle in short bursts rather than holding it down keeps the car's body closer to level on uneven terrain like ramps or bridges.

sections.heading: Different vehicles behave completely differently
sections.body: The vehicle changes across levels — a stretch limo handles nothing like a rocket-propelled car — so the same tap rhythm that cleared one level can immediately fail on the next. Treat each new vehicle's first obstacle as a calibration test for how sensitive its balance is before committing to full-speed inputs.

sections.heading: Surface changes momentum without warning
sections.body: Wooden bridges bounce, ramps add unexpected height, and ice removes traction almost entirely, all without any on-screen indicator before you reach them. Slowing down slightly on approach to any new surface type gives more room to correct if the car reacts differently than the previous stretch of road.

agario.metaDescription: Play Agar.io unblocked at Schplay. Move your cell with the mouse, press Space to split in two and lunge forward, or W to eject mass — eat pellets and smaller cells to grow while avoiding anything bigger than you on the shared leaderboard server.
agario.metaKeywords: Agar.io, agario unblocked, io game, cell eating game, mass split, schplay agario
agario.heroParagraph: Agar.io drops your cell onto a shared map with every other player currently connected, ranked live on a leaderboard by mass. Growth comes from eating colored pellets scattered across the map and absorbing any player cell smaller than your own; the only real threat is a cell large enough to eat you back.
instructions: Move the mouse to steer your cell in that direction; there is no keyboard movement, so positioning is entirely mouse-driven while Space and W handle the two special actions.

Press Space to split your cell into two smaller ones that can combine again after a cooldown — splitting lets a piece of your cell lunge forward past a smaller opponent that would otherwise outrun you, but it also leaves both halves temporarily weaker until they recombine.

Press W to eject a small piece of your own mass as a moving pellet, which is mainly used to feed a teammate's cell or to bait a much larger opponent's cell away from you rather than to attack directly.

sections.heading: Splitting is a lunge, not just a size trade
sections.body: A split sends one half of your cell shooting forward in the mouse's current direction, which is what actually lets you catch a smaller cell that would otherwise simply outrun your unsplit mass. The tradeoff is that both halves are smaller and vulnerable until the recombine cooldown finishes, so splitting next to a larger cell is dangerous.

sections.heading: Bigger cells move slower
sections.body: Cell speed drops as mass increases, so a much larger cell chasing you directly will rarely catch up on a straight line — the real danger is a large cell cutting off your path or trapping you against the edge of the map, not a head-on chase.

sections.heading: Ejecting mass has uses beyond feeding
sections.body: While W is mainly known for feeding mass to a teammate's cell to help them grow past a threshold, ejected mass can also be used to bait a large predator cell into moving in a specific direction, buying time to escape toward open space instead.

retrobowl.heroParagraph: Retro Bowl was built by New Star Games, the British studio founded by Simon Read that also made New Star Soccer, and released in January 2020. It puts you in charge of both coaching and playing quarterback: manage the roster and salary cap between games, then take direct control on the field to read the defense and find open receivers.
instructions: Use the on-screen joystick to move your quarterback in the pocket and your receivers after the snap, then swipe in the direction of an open receiver to throw; a quick swipe throws a normal pass while a double-tap throws a bullet pass that arrives faster but is harder to control.

Off the field, contract negotiations, player morale, and coaching staff upgrades all draw from the same limited salary cap, so a big free-agent signing at quarterback can leave no budget left to replace an aging offensive line.

Swipe down to call a timeout when a drive stalls or the play clock is about to run out; timeouts are limited per half, so saving at least one for a late defensive stop matters more than using it to reset an early third down.

sections.heading: Reading the pocket before you move
sections.body: Because you directly control the quarterback with the joystick, stepping up in the pocket too early walks you into a sack that a stationary quarterback would have avoided by throwing the ball away instead. Watch which receiver is breaking open before committing to a scramble.

sections.heading: Bullet passes trade accuracy for speed
sections.body: A double-tap bullet pass gets the ball to a receiver faster, which matters against tight coverage, but it is less forgiving of a mistimed throw than a normal swipe pass. Save bullet passes for receivers who are clearly open rather than using them as a default.

sections.heading: The salary cap connects every decision
sections.body: Retro Bowl ties contract offers, coaching upgrades, and player morale to one shared budget, so overspending to keep a star receiver can quietly weaken the rest of the roster for seasons afterward. Rebuilding the offensive line or defense often matters more long-term than chasing one flashy free agent.

ovo.heroParagraph: OvO is a momentum-driven stickman parkour game where the goal on every level is reaching a flag while avoiding spikes and other hazards. Speed carries between moves, so chaining a slide into a jump or a wall jump into another wall jump keeps momentum going in a way that stopping and restarting never can.
instructions: Move with the left/right arrow keys or A/D, jump with the up arrow or W, and slide under low obstacles with the down arrow or S while running — jumping out of a slide covers more horizontal distance than jumping from a standing start.

Press up while touching a wall to wall-jump off it; leaping toward a wall and pressing jump again the instant you touch it kicks you off in the opposite direction, and stringing several wall jumps together is how vertical shafts and wide gaps get crossed.

Pressing down while airborne triggers a smash attack that lets your stickman pass through certain transparent obstacles instead of bouncing off them — useful on levels that place a see-through barrier directly in your jump arc.

sections.heading: Momentum carries between moves
sections.body: A slide that transitions directly into a jump launches farther than a jump from a standstill, and a wall jump chained immediately into another wall jump keeps your speed climbing instead of resetting. Stopping to line up a jump costs more time than committing to the chain and adjusting mid-air.

sections.heading: Wall jumps need the timing, not just the wall
sections.body: Pressing jump on approach to a wall does nothing on its own — the kick-off only fires if you press again at the moment of contact. Jumping toward a wall too early or too late just results in sliding down it, so the input has to land on the touch itself.

sections.heading: Smash attacks pass through specific obstacles only
sections.body: The midair smash (press down while jumping) is built for see-through barriers that block a normal jump path, not for every hazard on a level — spikes and solid walls still end the run on contact, so smash is a targeted tool rather than a way to ignore obstacles generally.

idle-breakout.heroParagraph: Idle Breakout was made by Kodiqi and turns the classic brick-breaker into an incremental game: instead of controlling one paddle and ball, you buy automated balls that bounce around the screen on their own, breaking bricks and generating cash without needing constant input.
instructions: Click bricks directly with the mouse early on to earn starting cash, since manual clicks are the only income source before your first automated ball is purchased.

Spend earned cash on ball types with different behaviors — Plasma Balls deal splash damage to bricks near their impact point, while Sniper Balls hit a single brick harder — and buy more balls or upgrade existing ones to keep clearing bricks faster than new rows appear.

When progress on the current run slows down significantly, prestiging resets your bricks and cash in exchange for a permanent bonus on the next run, so the highest-value move late in a run is often prestiging rather than continuing to grind the same wall of bricks.

sections.heading: Manual clicking is only a bootstrap
sections.body: Clicking bricks by hand matters in the first few minutes to afford an initial ball, but it stops scaling almost immediately once automated balls are in play — time spent clicking after that point is better spent deciding which ball type or upgrade to buy next.

sections.heading: Match ball type to the wall you are facing
sections.body: Splash-damage balls like Plasma clear clustered groups of weak bricks fastest, while single-target balls like Sniper are worth prioritizing against walls with a few high-health bricks mixed into weaker ones. Buying only one ball type caps how fast either situation gets cleared.

sections.heading: Prestige when a run stalls, not before
sections.body: Prestiging wipes your current cash and bricks progress in exchange for a permanent multiplier on future runs, so resetting too early loses more than it gains — the right moment is when brick clearing has visibly slowed relative to earlier in the same run, not on a fixed timer.

sections.heading: Buildings compound faster than clicking
sections.body: Each building purchase increases that building's price for the next one, but total cookies-per-second from a full building lineup outpaces manual clicking almost immediately after the first few purchases. Prioritizing whichever building currently gives the best cookies-per-second for its price beats save-and-click strategies.

sections.heading: Golden Cookies reward attention, not idling
sections.body: Because Golden Cookies appear at random intervals and vanish if not clicked in time, a run played with the tab in the background misses bonuses that a run with the tab open and visible would catch — the random multiplier or cookie windfall from a Golden Cookie can be worth more than several minutes of normal production.

sections.heading: Minigames unlock progressively, not all at once
sections.body: The Garden, Grimoire, Pantheon, and Stock Market minigames each require owning enough of their linked building (Farms, Wizard Towers, Temples, and Banks respectively) before they become available, so ignoring a building type entirely also means permanently skipping the strategic options its minigame would unlock.

Hold the up arrow to accelerate and the down arrow to brake, and use the left and right arrow keys to lean your rider forward or backward in midair — landing a jump nose-first or tail-first crashes the bike even on a jump that was cleared with plenty of height.

Because the clock does not start until you press the gas, use the standing start to look ahead at the next obstacle, mine, or gap before committing, rather than launching immediately and reacting blind.

sections.heading: Landing angle matters more than jump height
sections.body: Clearing a gap or ramp is not enough on its own — leaning too far forward or backward with the arrow keys while airborne causes a crash on landing even when the jump itself was clean. Leveling the bike out before touchdown is the actual skill each level is testing.

sections.heading: The five games do not share progress

sections.heading: Use the pre-start pause deliberately
sections.body: Since the timer only begins once you accelerate, standing still at the start of a level to read the upcoming obstacles, explosive mines, or moving hazards costs zero time on the clock — a habit worth building on levels with obstacles placed close to the starting point.

blockblast.heroParagraph: Block Blast was released by Hungry Studio, a Hong Kong-based developer, in September 2022. Three block shapes are dealt at a time, each one placed exactly as shown with no rotation allowed, and the entire game is played on a fixed 8x8 grid.
instructions: Drag each of the three dealt block shapes onto the 8x8 grid one at a time; none can be rotated, so a shape that does not fit the current board layout has to be placed somewhere it still fits rather than turned to match a gap.

Filling every cell in a horizontal row or vertical column clears that entire row or column and scores points, and a single placement can clear more than one row or column at once if it completes several simultaneously.

All three current pieces must be placed before a new set of three is dealt, and the run ends immediately the moment any one of your current three pieces has no empty space left on the board that it can fit into — not when the board fully fills up.

sections.heading: Play the edges first, save the center
sections.body: Filling the outer rows and columns early keeps the center of the board open for large shapes like the 3x3 square or the 1x5 line, which are the pieces most likely to have nowhere to go if only small gaps remain. Placing large shapes into open center space first, before the edges fill in, prevents them from becoming unplaceable later.

sections.heading: A single stray cell can end the run
sections.body: Because the game ends the instant any one of your three current pieces cannot fit anywhere, a single awkward 1-cell gap left in the wrong spot can make an otherwise-placeable piece unplaceable. Avoid leaving isolated single-cell holes, since most shapes need at least two or three cells in a line to fit.

sections.heading: No rotation changes what "planning ahead" means
sections.body: Since none of the three shapes can be rotated, planning has to work around the exact orientation you are given rather than assuming a piece can be turned to fit a gap. Clearing a row or column to reset the board's open space is often more reliable than waiting for a shape that happens to match an awkward remaining gap.

subwaysurfer.heroParagraph: Subway Surfers was built by Kiloo and SYBO and launched in 2012; SYBO has run it solo since Kiloo stepped back from development in early 2020. Jake sprints down three train tracks that never stop generating new obstacles, and the run only ends when a train, barrier, or oncoming obstacle catches him.
instructions: The arrow keys stand in for the original swipe controls on this port: left and right switch between the three tracks, up jumps over low barriers and onto train cars, and down rolls or slides under overhead obstacles.

Pressing up a second time while already airborne triggers a double jump, which is the only way to clear obstacles positioned too high to reach with a single jump — timing the second press near the peak of the first jump gives the most extra height.

Coins scattered along all three tracks fund power-ups and character unlocks between runs, but chasing a coin into the wrong track is a common way to run straight into a barrier you would have otherwise had time to react to.

sections.heading: React to the lane, not just the obstacle type
sections.body: Because obstacles spawn across all three tracks independently, the actual decision on each obstacle is which lane to be in beforehand, not just whether to jump or roll. Committing to a lane change one obstacle early leaves more margin than reacting to what is directly in front of Jake.

sections.heading: Double jump timing is the ceiling on your run length
sections.body: Since the second jump input only adds height if pressed while still rising from the first, mistiming it into the descent wastes the double jump entirely on obstacles that specifically require the extra clearance. Practicing the press-timing on flat stretches with no obstacles builds the reflex before it matters.

sections.heading: Coins are a resource, not the objective
sections.body: Coins fund upgrades between runs but sit in the same lanes as obstacles, so treating every coin as worth collecting leads to unnecessary lane changes into danger. Prioritizing survival over a coin trail that crosses into a risky lane keeps runs going longer, which earns more coins overall than a short run chasing every one.

sections.heading: Power pellets are offense, not just defense

duckhunt.heroParagraph: This build is a Flash-era browser recreation of the Duck Hunt light-gun concept popularized by Nintendo's 1984 arcade release, running through the Ruffle Flash emulator since native Flash support was discontinued. instructions: Move the mouse to aim your crosshair and click to fire; unlike a keyboard-only shooter, aim is entirely analog through mouse position rather than snapping to discrete lanes or targets.

Press R to reload once your shots for the current wave run out — missing shots still counts against your limited ammo, so firing at a duck that has already changed direction wastes a shot that a wave often cannot afford to lose.

Press Space to start the next wave once the current one clears; ducks tend to move faster and change direction more abruptly as waves progress, so a shot pattern that worked on an early wave may not track a later wave's movement.

sections.heading: Lead the duck, don't chase it
sections.body: Because ducks change direction abruptly and the crosshair takes a moment to move with the mouse, clicking where a duck currently is often fires behind where it has already moved. Aiming slightly ahead of a duck's flight path lands more hits than tracking its exact current position.

sections.heading: Ammo is limited per wave, not per shot
sections.body: Since each wave gives a fixed number of shots before requiring a reload, missing early in a wave leaves fewer shots to clear the remaining ducks. Waiting half a second for a clean, close shot is usually worth more than firing early at a duck still far away or moving unpredictably.

sections.heading: Later waves need a faster aim update, not just faster clicking
sections.body: As waves progress, ducks move faster and change direction more abruptly, so the skill that scales is how quickly the aim adjusts to a duck's new heading, not how quickly the mouse button is clicked. A rushed shot on a wrong prediction wastes ammo that a later, corrected shot could have used instead.

bejeweled2.heroParagraph: Bejeweled 2 is PopCap Games' 2004 sequel to the original Bejeweled, adding special gems created by matching more than the minimum three: a four-gem match creates a Flame Gem, a five-in-a-row creates a Hypercube, and two matches intersecting in a T, L, or plus shape creates a Star Gem, each triggering a different clearing effect when detonated.
instructions: Click one gem, then click an adjacent gem to swap them; a swap that creates a horizontal or vertical match of three or more clears those gems, while a swap that creates no match reverses itself automatically.

Matching exactly four gems of the same color creates a Flame Gem that, when later matched, clears every gem in a 3x3 area around it, including triggering any other special gems caught in that blast radius.

Matching five gems in a row creates a Hypercube; swapping a Hypercube with any regular gem clears every gem of that gem's color from the entire board, making it the most valuable special gem to save for a color that has spread widely across the grid.

sections.heading: Star Gems come from intersections, not straight lines
sections.body: Unlike Flame Gems and Hypercubes, a Star Gem requires two matches crossing each other in a T, L, or plus shape rather than a longer straight line. When detonated, it clears its entire row and column plus triggers any special gems caught in that cross, making it useful for cutting through a cluttered board.

sections.heading: Save Hypercubes for spread-out colors
sections.body: Because a Hypercube clears every gem of whatever color it is swapped into, it delivers the most value when that color has spread across many separate clusters on the board rather than already being grouped into an easy match — using one on a color that was about to match normally anyway wastes its potential.

sections.heading: Chain reactions multiply special-gem value
sections.body: Detonating a Flame Gem or Star Gem near another special gem triggers both at once, and the gems that fall to refill the board can themselves complete new matches. Planning a match near an existing special gem, rather than in an empty part of the board, increases the odds of a chain reaction that clears far more than one match alone.

sections.heading: Glide angle is a constant tradeoff, not a set-and-forget input
sections.body: Holding the nose too high bleeds speed and stalls the glide early, while holding it too low dives into the water sooner than necessary. Making small corrections throughout the flight rather than picking one angle and holding it produces longer distances than either extreme.

sections.heading: Fire rockets after the glide stabilizes

Waiting until the glide is level before holding Space gets more usable distance out of the same rocket fuel.

sections.heading: Early runs are about coins, not distance records
sections.body: Since permanent upgrades to the ramp, glider, and rockets all come from coins earned by distance, treating the first several attempts as coin-farming runs rather than personal-best attempts builds toward genuinely longer flights faster than repeatedly trying to maximize an under-upgraded penguin's distance.

cut-the-rope.heroParagraph: Cut the Rope was released by ZeptoLab on October 4, 2010, and the goal in every level is the same: cut the ropes holding a piece of candy so it swings, falls, or bounces into the mouth of Om Nom, the small green creature waiting below, while collecting all three stars scattered along the way.
instructions: Click or swipe across a rope to cut it; the candy then swings or falls based on gravity and momentum, so cutting a rope at the wrong moment sends the candy in a direction that misses both the stars and Om Nom entirely.

Levels are grouped into boxes of 25, and each box introduces a new mechanic on top of the ones already learned — bubbles that float the candy upward, air cushions that bounce it, spikes that pop it instantly on contact — so a level pack later in the game combines mechanics rather than teaching them in isolation.

Collecting all three stars in a level is optional for finishing it but required in total count to unlock later boxes, so a level cleared by simply feeding Om Nom without the stars can still block progress if the box's star requirement is not met.

sections.heading: Order of cuts matters more than speed
sections.body: Because the candy's path depends on momentum built up from previous swings, cutting ropes in the wrong sequence can send it flying past a star or directly into a spike that a different cut order would have avoided entirely. Watching one full swing before committing to the next cut avoids compounding an early mistake.

sections.heading: Bubbles and cushions redirect, they don't just decorate
sections.body: A bubble carries the candy straight upward regardless of how it entered, and an air cushion bounces it in the direction the cushion is angled — both override the candy's existing momentum, so a rope cut that lines the candy up with a bubble or cushion is often more reliable than a direct swing toward Om Nom.

sections.heading: Star count gates progress, not just individual levels
sections.body: Since unlocking later boxes requires a minimum total star count rather than just clearing every level, skipping stars to rush through a box can leave you unable to access the next one even with every level technically completed. Replaying an early, easier level for its missed stars is often faster than struggling for stars on a harder one.

sections.heading: Bounced shots are a real threat, not a miss

sections.heading: Firepower pickups are worth contesting

sections.heading: Maze layout dictates safe firing lines more than direct aim
sections.body: Because walls both block and redirect bullets, understanding a specific maze's corridor layout matters more for landing hits than raw aiming precision — a shot lined up correctly for a particular maze's geometry can hit an opponent who has no direct line of sight to you at all.

sections.heading: The music box is a background timer, not a one-time task

Touching any spike, block edge, or hazard sends the attempt back to the very start of the level rather than a checkpoint, so a mistake near the end of a long level means replaying everything that came before it as well.

Because the course is fixed and repeatable, memorizing the exact timing of upcoming obstacle clusters through repeated attempts is the primary way levels get cleared, rather than reacting to obstacles in real time the way an unpredictable game would require.

sections.heading: No checkpoints means memorization compounds
sections.body: Since a single hit anywhere in the level sends the attempt back to the start rather than a nearby checkpoint, a section mastered early in a run still has to be executed perfectly again on every subsequent attempt, making earlier sections just as important to keep clean as the specific part that keeps causing a failure.

sections.heading: Auto-run means only timing matters, not positioning
sections.body: Because forward movement is entirely automatic, the only input decision at any moment is whether and when to jump — there is no lateral positioning to manage, so success comes down to internalizing the exact rhythm of upcoming obstacles rather than reacting to their horizontal position.

sections.heading: Fixed layouts reward practice runs, not reflexes
sections.body: Since the obstacle layout never changes between attempts, treating early attempts as practice runs for learning a section's specific timing — rather than expecting to clear it blind on reflex alone — matches how these levels are actually designed to be beaten.

tetris.heroParagraph: This build is an open-source HTML5 recreation of Tetris by developer Sandy Duan, built as a practice project rather than an official licensed release of Alexey Pajitnov's 1984 original — the falling-tetromino, line-clearing formula is the same one that made Tetris one of the most recognized puzzle games ever designed.
instructions: Use the left and right arrow keys to shift a falling tetromino sideways, the up arrow to rotate it, and the down arrow to drop it faster; each piece is one of seven fixed tetromino shapes, and placement decisions have to account for the shape of the stack already below.

A horizontal row that becomes completely filled across its width clears entirely, and everything above it shifts down to fill the gap — clearing multiple rows with a single piece placement scores more than clearing them one at a time across separate pieces.

The game ends when the stack of placed pieces reaches the top of the well, so leaving gaps or uneven surfaces that later pieces cannot fill cleanly is what typically causes the stack height to climb out of control rather than any single bad placement alone.

sections.heading: Flat surfaces prevent compounding gaps
sections.body: Because later tetromino shapes cannot always fill an oddly-shaped gap left by an earlier placement, keeping the top of the stack as flat and even as possible makes more of the seven piece shapes usable for the next drop, while an uneven surface narrows down which shapes can be placed without creating a new gap.

sections.heading: Clearing multiple rows at once is worth more than one at a time
sections.body: Since scoring rewards clearing several completed rows with a single piece placement more than clearing them individually across separate pieces, deliberately building up multiple near-complete rows before clearing them — rather than clearing each row the moment it completes — scores significantly higher over a full game.

sections.heading: Rotation should be planned before the piece reaches the stack
sections.body: Because a tetromino can only be rotated while it is still falling, waiting until a piece is already near the stack to decide its final orientation leaves little room to correct a bad rotation choice — deciding the target position and rotation as soon as a piece appears gives more time to adjust before it lands.

Press Q to use a currently held pill, card, or rune; these consumables have run-changing effects, and some are unidentified until used at least once, so using an unknown pill or card always carries some risk alongside its potential benefit.

Hold Ctrl to drop a held trinket or consumable, or to swap between multiple held consumables if an item has granted the ability to carry more than one at once — managing which consumable is active matters especially in a tough room where the right one used at the right moment can turn a fight around.

sections.heading: Kiting is the core combat skill
sections.body: Because movement and shooting are controlled independently, moving away from an enemy while still firing tears at it — rather than standing still to aim or moving directly toward danger — is the fundamental technique that makes most rooms survivable, especially against enemies that charge directly at Isaac.

sections.heading: Unidentified consumables carry real risk
sections.body: Since some pills and cards are unidentified until used, testing one in a safe moment (rather than as a desperate last resort mid-fight) reveals its effect for the rest of the run without gambling on an unknown, potentially harmful outcome exactly when survival is already on the line.

sections.heading: Procedural generation means item combinations vary every run
sections.body: Because room layouts and item drops are generated fresh each run, a build that relied heavily on one specific item combination in a previous run cannot be assumed to reappear — adapting strategy to whatever items actually drop in the current run matters more than replicating a build from a prior successful attempt.

A boss Galaga occasionally attempts to capture the fighter with a tractor beam instead of attacking directly; a captured fighter can be rescued by flying a second fighter into it, which merges the two into a dual fighter with additional firepower for the rest of that life.

sections.heading: Formation aliens are free points, not passive scenery

sections.heading: Boss Galaga tractor beams require needing two hits, not one

sections.heading: A captured fighter is a rescue opportunity, not a permanent loss
sections.body: Because a fighter captured by a tractor beam can be freed by flying a second fighter directly into it, losing a ship to a tractor beam is not necessarily the end of that life — successfully rescuing it creates a dual fighter with more firepower than either ship had alone, turning a capture into a net gain if timed correctly.

sections.heading: Coins must be collected before the exit counts
sections.body: Reaching the green exit box without having collected every yellow coin on the level does not complete it, so route planning has to account for every coin's position, not just the shortest path to the exit — a direct line to the exit that skips a coin accomplishes nothing.

sections.heading: Blue dot patterns are fixed, so timing is learnable
sections.body: Because each blue dot follows a consistent movement pattern rather than moving randomly, observing one full cycle of a dot's path before attempting to cross its area reveals a safe timing window — moving on a guess rather than a learned pattern is the most common way to restart a level.

sections.heading: Later levels stack independent patterns
sections.body: As the 30 levels progress, multiple blue dot patterns often overlap in the same space on different cycles, so a timing window that is safe for one dot's pattern is not automatically safe once a second pattern is also moving through that same area — both patterns need to be tracked together, not just the nearest one.

sections.heading: Each week resets note-pattern familiarity

sections.heading: Early or late hits both count against accuracy

sections.body: Since both ropes and bombs are carried in limited quantities rather than being freely available, using a bomb to blast through every wall out of curiosity or a rope on a fall that could be survived some other way leaves fewer available for a genuine emergency later in that same run.

sections.heading: Accumulated value is what the end-of-level cannon phase depends on

sections.heading: Merging with matching numbers compounds faster than collecting alone
sections.body: Because merging combines matching values into a single higher number rather than just adding to a count, seeking out numbers that match your character's current value produces bigger value jumps than picking up any nearby number regardless of whether it matches, similar to how matching tiles works in the original 2048.

sections.heading: Mechanisms only do what a single trigger allows

sections.heading: Flap timing gets stricter as your number grows

sections.heading: This is a parody built on two well-known mechanics, not a new one
sections.body: Because the game deliberately combines Flappy Bird's flap physics with 2048's merge-and-double logic, understanding either source game individually explains most of what Flappy 2048 is doing — the challenge comes from combining the two simultaneously, not from either mechanic being reinvented.

connect-3.heroParagraph: Connect 3 is a compact browser match-three built on an eight-by-eight board of seven tile types. What sets it apart from most match-three clones is that every colour is paired with its own shape - a plus, circle, triangle, square, hexagon, dash, or dot - so the board stays readable if you cannot separate the red and green tiles by hue alone. There is no timer, no move limit, and no fail state; the board simply refills forever and the only number that moves is your score.
instructions: Click a tile to select it, then click a tile directly above, below, left, or right of it to swap the two. Diagonal swaps are rejected outright, and clicking the selected tile a second time cancels the selection so you can pick somewhere else without committing to a move.

A swap is only allowed to stand if it creates a line of three or more matching tiles. If the pair you swapped produces nothing, the two tiles slide back to where they started after about a fifth of a second, so an illegal-looking move costs you nothing except the moment it took to try it.

Every tile cleared is worth 100 points, and clears are resolved in a loop rather than one pass. Tiles above a gap drop down, fresh tiles enter from the top row, and if that reshuffle happens to form another line the game clears that too and keeps going until the board settles.

sections.heading: Shapes do the work that colour usually does
sections.body: Each of the seven tile types carries a distinct outline as well as a distinct colour, which means you can scan a column for triangles rather than for yellow. That matters more than it sounds on an eight-by-eight board where the orange circles and the red dashes sit next to each other constantly, and it is the reason the board stays legible during a long cascade when tiles are still animating into place.

sections.heading: Play for the cascade, not the match
sections.body: Because clears resolve in a loop and new tiles fall in from the top, the highest-value moves are the ones made near the bottom of the board. Clearing low forces the entire column above to drop, which gives the game far more chances to form an accidental second or third line. A match made in the top row shifts almost nothing and usually scores exactly the tiles you lined up and no more.

sections.heading: The board never runs out of moves
sections.body: The opening board is scrubbed before you see it - the game repeatedly replaces tiles until no line of three exists - so your first move is always a real one. From there the refill is random rather than curated, so there is no shuffle button and no deadlock check. Since nothing is lost by trying, probing an uncertain swap is genuinely free, and the failed attempt shows you a little more of the board.

captain-callisto.heroParagraph: The Adventures of Captain Callisto is a 3D platformer written by Cody Ebberson for js13kGames 2021, the annual competition where the entire game - code, textures, audio and levels - has to fit inside 13 kilobytes with no external files of any kind. It placed third overall out of 223 entries and was voted second for its use of the contest theme and fourth for graphics, which is remarkable company for a game smaller than most single photographs.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys or WASD and jump with Z or the space bar. The camera sits behind the Captain in true 3D rather than the flat side-on view most 13 kilobyte entries settle for, so watch the shadow beneath him to judge where a landing will actually put you before committing to a jump.

The jetpack is the mechanic that defines the game. Hold X or shift to fire it and gain height in mid-air, which turns almost every gap into a question of fuel management rather than timing. A jump you have already committed to badly can often still be rescued with a short burst, so reach for the jetpack rather than accepting the fall.

Press R at any point to restart the current level instantly, M to toggle the music, and escape to return to the main menu. The quick restart is there because the game is built around learning a level's layout through repetition - failing a section, seeing exactly what caught you out, and clearing it on the next attempt.

sections.heading: Why a 13 kilobyte 3D game is remarkable
sections.body: js13kGames forbids external resources entirely, so there is no CDN request, no texture download and no audio file. Everything Captain Callisto renders is produced by the code itself at load time, and the zipped bundle still has to come in under 13,312 bytes. Third place out of 223 entries was won against a field that mostly stayed two-dimensional precisely because 3D consumes so much of that budget.

sections.heading: Read the shadow, not the character
sections.body: The most useful habit in any third-person 3D platformer is to track the shadow rather than the character. Depth is genuinely ambiguous from a camera sitting behind the player, and the shadow is the only element on screen that tells you which platform you are actually above. Players who miss jumps here are almost always misjudging depth rather than distance.

sections.heading: Jetpack fuel is the real resource
sections.body: Because the jetpack can extend or rescue nearly any jump, the interesting decisions are about when not to use it. Burning fuel early to clear a gap you could have jumped normally leaves nothing for the recovery you will need thirty seconds later, and since R restarts a level instantly, the cheapest way to learn a section's fuel budget is simply to run it a few times and watch where you run dry.

packabunchas.heroParagraph: PACKABUNCHAS is a tiling puzzle by Italian developer Mattia Fortunati, made for js13kGames 2021 on the theme of Space. The premise is that a crowd of space creatures need rescuing and the only way to save them is to pack them together, which turns the whole game into a polyomino fitting problem wrapped in soft pastel artwork Fortunati has credited to Sanrio and San-x. GitHub picked it out as one of their favourite entries from that year's competition.
instructions: Every creature is a polyomino - a shape built from squares, like a tetromino with more variety. Click or tap one to pick it up, drag it over the bin, and release to drop it in. Everything is done with clicks or taps and nothing else, which is why the game plays the same on a school Chromebook as it does on a phone.

Levels are generated rather than hand-built, so the bins vary in shape from one to the next and some of them contain holes you have to work around. Read the container before you place anything: an awkward notch in the wall dictates which piece has to go there far more than your preferred order of play does.

Place the least flexible shapes first. A long bar or an L-bend has only a handful of legal positions against an edge and dozens in open ground, so committing those early and filling the middle with compact pieces avoids the usual failure - stranding a one-square gap that nothing left in your set can reach.

sections.heading: It is a packing problem, not a Tetris clone
sections.body: Nothing falls and nothing is on a timer, which changes the skill entirely. Tetris asks you to react under pressure; PACKABUNCHAS asks you to solve a static arrangement before you commit to it. There is no score chasing you either - the framing is a running joke about rescuing thirteen thousand creatures, a nod to the competition's 13 kilobyte limit, spread across a sequence of levels.

sections.heading: Look at what a placement leaves behind
sections.body: The reliable way to lose a level is to create a gap in a shape that none of your remaining creatures matches. Before dropping a piece into open ground, check what the placement carves the empty space into. Splitting the bin into two regions when your smallest remaining piece covers three squares means a two-square region is already dead, even though the container still looks mostly empty.

sections.heading: A tutorial and a mascot, inside 13 kilobytes
sections.body: A mascot character walks you through the first level and keeps up ambient chatter and hints as you play, which is an unusual thing to spend bytes on when the entire game has to fit in 13,312 of them. The audio is generated in code with the ZzFX and ZzFXM micro-libraries rather than loaded as files, and that is what buys the room for music, sound effects and a talking guide at the same time.

q1k3.heroParagraph: Q1K3 is a working first-person shooter that fits in 13 kilobytes, written by Dominic Szablewski - better known as phoboslab - for js13kGames 2021, with music by Andreas Loesch of no-fate.net. The competition theme that year was Space and Szablewski ignored it completely, building a tribute to id Software's Quake instead because the original had just turned twenty-five. What fits inside the size limit is genuinely startling: two levels, five enemy types, three weapons, roughly thirty textures, dynamic lighting, working doors and a soundtrack.
instructions: Click the title screen to start, which hands the game pointer lock - press escape when you want the cursor back. Move with WASD or the arrow keys, look with the mouse and fire with left click. Jump with space or right click, and cycle the three weapons with Q and E or the mousewheel. The title screen also carries a mouse-speed slider, an invert toggle and a fullscreen button, all worth setting before your first run.

This is deliberately pre-modern shooter design, which means there is no reloading, no ironsights and no regenerating health. Ammunition and health are objects lying in the level, so exploring side rooms is not optional decoration - it is the only supply line you have, and a corridor you skipped is ammunition you do not get back.

Enemies do not take cover or flank, but they do fire the moment they have line of sight, and several of the five types lead their shots. Strafing sideways while keeping your crosshair on a target beats backing away in a straight line, because retreating in a straight line keeps you inside the firing solution they already have.

sections.heading: How a whole FPS fits in 13 kilobytes
sections.body: There are no image or audio files in Q1K3. Every texture is generated procedurally when the game loads, the music and sound effects are synthesised in code, and the level geometry is stored as a compact description rather than a model file. It still finds room for spatial audio with stereo separation and distance-based volume falloff, so you can hear roughly where an enemy is before you see it. Szablewski published a detailed making-of and the source under the MIT licence, and the game is still studied as a reference for extreme size optimisation.

sections.heading: Movement speed is the mechanic
sections.body: Quake-lineage shooters move much faster than modern ones, and Q1K3 keeps that. You outrun most incoming fire simply by never standing still, and the level layouts are built around that assumption - open arenas with pillars to break line of sight rather than corridors with cover points. Playing it like a cover shooter, stopping behind geometry to trade shots, works badly.

sections.heading: Two levels, and they are meant to be replayed
sections.body: The game is short by design because the byte budget went into systems rather than content. Both levels contain secrets and supply caches that are easy to miss on a first run, and because health does not regenerate, a second attempt with knowledge of where the armour is plays very differently from a blind one. Treat the first run as reconnaissance.

instructions: Thrust with W, Z or the up arrow and turn with A and D or the arrow keys; S brakes with reverse thrust. The craft handles differently depending on where it is - in open space the direction keys rotate you and thrust pushes you along your facing, while standing on a planet's surface the same keys run and jump instead.

Your goal is to find planets and complete them by charging up their sectors. Each planet you finish rewards you with a companion sprite that orbits you from then on, and those companions are not decoration - they feed you energy and fight for you, which is what makes the back half of a run survivable.

Energy is the resource everything runs on and thrusting spends it. The game's own advice is to find energy mass to absorb or fly near a completed planet to recharge, so the loop is to build up a small network of finished planets early and then use them as refuelling points while you push further out into unexplored space.

sections.heading: The red drain your energy, and you cannot shoot them
sections.body: Red harvesters guard the planets and steal energy from you when you get close, and the game is explicit that they can only be killed by planet sprites - the companions you earn by completing planets. Until you have some, the correct answer to a harvester is distance, not aggression. Giant drones show up later and attack the planets you have already finished, so a completed system still needs defending.

sections.body: The display tracks energy remaining, a circular indicator pointing at nearby planets, and running totals of planets discovered against planets completed. Because thrust is the main energy cost, checking the planet indicator before committing to a direction is the difference between arriving somewhere with enough charge to do the work and drifting into empty space with nothing left to recharge from.

sudoku.heroParagraph: Sudoku is the number-placement puzzle that ran in Japanese magazines through the 1980s under the name Suuji wa dokushin ni kagiru before Wayne Gould's computer-generated grids took it worldwide in British newspapers in 2004. This build is a deliberately plain browser version of the classic rules: one fixed nine-by-nine grid with 35 digits already placed and 46 blank squares for you to fill, plus a button that checks your work whenever you want it.
instructions: Fill every empty square so that each row, each column, and each of the nine three-by-three boxes contains the digits 1 through 9 exactly once. Click or tap a blank square to select it and type a number to place it. The 35 digits printed at the start are fixed clues and cannot be edited, so the puzzle always has the same solution.

Use the 'how am I going?' button whenever you want a check. It scans the grid and tells you one of three things: that there are duplicates, that there are no duplicates but empty cells remain, or that you have finished. Squares involved in a duplicate are highlighted so you can see exactly which pair of digits is in conflict.

Note that the checker only looks for repeated digits - it does not tell you whether a legal-looking digit is the correct one for the final solution. A grid can be entirely free of duplicates and still be wrong, so treat a clean check as evidence that you have not broken a rule yet rather than confirmation that you are on the solution path.

sections.heading: Start with the constraint, not the empty square
sections.body: The instinct is to pick a blank square and ask what could go there, which on a grid with 46 blanks gives you far too many candidates to hold in your head. The faster approach reverses it: take a digit, look at the three boxes in a band, and ask where that digit can still legally go. Rows and columns that already contain it eliminate most positions immediately, and often only one square survives.

sections.heading: Scan bands and stacks, not the whole grid
sections.body: A nine-by-nine grid is really three horizontal bands and three vertical stacks of three boxes each. Because a digit must appear exactly once in each box of a band, placing it in two boxes of that band usually forces its position in the third. Working band by band rather than sweeping the whole grid is what turns a puzzle that looks intimidating into a sequence of small, closed questions.

sections.heading: One fixed puzzle, which changes how you use it
sections.body: This version serves a single hand-placed grid rather than generating a new one each visit, so refreshing gives you the same 35 clues again. That makes it a poor choice for daily practice but a good one for learning technique, since you can abandon a half-finished attempt, come back later, and work the same position again with a different method to see which approach actually cracks it faster.

A 'how am I going?' button checks the grid and reports duplicates, remaining empty cells, or completion, highlighting any conflicting squares. The checker detects repeated digits only, so a grid with no duplicates is not necessarily on the correct solution path.

konnekt.heroParagraph: Konnekt is a real-time conquest game built by the developer monsterkodi for js13kGames 2018, and its defining idea is that the board is a sphere rather than a flat plane. Nodes sit at points on a globe you can rotate, and the connections between them curve around its surface, which means a position that looks safe from one angle can be surrounded from the side you cannot currently see. The whole thing is rendered as SVG in under 13 kilobytes.
instructions: Every node you own accumulates units over time, shown as a filling arc around it. Drag from one of your nodes to another to dispatch exactly half of its garrison along that link, and note that a node has to be holding at least twelve units before it is allowed to send anything at all. Nodes fill to a ceiling of 360, so a full one sitting idle is wasted production.

Distance costs you units, but only when you attack. Sending to a neutral or enemy node loses a share of the force in transit that scales with how far apart the two nodes are, while reinforcing one of your own nodes arrives at full strength no matter how far it travels. That single asymmetry is what makes short, local attacks and long, safe reinforcement the correct shape of most winning games.

An attack resolves as a straight comparison of the numbers that actually arrive. More than the defender and you capture the node with the surplus as its new garrison; fewer and you simply reduce it while it holds. An exact tie is reported as a draw and leaves the node empty for either side to take, which is usually the worst outcome available to you.

sections.heading: Twelve levels that escalate by economy, not intelligence
sections.body: Five tutorials lead into named boards - Easy, Circles, Ring, Close, Poles, Unfair, Frenzy and a randomised layout. What changes as you climb is the rate at which nodes generate units, which starts at zero in the tutorials and rises steeply by the time you reach Unfair and Frenzy. The opponent does not get cleverer, it gets richer, so those levels are won on tempo - striking during the window before its production advantage compounds.

sections.heading: The sphere is the whole design
sections.body: On a flat conquest map you can see every threat at once. On a globe you cannot, and Konnekt uses that constantly - the Poles and Ring levels are built specifically around positions that are adjacent on the sphere but appear far apart from a given camera angle. Rotating to check the far side before committing units is not a convenience here, it is a core part of playing well.

sections.heading: Half-strength attacks are the common mistake
sections.body: Because a send dispatches only part of a node's garrison, launching two attacks from the same node in quick succession usually delivers two forces that are each too small to take anything, while leaving the origin node stripped and vulnerable. Waiting for one node to fill and sending a single decisive wave beats trickling units at a target almost every time.

sections.heading: Sound that is generated, not recorded
sections.body: Each level assigns different synthesised instruments to you and to the opponent - piano, bells, organ, strings and flute across the level list - so the note you hear tells you whose move just resolved without your having to look. It is also a practical necessity: with a 13 kilobyte budget and no audio files allowed, every sound in the game has to be produced by code at the moment it plays.

Nodes you own gain units over time, and dragging from one node to another sends part of its garrison to reinforce or attack. Combat compares numbers directly - more units captures the node, fewer only reduces it, and a tie empties it. Five tutorials lead into named levels including Circles, Ring, Poles, Unfair and Frenzy, where the opponent's unit growth rate rises rather than its intelligence.

roadblocks.heroParagraph: Road Blocks is an isometric drag-and-drop puzzle written by Australian developer Ash Kyd for js13kGames 2015, whose theme that year was Reversed - an idea the game picks up directly in a level called Reverse the Flow. You build a working road across a small isometric town by pulling tiles from a tray at the top of the screen, and the entire thing, including the isometric renderer and the sound effects, fits inside 13 kilobytes.
instructions: Drag tiles down from the tray at the top of the screen and drop them onto the map to build a continuous road connecting the left edge to the right. Tiles snap to the isometric grid, and a placement that cannot legally connect is refused rather than silently accepted, so an invalid drop costs you nothing.

You are not limited to road. Water, forest and helipad tiles appear as the puzzles progress, each with its own rule - forest tiles award bonus points, and the helipad lets you stack a tile aside for later rather than committing it immediately. Long-press any tile you have already placed to bulldoze it and free that square up again.

Puzzle mode runs through a sequence of named levels including Roads 101, Town Planning, Reverse the Flow, The Block Forest, Dual Carriageway and Little Condo by the Sea, each introducing one new idea. Completing enough of them unlocks Free Map mode from the main menu, where there is no objective and you simply build a town for its own sake.

sections.heading: The tray order is the real constraint
sections.body: Tiles arrive in a fixed sequence and you have to take them as they come, so the puzzle is less about where the road should go than about what you can afford to do with the piece currently in your hand. Placing a straight where a corner is coming is how most levels are lost, and the helipad exists precisely so you can park an awkward tile instead of forcing it somewhere damaging.

sections.heading: Bulldozing is part of the loop, not a penalty
sections.body: Long-pressing to demolish a tile is not an admission of failure - several levels are difficult to solve without it, because committing early to a route and then adapting is cheaper than trying to plan the entire path before you know which tiles are coming. If a level tells you that you are stuck, the fix is almost always removing one badly-placed tile rather than restarting.

sections.heading: Free Map is the reward, and it is worth unlocking
sections.body: The mode you unlock by clearing puzzles removes the win condition entirely and gives you the full tile set to build with. There is a camera button that exports whatever you have made as an image file, which in 2015 was an unusually generous feature to spend precious bytes on and remains the reason people still share screenshots of towns built in this game.

spacehuggers.heroParagraph: Space Huggers is a run-and-gun roguelike by Frank Force, who publishes as KilledByAPixel, built for js13kGames 2021 and openly modelled on Broforce, Metal Slug and Contra. It finished eighth out of 223 entries and took second place in both the fun and the gameplay categories. The engine Force wrote to make it fit in 13 kilobytes was later released on its own as LittleJS, which is now a widely used open-source JavaScript game engine.
instructions: Run and jump on the keyboard while aiming independently with the mouse. That separation of aim from movement is the core of the game - you are expected to be firing in one direction while running in another, and players who stop moving to line up a shot tend not to last long. Analog gamepads and touchscreens are supported too, through the engine Force wrote for it.

Levels are procedurally generated, so there is no layout to memorise between runs, and much of the terrain is destructible. Shooting through a wall to make your own route is a legitimate tactic rather than an exploit, and it is often safer than taking the corridor an enemy is already covering.

As a roguelike it expects repeated runs rather than one long attempt. Death sends you back to the start with a fresh layout, and the skill you carry forward is reading generated terrain quickly - spotting which platforms are shootable, where the drop-offs are, and which enemy groupings are worth avoiding entirely.

sections.heading: Destructible terrain changes every fight
sections.body: Because the environment can be shot away, cover is temporary for both sides. An enemy behind a block is protected only until you remove the block, and the platform you are standing on is subject to the same rule. The most common self-inflicted death in the game is destroying the floor beneath your own feet during a firefight, so watch what your stray shots are hitting.

sections.heading: The engine outlived the competition
sections.body: Force built the renderer, physics, particle system and audio from scratch to fit the 13 kilobyte limit, then open-sourced that work as LittleJS. That lineage is why the game feels heavier and more responsive than most jam entries - the particle effects, screen shake and physics were engineered as a reusable engine rather than assembled just far enough to submit before the deadline.

sections.heading: Four-player co-op, a first for the competition
sections.body: Space Huggers supports up to four players in local cooperative play, which Force has noted was a first for js13kGames, alongside keyboard, mouse, touch and analog gamepad input. Co-op changes the game noticeably because every player can destroy the same terrain, so a second player is both extra firepower and an extra source of collapsing floors underneath you.

asciispace.heroParagraph: Adventure in ASCII Space is a space shooter drawn entirely with text characters, written by Nicklas Lof for js13kGames 2021 and placed sixteenth in that year's competition. The premise is as direct as the presentation: you fly through a galaxy rendered in ASCII hunting a hostile entity known only as the evil O. It was the main entry of three that Lof submitted to the 2021 contest.
instructions: Fly with W, A, S and D and shoot with the space bar. The entire playfield is built from text characters, so learning to read the screen is part of the challenge - enemies, projectiles and terrain are all distinguished by glyph and colour rather than by shape, and the display becomes dense quickly once a fight starts.

Press E to open the upgrade panel. This is the progression system and it is easy to miss entirely, since nothing forces you to open it - spending what you have collected on improving your ship between engagements is what makes the later parts of the run survivable.

Gamepad support is built in and was tested against Xbox controllers, so a pad works if you have one connected. Whichever input you use, keep moving: the ship has no shield and no invulnerability window, and the ASCII projectiles travel fast enough that a stationary target is hit almost immediately.

sections.heading: Reading a screen made of letters
sections.body: The visual language takes a minute to learn because everything is the same size - a hazard and a pickup occupy exactly one character cell. Colour is doing most of the work of telling you what matters, so the practical advice is to learn the palette before you learn the glyphs. Once that clicks, the ASCII presentation becomes an advantage: the screen is far less visually noisy than a comparable sprite-based shooter.

sections.heading: The upgrade panel is not optional
sections.body: Because E opens a panel rather than pausing into an obvious menu, plenty of players finish a run without ever using it and conclude the game is harder than it is. Treat opening it as a routine step between fights. Progression is the intended counterweight to the difficulty curve, and skipping it means facing later enemies with a starting ship.

sections.heading: Why text rendering suits a 13KB budget
sections.body: Drawing with characters costs almost nothing - there are no sprites to store or generate, and the font is already on the machine. That freed Lof to spend the byte budget on the systems instead: enemy behaviour, the upgrade tree and the generated galaxy. It is a common strategy among js13kGames entries, and this one is a particularly clean demonstration of what it buys you.

backcountry.heroParagraph: Backcountry is a low-polygon Wild West game built by Michal Budzynski and Stanislaw Malolepszy - the piesku pair - for js13kGames 2019, whose theme that year was Back. You ride out to track down bandits and collect the bounty on them, and the whole thing was written in 31 days between the 13th of August and the 13th of September 2019, finishing at 13,304 bytes. It placed third in the competition's monetization category and was later shown at the MozFest Arcade booth in London.
instructions: The title screen frames every session the same way: earn as much money as you can in today's challenge. That daily framing is the point of the scoring - you are not working through a campaign towards an ending, you are trying to beat a number, and the run resets so you can immediately try a better line through the same territory.

Play is driven with the mouse or by tapping, so it works on a school Chromebook and a phone without any change. Bandits are what pay, so the loop is to find them, deal with them, and bring the bounty home rather than exploring the landscape for its own sake.

The world is rendered as untextured low-poly geometry in a flat red and tan palette. That is a size decision rather than a stylistic accident - with no room for texture files in 13 kilobytes, the terrain is built from coloured polygons, which is why silhouettes and shape read more clearly here than surface detail does.

sections.heading: Built on an engine the authors gave away
sections.body: Backcountry runs on goodluck, the piesku team's own template for tiny browser games, which they publish openly for anyone to clone and build on. That is worth knowing because it explains the game's shape: goodluck supplies a game loop and a rendering pipeline and deliberately not much else, so what you are playing is close to raw WebGL with the fat cut away to fit the byte limit.

sections.heading: The daily challenge is the replay hook
sections.body: Because a session is scored in money earned rather than progress made, the game is designed around short repeated attempts. Knowing where bandits tend to appear is worth more than reflexes, and the second or third run through a given day's challenge is usually worth several times the first, which is the intended curve rather than a sign you played badly the first time.

sections.heading: Hats, web monetization and a third-place finish
sections.body: js13kGames 2019 ran a separate monetization category using the Web Monetization standard, and Backcountry's entry into it let supporters pick different hats for their character - a cosmetic reward rather than a gameplay advantage. It took third in that category. The cosmetic unlocks are inactive here, but nothing about the core bounty hunting depends on them.

black-hole-square.heroParagraph: Black Hole Square is a minimalist puzzle game built by the developer Quinten for js13kGames 2021 on the theme of Space. Its entire instruction set, in the author's own words, is to clean up all the other squares in the universe by tapping them and seeing what happens - there is no tutorial, no text explaining the rules, and working out what each square does when you touch it is the actual game rather than a preamble to it.
instructions: Tap or click a square to activate it. Different squares behave differently and the game never tells you which is which, so early puzzles are effectively a laboratory: touch something, watch what it does to its neighbours, and build up a mental rulebook you can apply when the layouts get harder.

Swipe right to reset the puzzle you are on, or to travel back to puzzles you have already finished. Because experimentation is the intended method, resetting is cheap and expected - there is no penalty for wrecking a board to find out how a piece behaves.

Swipe left to skip a puzzle entirely. That escape hatch matters in a game that refuses to explain itself: if one layout has you stuck, moving on and meeting the same square type in a simpler arrangement often teaches you the rule you were missing, and you can swipe back afterwards.

sections.heading: A game that withholds its own rules
sections.body: Most puzzle games front-load an explanation and then test you on it. Black Hole Square inverts that: the mechanics are the puzzle, and each new square type is a small mystery you solve by experiment. It is a design that only works at this scale, because a long game built this way would exhaust the player - here the whole thing is short enough that curiosity carries you to the end.

sections.heading: Minimal by constraint, not just by taste
sections.body: The stark black field with sparse geometric shards is what a 13 kilobyte budget buys once you have spent the space on puzzle logic. There are no sprites and no texture files anywhere in the bundle, so every shape on screen is drawn mathematically at runtime. The look and the size limit are the same decision seen from two directions.

sections.heading: It installs like an app
sections.body: The game ships a web manifest and a service worker, which is unusual for a jam entry and means your browser can install it to a home screen and run it with no network at all after the first visit. Three additional bonus puzzles were originally gated behind Web Monetization support during the competition; the main sequence has never required it.

chroma-incident.heroParagraph: The Chroma Incident is a twin-stick shooter built by Ryan Malm, who works as Rybar, for js13kGames 2018. The premise is that colour itself has been stolen from the world by a faction called the Achromats and your job is to take it back, which is why the game opens in stark monochrome pixel art. Malm went on to win the competition outright three years later with Space Garden, and the same instinct for making a 13 kilobyte budget look deliberate is already visible here.
instructions: Move with WASD, or with ZQSD if you are on an AZERTY keyboard - the game supports both layouts from the title screen. Aim with the mouse and hold the button to shoot. Movement and aim are fully independent, which is what makes this a twin-stick shooter rather than a run-and-gun.

Gamepads are supported and the title screen tells you how to switch: press any button on a connected controller and the game picks it up. On a pad the two sticks map to movement and aim directly, which is the control scheme the genre was designed around.

Because you can shoot in one direction while retreating in another, the correct habit is to keep circling rather than backing straight away from a threat. Retreating in a straight line keeps you inside the path enemies are already firing along, while orbiting them buys distance without ever taking your crosshair off the target.

sections.heading: Monochrome as a premise, not a limitation
sections.body: Plenty of 13 kilobyte games are visually plain because colour data costs bytes. The Chroma Incident turns that constraint into its story: the Achromats have drained the world, so the starting palette is deliberately bleached and recovering colour is the goal you are working toward. It is a neat piece of design economy, using the jam's hardest restriction as the thing the game is about.

sections.heading: The same author who won js13kGames outright
sections.body: Rybar is Ryan Malm, who took first place in the 2021 competition with Space Garden. Playing the two back to back is a useful lesson in what these constraints reward - both games generate all their visuals in code, both lean on a single strong colour idea, and both are built to be readable instantly on a small screen rather than detailed up close.

sections.heading: Keep moving, always
sections.body: There is no cover system, no dash and no invulnerability window, so survival is entirely a matter of positioning. The most common way players lose a twin-stick shooter is standing still to improve their aim, which trades a small accuracy gain for a very large increase in how easy you are to hit. Fire while strafing and accept a few missed shots.
