evil-glitch.heroParagraph: Evil Glitch won js13kGames 2016. Built by Colombian developer Giovanny Beltran, who publishes as agar3s, it is an arcade shoot-'em-up with a neon WebGL look inspired by 1980s media, and its enemies are drawn from what Beltran describes as crazy sacred geometry. He has said the game came out of an obsession with making sprites that glow like neon, something he only managed once he moved the rendering to WebGL. The final entry compressed to 13,225 bytes.
instructions: The game follows your cursor - move the mouse and your craft goes where you point it, with no separate movement keys to fight against. Hold the mouse button to keep firing. That leaves you one continuous decision to make at any moment, which is where the arcade pressure comes from.

The title screen carries a Controls entry alongside a fullscreen toggle, and it is worth opening before your first run since the game also accepts keyboard input. Fullscreen is more than cosmetic here: the neon effects and the CRT-style distortion read very differently at size than they do in a small embedded frame.

Enemies arrive as geometric shapes that split, rotate and multiply rather than flying fixed attack patterns. Because the whole screen is glitching by design, the reliable way to track danger is to watch the shapes rather than the colours, which are deliberately unstable.

sections.heading: What winning js13kGames 2016 meant
sections.body: The 2016 theme was Glitch, and Evil Glitch took the competition's top prize by committing to it completely - the visual noise, the tearing and the unstable palette are the game rather than an effect layered on top. Beltran was later interviewed by Mozilla about the win. Every entry had to fit in 13 kilobytes with no external image or audio files of any kind.

sections.heading: Neon sprites, and why WebGL was the unlock
sections.body: Beltran has written that he wanted glowing neon sprites for a long time and could not get there until he used WebGL. That matters for a 13 kilobyte budget because shader code is tiny compared with the artwork it replaces - a few lines of GLSL produce a glow that would cost kilobytes as pre-rendered images, which is what makes the look affordable at this size.

sections.heading: An arcade score chase, not a campaign
sections.body: There is no story mode and no ending to reach; the game is built around surviving escalating waves and posting a better number than last time. Beltran later released an expanded arcade version with global scoreboards, which tells you how the original was meant to be played - short repeated runs where each attempt teaches you one more enemy behaviour.

ninja-vs-evilcorp.heroParagraph: Ninja vs EVILCORP is a stealth platformer written by Remi Vansteelandt, who publishes as remvst, for js13kGames 2020. He has named Super Meat Boy and Stealth Bastard Deluxe as the games it is built after, and the goal is exactly as blunt as the title suggests: scale a corporate tower to find the evil plans without ever being spotted. Levels are laid out with an obvious route and a harder alternate one, and a timer runs so the whole thing can be speedrun.
instructions: Move and climb with the arrow keys or WASD, jumping with up, W or space. The Super Meat Boy lineage shows in the handling - the ninja is fast, wall-jumps are central to vertical progress, and levels expect you to chain movement rather than take each jump as a separate considered decision.

Getting spotted is the fail condition, not taking damage. That changes how you approach a room: the question is never whether you can survive crossing it, but whether anything has line of sight while you do. Waiting a beat for a guard to look away is almost always cheaper than trying to outrun detection.

Every level has a straightforward path and at least one more difficult route that saves time, and the on-screen timer exists so you can chase those. The intended arc is to clear a level however you can first, then come back and find the faster line once you know where the sightlines are.

sections.heading: Stealth measured in sightlines, not noise
sections.body: Unlike stealth games that track sound, suspicion meters and alert states, this one reduces the genre to a single readable rule - can something see you right now. That is partly a byte-budget decision and partly what makes it work as a platformer: you can evaluate a room at a glance and commit to a run through it, which keeps the pace much closer to Super Meat Boy than to a conventional stealth game.

sections.heading: Two routes per level, by design
sections.body: Vansteelandt has said the levels were deliberately built with obvious routes alongside more difficult alternates. That structure is what gives a short jam game replay value - the first clear teaches you the room, and the second run is about spotting the wall-jump chain or the gap in patrol timing that the safe route was letting you avoid.

sections.heading: Made for the 404 theme

sections.heading: Two genres that should not fit together

Its setup is that something is stealing time itself - today was yesterday and tomorrow is nowhere to be found - and Detective Clay is on the case. Hovering over certain shapes changes how time flows. That is the central mechanic and it is not limited to slowing things down: you can wind time backwards, including further back than your own character has actually experienced, which is what turns some apparently impossible rooms into solvable ones.

Because time itself is the tool, the solution to a blocked path is often temporal rather than spatial. If there is no route past a hazard, the question to ask is not which way around it goes but what the room looked like at a different moment, and whether you can get the room back to that state.

sections.heading: Rewinding past your own timeline

It is a genuinely unusual mechanic and the source of the game's best puzzles.

sections.heading: How this version differs from the original
sections.body: Neal Agarwal's original Infinite Craft is genuinely open-ended because it asks a language model to invent a result whenever it meets a pair it has not seen, which requires a live server. This build ships a fixed recipe table instead, so its tree is finite and identical every time you play. That trade buys something the original cannot offer: it runs entirely offline, on any locked-down network.

sections.heading: A finite tree is a different game
sections.body: Because the recipe list is fixed at 508 combinations, this version has an actual completion state - there is a definite set of 458 things to find rather than an endless generated space. That makes it closer to a collection puzzle than a sandbox, and the interesting question shifts from what will it invent to what have I not tried yet.

sections.heading: Start broad, then go deep
sections.body: The efficient opening is to combine all four starting elements with each other in every pairing before chasing any single chain, because those six results are the roots almost everything else grows from. Players who immediately follow one promising line tend to stall, while players who widen their base first find the later branches open much faster.

line-rider.heroParagraph: Line Rider was made in September 2006 by Boštjan Čadež, a Slovenian student who published under the name fšk, as part of his university design work. He posted it to DeviantArt and then Newgrounds and it became an internet phenomenon within weeks - there is no score, no goal and no way to win, only a boy called Bosh on a sled and whatever track you choose to draw for him.
instructions: Draw with the mouse. Every line you drag becomes solid ground, and when you press play Bosh sets off from the start and travels along whatever you have built, governed by a simulated physics model that handles momentum and gravity rather than following your line as a fixed path.

Smoothness is everything. A track made of short segments meeting at sharp angles will throw the rider off his sled, so long gentle curves built from overlapping strokes are what carry speed. Most of the skill in Line Rider is learning to draw a curve the physics will accept.

There is no failure state to avoid and nothing to complete, so the game rewards iteration rather than caution. Draw a section, run it, watch where the rider comes off, adjust that one corner and run it again - the entire community that grew around this game works that way.

sections.heading: A toy, not a game
sections.body: Line Rider ships with no objective at all, which is why it was voted best webtoy rather than best game in 2006. That absence turned out to be its strength: without a designer's goal to satisfy, players invented their own, and elaborate hand-drawn courses synchronised to music became a genre of their own on early YouTube.

sections.heading: From student project to McDonald's advert
sections.body: Čadež built it as coursework and it escaped almost immediately, picked up by Yahoo and Time's website and eventually appearing in McDonald's advertising in 2008. offline-paradise.heroParagraph: Offline Paradise is a platformer built by the developer sirxemic for js13kGames 2018, whose theme that year was offline. It is a deliberately simple game in shape - run, jump, reach the end - and the interest is in how tightly it is tuned inside a 13 kilobyte budget that also had room for a level editor the author shipped alongside the source.
instructions: Run with the arrow keys or WASD and jump with up, W or space. Falls are cheap and restarts are immediate, which is the design contract of a precision platformer. You are expected to fail a jump repeatedly while working out its timing, so treat the first several attempts at any new section as measurement rather than as mistakes.

Momentum carries between jumps, so a sequence of gaps usually has to be run as one continuous movement rather than as separate hops with pauses between them. When a stretch feels impossible, the usual cause is stopping to line up each jump instead of committing to the whole run.

sections.heading: The theme was offline, and the game means it

ducktales.heroParagraph: DuckTales was developed and published by Capcom for the NES, arriving in North America in October 1989 and adapting the Disney cartoon that had launched two years earlier. It is remembered for two things: Scrooge McDuck's pogo cane, which turns his walking stick into the movement system the whole game is built around, and Hiroshige Tonomura's soundtrack, whose Moon stage theme became one of the most widely covered pieces of music the console produced.
instructions: Press enter to start, move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and use X for the cane. The pogo is the technique that matters: hold down while airborne and press the cane button to bounce, which lets Scrooge cross spikes and enemies that would otherwise be lethal and gains height with each successful bounce.

There are five stages - the Amazon, Transylvania, African Mines, the Himalayas and the Moon - and you may tackle them in any order from a world map. That structure was unusual for the time and rewards knowing which stage's treasure makes the others easier before you commit.

The cane also serves as a tool on the ground: swing it at loose blocks and chests to clear paths and uncover money. Since your final score is Scrooge's fortune, exploring for hidden treasure is not optional flourish but the actual objective the ending is graded on.

sections.heading: The pogo is the entire movement system
sections.body: Most platformers of the era gave you a jump and an attack as separate ideas. DuckTales fuses them - bouncing on the cane is simultaneously how you kill things, how you cross hazards and how you gain height, which means skilled play looks nothing like walking. Players who never learn the pogo find the game punishing; players who do rarely touch the ground.

sections.heading: Why the Moon theme outlived the game
sections.body: Hiroshige Tonomura worked at Capcom for only two years, from 1988 to 1990, and the music he wrote for the fifth stage has long outlasted that tenure. The Moon theme has been rearranged, covered and remixed continuously for over three decades, and it is routinely cited among the finest compositions ever written for the NES sound hardware.

edge-not-found.heroParagraph: Edge Not Found is a block-pushing puzzle by Tom Hermans, who publishes as Auroriax, built for js13kGames 2020 on the theme 404. He described the project as making an infinitely wrapping Sokoban-type puzzle, and the title is the joke that follows from it - walk off the right side of the board and you reappear on the left, because the edge genuinely is not there.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys or WASD, pushing any block you walk into. The standard Sokoban rules apply otherwise - you can push but never pull, so a block driven into a bad position stays there until you undo.

The board wraps on every axis. A block pushed off the right edge arrives at the left, and the same is true vertically, which means the shortest route to a target is often through a wall you thought was a boundary. Reading the grid as a torus rather than a rectangle is the whole adjustment the game asks you to make.

Undo and restart are both bound and both are essential. In a wrapping puzzle the consequences of a push are much harder to see coming than in a normal one, because a block can travel around and collide with something on the far side of the board, so stepping back a move is routine rather than an admission of defeat.

sections.heading: Wrapping breaks your spatial intuition
sections.body: Sokoban players build a strong instinct that walls are safe boundaries and corners are traps. Remove the edges and both intuitions invert: there are no corners in the usual sense, and a block you push away from you may arrive behind you. The puzzles are constructed specifically around the moments where that inversion matters.

sections.heading: A neat reading of the 404 theme
sections.body: The competition's 2020 theme was 404, the web's not-found error. Rather than building a game about broken links, Hermans applied the idea to geometry - the edge of the board is the thing that cannot be found. It is a much better fit for a puzzle mechanic than the literal reading, and it gives the game its title.

sections.heading: Think in destinations, not directions
sections.body: Because a push can send a block all the way around the board, planning by direction stops working. The productive method is to identify which square each block must end on, then work out which single push lands it there - counting the wrap if necessary - rather than nudging blocks gradually toward a goal.

contra.heroParagraph: Contra is Konami's run-and-gun benchmark, and the title screen on this cartridge carries a 1988 copyright for the North American NES release, a year after the coin-op original reached arcades. You play Bill Rizer or Lance Bean fighting through eight stages of the Galuga archipelago, and the game is famous for two things in roughly equal measure: the Spread gun, and how brutally quickly it kills you without one.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and fire with X, then press Enter to start. Holding a direction while you fire aims the shot, so up-and-right sends bullets diagonally, and pressing down while airborne drops you through a platform. Learning to shoot on a diagonal while jumping is most of the skill ceiling in the first three stages.

Weapon pods float past carrying letters, and the one worth chasing is S for Spread. It fires five bullets in a fan and roughly triples your effective coverage, which matters because you die in one hit and lose the weapon when you do. L is the laser, F is flame, M is a faster machine gun and R reverses nothing useful - most players ignore everything that is not S.

You get three lives and one hit each, so the safest approach is to stay low and keep moving right. The Konami Code - up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, then B and A, entered on the title screen - grants thirty lives, and on this ROM B and A are the X and Z keys. Press V beforehand if you want two-player mode.

sections.heading: Two kinds of stage, two kinds of game
sections.body: Most of Contra scrolls sideways or upward as a conventional platformer, but the Base stages switch to a pseudo-3D corridor viewed head-on, where you advance into the screen dodging electric barriers and shooting a core at the far end. That change of camera is why the game still feels varied thirty-odd years on - it never runs the same stage layout twice, and the corridor sections demand pattern recognition rather than reflexes.

sections.heading: Co-op is the way it was meant to be played
sections.body: Press SELECT before starting and a second soldier joins. Two players share the screen and cannot scroll apart, so the mode is genuinely cooperative in the awkward sense - a partner who rushes ahead drags you into enemies you have not seen. The trade-off is worth it, because two Spread guns clear the waterfall stage and the final alien lair far faster than one, and a partner keeps the run alive when you lose your weapon.

sections.heading: Why one hit kills, and what to do about it
sections.body: Contra gives you no health bar at all, which sounds punishing until you notice how much of the difficulty is memorisation rather than reaction. Enemy spawns are fixed, so each attempt teaches you where the turrets and snipers sit. The practical habits are simple: keep crouched when you can, never stand still on open ground, and treat every weapon pod as more important than any individual enemy on screen.

sections.heading: Playing it on a keyboard in 2026
sections.body: The NES pad had two face buttons and this runs them on Z and X, which puts jump and fire under two fingers of one hand while the other works the arrows. That is a comfortable layout for Contra specifically, because the game asks you to hold a diagonal and fire at the same time far more often than it asks you to jump and shoot together. The emulator also offers save states from its menu, and while purists will object, using one at the start of the waterfall stage is the difference between learning that section and giving up on it. Control bindings can be remapped from the same menu if the defaults do not suit you.

kid-icarus.heroParagraph: Kid Icarus carries the subtitle Angel Land Story on its title screen along with a 1986 Nintendo copyright, and it is the odd sibling to Metroid - built by the same Nintendo R&D1 team, on closely related technology, released within months of it. You play Pit, an angel armed with a bow, climbing out of the underworld to rescue the goddess Palutena from Medusa, and the game is remembered as much for its difficulty as for its charm.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and fire arrows with X, then press Enter to start. Pit shoots straight ahead by default and can aim upward while standing still, which is essential because a great many enemies approach from above in the climbing stages.

The first three stages scroll vertically, and this is where new players lose runs. The screen only moves upward - fall below the bottom edge and you die instantly, no matter how much health you have. Treat every jump as one-way and never drop back down to collect something you missed.

Hearts dropped by enemies are the game's currency, not score. Spend them in the shops hidden behind doors on each stage, where you can buy health restoration, arrow upgrades and useful items. Saving hearts for a shop is almost always better than pushing on underequipped, because the fortress stages punish a weak bow badly.

sections.heading: Three level types, and each plays differently
sections.body: Angel Land is split into vertically scrolling climbs, horizontally scrolling stretches and enclosed fortress mazes that end in a boss. The fortresses are the sharpest change: they are room-to-room labyrinths rather than a straight route, and you need the Pencil item or a good memory to map them. That structural variety is what makes Kid Icarus feel closer to an action adventure than a pure platformer.

sections.heading: The famous eggplant problem
sections.body: The Eggplant Wizard is one of the best-known enemies in the NES library for a reason. Being hit by its projectile turns Pit into a walking eggplant who cannot attack at all, and the only cure is to reach a hospital room inside the fortress. It is a status effect rather than damage, and it is the moment most players discover that Kid Icarus is willing to make life genuinely inconvenient rather than simply hard.

sections.heading: Passwords instead of saves
sections.body: Like most cartridges of the era Kid Icarus has no battery save, and instead gives you a password when you finish a stage. Write it down if you want to continue later, because a browser tab closing takes your progress with it. The password system is also notoriously exploitable - the game encodes your stats loosely enough that hand-edited passwords have been a part of its culture for decades.

sections.heading: How the difficulty actually works
sections.body: Kid Icarus has a reputation for being unfair, but most of what kills new players is a single design decision: enemies respawn continuously while you climb, and the spawn rate does not slow down if you stop to fight. Standing your ground is therefore always the wrong answer in the vertical stages, because the game can generate enemies faster than you can shoot them. Keep climbing and accept the hits you cannot avoid. The game also tracks a hidden score that determines which ending you get and how strong Pit becomes, which rewards thorough play in the fortresses even though nothing on screen tells you so.

battletoads.heroParagraph: Battletoads is Rare's 1991 NES beat 'em up, and it has spent three decades as shorthand for video game difficulty. You play Rash or Zitz, anthropomorphic toads whose limbs turn into oversized boots and horns mid-swing, working through twelve wildly varied stages to rescue Pimple and Princess Angelica from the Dark Queen. The animation was extraordinary for the hardware and the difficulty curve is close to a cliff.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and attack with X, then press Enter to start. The attack button is contextual - a normal punch connects as a punch, but the final hit of a combo turns your fist into something absurd and does far more damage, so finishing combos matters more than mashing.

Grab enemies and throw them. Walking into a stunned enemy and pressing attack picks them up, and thrown bodies damage anything they hit. In the beat 'em up stages this is more efficient than trading blows, because it removes two enemies from the screen with one action and leaves you out of counterattack range.

Level three is the Turbo Tunnel and it is where most runs end. You ride a speeder bike down a corridor of walls that must be dodged by memorised timing, at a speed that steadily increases. There is no trick beyond repetition - the wall pattern is fixed, so treat each attempt as learning the next few seconds of the sequence.

sections.heading: Twelve stages, barely any of them the same genre
sections.body: Battletoads refuses to stay a beat 'em up. Across its run it becomes a vertical rope descent, a speeder-bike race, a surfing level, a snake-riding climb and a sequence where you outrun a giant rotating drill. Each one arrives with its own control conventions and almost no tutorial, which is a large part of why the game is hard: you are constantly a beginner again.

sections.heading: The two-player mode has a famous flaw
sections.body: Two players can fight side by side, and friendly fire is on - you can and will hit your partner, who is stunned by it. Worse, the original cartridge has a well-documented bug that hangs the game in two-player mode on the Wookie Hole stage, which is why serious attempts at finishing Battletoads have historically been solo runs. Play co-op for the early stages and the chaos, not for a completion.

sections.heading: Difficulty as a design decision
sections.body: Rare built Battletoads with limited continues and no password system, in an era when rental shops meant a short game was a commercial risk. The result is a title that is genuinely unfair in places and genuinely brilliant in others, and its reputation has outlived most of its contemporaries. Playing it in a browser with save states available is, frankly, a kinder experience than anyone had in 1991.

sections.heading: What to expect from the first three stages
sections.body: Ragnarok's Canyon opens the game gently as a straightforward brawl with a descent on a rope, and it exists to teach you the combat rhythm. Wookie Hole follows, a vertical abseiling stage where you rappel down a shaft dodging obstacles and gravity does most of the work against you. Then comes the Turbo Tunnel, and the difficulty jumps so sharply that many players in 1991 never saw a fourth stage at all. If you want to see the rest of the game, the honest advice is to use the emulator's save state feature at the tunnel entrance rather than restarting from the beginning every time.

battletoads.plainText: Battletoads is a 1991 NES beat 'em up developed by Rare, in which Rash and Zitz fight through twelve stages to rescue Pimple and Princess Angelica from the Dark Queen. Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z, attack with X and press Enter to start. The final hit of a combo transforms the toad's limb into an oversized weapon and deals much more damage, and grabbing stunned enemies to throw them is more efficient than trading hits. The stages change genre repeatedly, including a rope descent, a surfing level and the notorious Turbo Tunnel speeder bike sequence in level three, where a fixed pattern of walls must be dodged from memory at increasing speed. Two-player co-op has friendly fire, and the original cartridge has a known bug that hangs two-player games at the Wookie Hole stage.

kirbys-dream-land.heroParagraph: Kirby's Dream Land is where Kirby began. The title screen credits HAL Laboratory and Nintendo with a 1992 copyright, and the game was directed by Masahiro Sakurai, who was still in his early twenties and would go on to create Super Smash Bros. It is short, generous and built deliberately as an entry point - and it is the one Kirby game where he cannot copy an enemy's power, because that idea had not been invented yet.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and inhale with X, then press Enter to start. Holding X pulls in nearby enemies and loose blocks; once one is in your mouth, pressing X again fires it out as a projectile that damages whatever it hits. That inhale-and-spit loop is the entire combat system.

You can fly whenever you want. Pressing up or tapping jump repeatedly makes Kirby gulp air and float upward indefinitely, which trivialises most pits and lets you skip large sections of level geometry. The cost is that you must exhale to land or attack, and that puff of air is a weak shot, so flying into a room full of enemies leaves you briefly defenceless.

There are five levels: Green Greens, Castle Lololo, Float Islands, Bubbly Clouds and Mt. Dedede. Look for food items, which restore health, and the Superspicy Curry, Mint Leaf and Mike power-ups hidden in each stage - they are temporary rather than permanent, so use them on the sections you find hardest rather than saving them.

sections.heading: No copy abilities - and that is the point
sections.body: Every later Kirby game is built on swallowing an enemy and stealing its power. That mechanic debuted in Kirby's Adventure on the NES a year later, not here. In Dream Land, an inhaled enemy is only ever ammunition. The result is a purer, simpler platformer, and playing it now is a useful reminder that a series' defining idea often arrives in the sequel rather than the original.

sections.heading: Designed to be finished
sections.body: Sakurai has been open about building Dream Land for players who were not already good at games, and the design shows it: unlimited flight removes most platforming failure, health is plentiful and the whole game runs about half an hour. A hidden Extra Game unlocked after finishing it raises enemy speed and damage substantially for anyone who wants the harder version, which is a neater solution than a difficulty menu.

sections.heading: A monochrome game worth seeing in monochrome
sections.body: This runs as the original Game Boy release rather than a Game Boy Color or Super Game Boy version, so the art is the four-shade greyscale that HAL actually drew for. Kirby's famous pink came later - on the original packaging outside Japan he was rendered white, reportedly because nobody outside the development team knew what colour a shape defined only in grey was supposed to be.

sections.heading: The bosses, and a famous final stage
sections.body: Each of the five levels ends with a boss, and they are the parts of Dream Land that actually require the inhale mechanic rather than flight. Whispy Woods drops apples you swallow and fire back; Lololo and Lalala push blocks at you along tracks; Kracko is a cloud with an eye. Mt. Dedede finishes with a rematch against every previous boss in sequence before King Dedede himself, which is a structure Kirby games have reused ever since. Dedede fights by inhaling you and spitting you into walls, turning your own signature move against you.

bounce-back.heroParagraph: Bounce Back is a boomerang roguelite built by Frank Force for js13kGames 2019, whose theme was Back - answered here with a weapon that comes back to you. The whole game, engine, art and procedurally generated music included, fits inside 13 kilobytes. It has ten procedurally generated levels, three enemy types, a shop, a final boss and a persistent save, which is a remarkable amount of game for the size.
instructions: Move with WASD, aim with the mouse and click to throw your boomerang. The throw is the only attack you have and the boomerang has to return before you can throw again, so every shot commits you to a second or two of being unarmed. Missing is punished less by the damage you did not do than by the window you spent waiting.

Press space to dash, and note what the game's own hints say: you take no damage while dashing. That makes the dash a defensive tool first and a movement tool second - dashing through an enemy charge is safer than trying to outrun it, and it is the correct answer to almost every situation where you are cornered.

You keep your gems when you die. That is the central concession that makes the roguelite loop work: a failed run still funds the shop, so buying items early is never wasted. A lost boomerang shows up as a large marker on the minimap, sand slows both you and your enemies, and beating the game unlocks a separate speed run mode that leaves your normal save alone.

sections.heading: Two boomerangs worth buying
sections.body: The shop sells coloured boomerangs with distinct behaviours, and two are worth singling out. The yellow one collects pickups on its flight path, which turns every throw into a way to gather gems and health without walking into open ground. The blue one does double damage. Which you want depends on whether your runs are ending because you cannot kill things fast enough or because you keep getting hit while looting.

sections.heading: Ten levels, generated but bounded
sections.body: There are exactly ten levels and then a boss, so this is a roguelite with a defined ending rather than an endless climb. Layouts are procedurally generated, and giant and invisible variants of the standard enemies appear as you go deeper. Knowing the run has a finish line changes how you spend gems - there is no point hoarding for a run that does not exist, so spend aggressively as you approach the later levels.

sections.heading: An engine written to be shrunk
sections.body: Force separated the game code from a reusable 2D engine with a physics system, tile collision, particles, pseudo-3D shadows and cached level rendering, then stripped the debug layer and compressed the result down under the limit. The sixteen sound effects are synthesised at runtime with zzfx and the music is generated rather than stored, which is the standard answer to fitting audio into a budget this small.

sections.heading: Reading the minimap
sections.body: A minimap sits on screen throughout, and it does more than show walls. A boomerang you have thrown and lost track of appears on it as an oversized marker, which matters because you cannot throw again until it returns and a boomerang stuck behind geometry effectively disarms you. Health warnings escalate visibly as you drop low rather than being buried in a number. Between those two readouts the game tells you the only two things that decide a run - where your weapon is and how close you are to dying - without spending bytes on a conventional interface.

chrome-easter-egg-t-rex-runner.heroParagraph: This is the dinosaur that appears in Google Chrome when your connection drops, lifted directly out of the Chromium source tree - specifically the offline error page's own game code, taken at commit 24d8c44. It was added to Chrome in 2014 as a joke about being offline, and became one of the most played games in the world by accident, entirely because of where it lives.
instructions: Press the space bar to start running and to jump. Hold it slightly longer for a higher jump - the height scales with how long the key is held, which matters once cacti start appearing in clusters of three that need a full-height leap to clear.

Press the down arrow to duck. Pterodactyls appear later in a run and fly at three different heights: the low ones must be jumped, the high ones can be run straight under, and the middle ones require a duck. Reading their height quickly is the main thing separating a score of 500 from a score of 2000.

You can also press down while in the air to drop faster. This is the technique that most people never discover, and it matters at high speed - a fast landing after a jump gets you back in control before the next obstacle, where a floaty arc would carry you into it.

sections.heading: It speeds up forever, and night falls
sections.body: The run has no levels and no end. Speed increases continuously with distance, and at intervals the palette inverts into a night mode with white obstacles on black. The switch is purely cosmetic but it is disorienting the first few times, and it arrives around the same distance that pterodactyls start appearing, which is why so many runs die shortly after it.

sections.heading: Where the dinosaur came from
sections.body: The offline page's dinosaur was drawn by Sebastien Gabriel, a Chrome designer, and the team has described it as a deliberate nod to prehistory - a joke about connections going extinct. The pixel style was chosen partly because the error page had to stay tiny and could not depend on loading external assets, which is the same constraint that makes it work well on a blocked school network.

sections.heading: You do not actually need to be offline
sections.body: In Chrome you can reach the same game any time by typing chrome://dino into the address bar, which opens it in a full window rather than squeezed onto an error page. That version and this one are the same code. Running it here simply means you do not have to leave the page you are on, and it works in browsers other than Chrome.

sections.heading: Scoring, and what a good run looks like
sections.body: Score is simply distance, ticking up continuously, with a high score stored in the browser and shown as HI at the top right. There are no points for near misses and no bonus for style. A first attempt usually ends somewhere under 500, a comfortable player sits around 1000 to 2000, and past that the speed is high enough that cactus clusters and pterodactyls arrive together and reaction time stops being sufficient on its own. Beyond roughly 1500 the game stops adding new obstacle types and only increases speed, so the ceiling on a run is your reflexes rather than anything the game introduces.

wordle.heroParagraph: This is Wordle+, an open-source recreation of Josh Wardle's word game written in Svelte and TypeScript by the developer MikhaD, and the game says so itself on its own how-to-play screen. It is not the New York Times version and does not share its answers. What it adds is the thing the original deliberately withholds: you can play more than once a day.
instructions: Guess a five-letter word and press Enter. Each tile then changes colour - green means the letter is correct and in the right position, yellow means the letter is in the word but somewhere else, and grey means it is not in the word at all. You have six guesses.

Open the settings menu with the gear icon to pick your mode. Daily gives everyone the same word once per day, Hourly rotates a new word every hour, and Infinite lets you play back-to-back with no waiting - which is the mode most people actually want when they have twenty minutes rather than one puzzle's worth of attention.

Hard Mode, also in settings, forces you to reuse every hint you have found: any green letter must stay in place and any yellow letter must appear somewhere in your next guess. It removes the common tactic of burning a guess on five fresh letters to gather information, and it is the setting to turn on once ordinary Wordle stops being difficult.

sections.heading: Two word lists, and why that matters
sections.body: The game carries two separate dictionaries: roughly 2,300 possible answers and about 10,650 words it will accept as valid guesses. That split is inherited from the original design and it is genuinely useful - it means obscure words like AALII are legal to guess for their letters even though they will never be the answer, so you can probe with unusual letter combinations without wasting a turn on something the game rejects outright.

sections.heading: Opening words are about letter coverage
sections.body: A good opener is not a likely answer, it is a wide net. Words such as CRANE, SLATE and AUDIO score well because they cover common consonants and vowels without repeating a letter, and a repeated letter effectively wastes one of your five slots on information you already have. The strongest practical habit is to spend guesses one and two on ten distinct common letters, then solve with the remaining four.

sections.heading: Streaks, stats and settings that stay put
sections.body: The game tracks your current and maximum streak alongside a distribution of how many guesses your wins took, kept separately for each mode. A high-contrast colourblind palette swaps the green and yellow for colours that stay distinguishable, and a dark theme is on by default. All of it is stored in your browser, so it persists between visits on the same machine but does not follow you to another one.

sections.heading: Yellow tiles carry more information than they look like they do
sections.body: A yellow tile tells you two facts, not one: the letter is in the word, and it is not in that position. Players routinely use the first half and forget the second, then waste a guess putting the same letter back in a square already ruled out. Duplicate letters are the other common trap - if you guess a word with two Es and the answer has one, the game marks one E and greys the other, which reads as contradictory until you know the rule. Treating grey as 'not here again' rather than 'not in the word' when the letter appears twice will save a guess more often than any clever opening word.

asteroids.heroParagraph: This is Doug McInnes's HTML5 recreation of Asteroids, written in 2010 and released under an MIT licence. It reproduces the 1979 Atari coin-op that defined vector arcade gaming: white outlines on a blank field, a ship that drifts forever because nothing in space slows it down, and rocks that split into smaller and faster rocks every time you shoot one.
instructions: Press space to start, rotate with the left and right arrows, thrust with up and fire with space. The single most important thing to understand is that thrust adds momentum rather than setting a direction - let go and you keep travelling exactly as you were. Stopping requires turning around and thrusting against your own drift.

Shooting a large asteroid does not remove it, it breaks it into two medium ones, which break into two small ones each. A screen you have half-cleared is usually more dangerous than the one you started with, because the fragments move faster. Clear one rock completely before starting on the next rather than spraying shots across the field.

The screen wraps on all four edges, and so do you, your bullets and every asteroid. That is a tool, not just a quirk - flying off one edge to escape a crowded corner puts you somewhere empty, and a shot fired into open space can come back around and hit something behind you.

sections.heading: The flying saucers are the real threat
sections.body: About half a minute into a game, a saucer appears and starts shooting back. The large one fires roughly in your direction; the small one aims properly and is worth considerably more points, 200 against the 120-and-up that asteroids pay depending on their size. Saucers keep arriving at intervals for the rest of the run, so a field cleared of rocks is not a field that is safe.

sections.heading: No hyperspace in this version
sections.body: The 1979 cabinet had a hyperspace button that teleported you to a random location, sometimes fatally. This port does not implement it, which is worth knowing because the standard advice for the original arcade game - panic, hit hyperspace, hope - simply is not available here. Your only escape from a bad position is the screen-wrap and good thrust management.

sections.heading: Why it still looks like this
sections.body: Asteroids ran on a vector monitor that drew lines directly with an electron beam rather than filling a grid of pixels, which is why the shapes are crisp outlines and there is no shading anywhere. McInnes's version renders that same look on an HTML5 canvas, right down to the Vector Battle typeface used for the score. You get three ships per game and the sound effects are the original arcade samples.

sections.heading: Staying alive past the third wave
sections.body: Each cleared field is replaced by a denser one, and the practical limit for most players arrives around the third or fourth wave when there is no longer an empty quadrant to retreat to. Two habits extend a run substantially. The first is to keep your speed low and make small corrective thrusts rather than long burns, because a fast ship cannot react to a fragment appearing in front of it. The second is to shoot rocks that are heading away from you rather than the ones bearing down, since splitting an incoming asteroid creates two fast fragments already pointed at your hull.

shift.heroParagraph: Shift is a puzzle platformer published by Armor Games in 2008, and its menu screen still carries that copyright. It is drawn entirely in black and white, and its single idea is in the title: press the Shift key and the world turns over. What was solid floor becomes empty air, what was empty air becomes floor, and your character walks on the other side of the same line.
instructions: Use the arrow keys to run left and right, press space to jump, and stand in front of a door to move on to the next level. Press P at any point to open the menu. The game states all of this in the level geometry itself rather than in a manual - the first few stages have the instructions painted into the scenery.

Press Shift to flip. The entire level rotates 180 degrees and the colours invert, so you end up standing on what was previously the ceiling. This is not a cosmetic effect and it is not a colour filter: it is the actual solution to nearly every obstacle in the game. A gap you cannot jump becomes a platform once you are on the other side of it.

Flipping only works where there is room for you on the other side. If the black space above you is too thin to hold your body, the shift will not happen, so position matters as much as timing. The habit to build is to look at the negative space in a room before you look at the floor - the shape you are not standing on is the level you are about to be in.

sections.heading: Figure and ground as a game mechanic
sections.body: Shift borrows directly from optical illusions where a silhouette can be read two ways depending on which region you treat as the subject. The game makes that readable-both-ways property literal and playable, and it is why the art has to be pure black and white with no shading - any gradient or texture would tell you which half is meant to be solid and spoil the ambiguity the puzzles depend on.

sections.heading: Keys, locks and spikes
sections.body: Beyond the flip, the levels introduce a small set of complications. Spikes kill on contact and are usually placed so the obvious route runs straight into them. Keys must be collected to rotate the locks that block certain doors, which forces detours rather than a straight run to the exit. The combination is enough to keep the single mechanic productive across the full run of levels.

sections.heading: Flash, preserved
sections.body: Shift was built in Flash, which browsers stopped supporting at the end of 2020. It runs here through Ruffle, an open-source reimplementation of the Flash player written in Rust, loaded from this site rather than from an external CDN - so it works on networks that block outside domains. Antony Lavelle's series went on to several sequels and a DSiWare release.

sections.heading: Thinking in silhouettes
sections.body: The mental adjustment Shift asks for is genuinely unusual, and most players hit a wall somewhere in the middle levels where the answer stops being visible. The reliable method is to stop reading the screen as a platformer level and start reading it as two overlapping levels that share an outline. Before you move, look at where you would be standing after a flip and whether a route exists there. Puzzles that appear to have no solution almost always have one that begins with flipping first and moving second, which is the opposite of the instinct the genre trains.

bubble-shooter.heroParagraph: Bubble Shooter is the Absolutist original - the game that took the mechanic from Taito's arcade title Puzzle Bobble, put it in a browser window, and became the template that thousands of imitators copied. A grid of coloured bubbles fills the top of the board, you fire from the bottom, and matching three or more of a colour drops them out of the ceiling.
instructions: Move the mouse to aim the launcher and click to fire. The next bubble waiting in the launcher is always visible, so you can plan two shots ahead rather than one - and planning two ahead is most of what separates a cleared board from a stuck one.

Three bubbles of the same colour touching is enough to pop them. The important detail is what happens next: any bubbles left hanging with no path back to the ceiling fall as well, and they score more than the ones you popped directly. Bringing down a large hanging cluster with one well-placed shot is how the big scores are made.

Bank shots off the side walls. Bubbles bounce off the left and right edges at a mirrored angle, which is the only way to reach a target tucked under an overhang. This is the technique most casual players never use, and it is what makes otherwise impossible pockets reachable late in a board.

sections.heading: Aim for the ceiling anchors, not the nearest match
sections.body: Because unattached bubbles fall, the efficient strategy is structural rather than greedy. Look for the small groups holding a large section to the roof and break those, instead of popping whichever match is easiest to reach. Clearing three bubbles that were supporting twenty is a far better shot than clearing five that were supporting nothing.

sections.heading: Difficulty levels and a score table
sections.body: The game opens on Novice and includes a Setup screen for changing difficulty, along with a Top 10 table and a Help page. Higher difficulties add colours to the mix, which matters more than it sounds: every additional colour reduces the chance that the bubble you have been handed is useful anywhere near where you want to shoot, and forces more defensive parking of unwanted bubbles.

sections.heading: Where the genre came from
sections.body: The bubble-matching mechanic originates with Taito's Puzzle Bobble in 1994, an arcade spin-off of Bubble Bobble. Absolutist's browser version, first published in the early 2000s, is what carried it to the web and made it a fixture of free game portals for two decades. It runs here through Ruffle, since Flash itself was discontinued at the end of 2020.

sections.heading: Parking a bubble you cannot use
sections.body: Sooner or later the launcher hands you a colour with no useful target anywhere on the board, and what you do with it decides how the rest of the game goes. Firing it straight up into the middle of the cluster is the worst option, because it adds a bubble to the structure you are trying to dismantle and often blocks a pocket you needed. Park it instead at the far edge of a row, where it stays out of the way and may become the third of a match later. Good players are effectively building a small reserve of spare colours along the walls throughout a board.

mega-man-2.heroParagraph: Mega Man 2 is the game that turned a modest Capcom series into an institution, and it is widely held to be the best of the NES run. You pick any of eight Robot Masters, beat them in whatever order you like, and take their weapon when they fall - and each weapon is the answer to some other boss, so the game is a puzzle about ordering as much as it is a platformer. This cartridge also carries the Normal and Difficult modes added for the Western release.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and shoot with X. Press Enter to open the weapon menu at any time, which pauses the action and lets you switch to whatever you have collected. Getting comfortable with pausing mid-fight to swap weapons is essential, because the right weapon often kills a boss in a handful of hits.

Start with Metal Man. His Metal Blade is thrown in eight directions, costs almost nothing per shot and shreds a large fraction of the rest of the roster - it is frequently described as the most overpowered weapon in the series. From there the widely used route runs Metal, Air, Crash, Flash, Quick, Wood, Heat, Bubble.

Watch your footing more than your health bar. Mega Man 2 kills far more players with spikes and bottomless pits than with damage, and spikes are instant death regardless of how much energy you have. Items 1, 2 and 3, taken from Heat Man, Air Man and Flash Man, are platforms you deploy yourself and they exist precisely to cross what looks impassable.

sections.heading: Choosing your own order was still a new idea
sections.body: The stage select screen is so familiar now that it is easy to miss how unusual it was. Rather than a fixed sequence, you are handed eight self-contained levels and left to work out the dependency graph yourself. Beating a boss with only the starting Mega Buster is always possible but rarely pleasant, so the game quietly teaches you to experiment, fail, and come back with the right tool.

sections.heading: Normal and Difficult, and why they exist
sections.body: The title screen here offers a choice the Japanese original did not have. Capcom judged the game too hard for the North American market and added a Normal mode that roughly doubles your damage output, keeping the Japanese balance as Difficult. If you are new to the series, Normal is the honest recommendation - it is still a demanding game, and the level design is the point rather than the damage numbers.

sections.heading: A password system with no save battery
sections.body: Finishing a Robot Master gives you a password on a grid of red dots, which restores your progress and your weapons but not your extra lives or energy tanks. Write it down before you close the tab. The grid encoding is simple enough that players worked out how to construct passwords by hand, including the well-known code that grants every weapon and four energy tanks at once.

sections.heading: The soundtrack people still cover
sections.body: Takashi Tateishi's score is the reason a lot of people remember this game at all, and the Dr. Wily Stage 1 theme in particular has been covered, remixed and performed live for over thirty years. It is a genuinely remarkable piece of work given the NES sound hardware offers two pulse channels, a triangle wave and a noise channel, with no sampling to fall back on.

metroid-ii.heroParagraph: Metroid II: Return of Samus took a series built on wide-open exploration and squeezed it onto a monochrome handheld, which forced a genuinely different design. Samus lands on SR388 with one job - exterminate the Metroid species at its source - and a counter on the bottom of the screen tells you exactly how many are left. It starts at 39, and it is the closest thing the game has to a map.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and shoot with X. Press V to toggle between your beam and missiles, and Enter to check your equipment. Holding a direction before jumping gives you the spin jump, which is what you need for distance and for the screw attack later on.

The Metroid counter is your objective marker. The planet is gated by lava that recedes only when you have killed every Metroid in the current area, so if you cannot find a way forward, the answer is always that one more Metroid is hiding somewhere behind you. Sweep the area again rather than hunting for a secret passage.

Save at the Chozo statue save points and refill at the recharge stations, and do it often. The Game Boy screen shows very little of the world at once, so getting lost is normal and backtracking is expensive - a save before exploring somewhere unfamiliar costs you seconds and can spare you twenty minutes.

sections.heading: The counter replaces the map
sections.body: The original Metroid gave you a sprawling interconnected world; this one gives you a vertical descent through a series of gated regions and a number that ticks down. That is partly a hardware concession - there is no map screen and the viewport is tiny - but it turns the game into something more focused and more oppressive. You are not exploring so much as clearing, floor by floor.

sections.heading: Metroids that grow up
sections.body: The species evolves in front of you. Larvae become Alpha, then Gamma, Zeta and finally Omega Metroids, each larger, tougher and more aggressive than the last, and each requiring more missiles and better positioning. Watching the enemy roster escalate as the counter falls is the clearest sense of progress the game offers, and it lands harder than a percentage complete ever would.

sections.heading: The upgrades that changed the series
sections.body: Metroid II introduced the Spider Ball, which lets morph-ball Samus cling to and roll along walls and ceilings, the Space Jump for repeated mid-air jumps, and the Plasma Beam. It also debuted the Varia Suit's visible sprite change. Several of these became permanent series fixtures, so this handheld entry has more influence on later Metroid design than its reputation suggests.

The sprites are large relative to the screen, which was a deliberate choice for a display measuring a couple of inches and reads differently on a monitor - Samus is imposing here in a way she is not in the NES original. The emulator's save states are worth using alongside the in-game save points, since a browser tab closing will not preserve battery saves reliably.

sections.heading: How it fits between Metroid and Super Metroid
sections.body: Chronologically this sits between the NES original and Super Metroid, and it carries the plot point the whole series turns on - the larva that hatches at the end and imprints on Samus becomes the emotional core of the next game. Playing it makes Super Metroid's opening land properly, which is a good reason to spend time with it even though the handheld hardware makes it the roughest of the three to go back to.

mike-tysons-punch-out.heroParagraph: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!! is a boxing game in the same way that a rhythm game is about music. You play Little Mac, a small fighter working up through a roster of enormous cartoon opponents with his trainer Doc Louis in his corner, and you win not by out-boxing anyone but by learning the precise tell that precedes each attack and answering it on the exact frame.
instructions: Dodge left or right with the arrow keys, block or duck with down, and punch with Z and X. Holding up while you punch aims at the head instead of the body. Head shots do more damage but leave you exposed for longer, so the standard rhythm is to dodge, land one or two body blows, and reset.

Every opponent telegraphs. Glass Joe drops his guard, King Hippo opens his mouth before he swings and his trunks fall down when you hit him there, Bald Bull charges the length of the ring. None of it is random - each fighter runs a fixed script, and a fight you cannot win is simply one whose tells you have not learned yet.

Landing a counter at the right moment earns a star, shown under your health. Press Enter while holding stars to throw a knockout uppercut, which does enormous damage. Stars are lost if you get hit, so the tension in every round is whether to spend them now or risk holding them for a cleaner opening.

sections.heading: The licence expired, and the game was renamed
sections.body: Nintendo's contract with Mike Tyson ran out in 1990, and the game was reissued as Punch-Out!! with the final opponent replaced by a fighter called Mr. Dream. This is the original version with Tyson in it, and his fight is famous for a reason - in the first ninety seconds he can knock you out in a single punch, which makes the opening of that bout a pure test of dodging with no offence at all.

sections.heading: Learning a fight is the whole game
sections.body: There is no difficulty setting and no way to grind. Progress comes entirely from pattern recognition, and the correct way to treat a loss is as information rather than failure. Most players find the difficulty curve spikes hard at Bald Bull's second fight and again at Soda Popinski. Both become almost mechanical once the tell clicks, which is exactly the design working as intended.

sections.heading: Doc Louis is telling you something
sections.body: The advice your trainer gives between rounds is not flavour text. His hints point at each opponent's actual weakness, and the game expects you to read them - it is one of the earliest examples of a title using a character to deliver a mechanical tutorial rather than a manual. Pay attention to the corner sequences instead of pressing through them.

sections.heading: Why the sprites are so big
sections.body: Little Mac is drawn small and semi-transparent so the game can render enormous, heavily animated opponents without the NES running out of sprite budget on a single scanline. It is a technical constraint that turned into the series' visual identity, and it also serves the fiction - you are meant to feel outmatched by everyone you face.

sections.heading: Where new players should expect to stall
sections.body: Glass Joe and Von Kaiser exist to teach the rhythm and go down quickly. Piston Honda is the first opponent who punishes sloppiness, King Hippo is a puzzle rather than a fight, and Bald Bull's charge is the first attack that demands frame-accurate timing. If you are stuck, the answer is almost never to punch more - it is to spend a full round doing nothing but dodging until the pattern becomes obvious.

ninja-gaiden.heroParagraph: Ninja Gaiden opens with a swordfight silhouetted against a full moon, and that cutscene is why the game matters historically - Tecmo built a cinematic storytelling style into a 1989 NES action game at a time when almost nothing else on the console bothered. What follows is Ryu Hayabusa moving through six acts at high speed, and a difficulty that has kept the game in arguments for three decades.
instructions: Run with the arrow keys, jump with Z and swing the Dragon Sword with X. The wall cling is the mechanic everything else is built on: jump into a wall and Ryu grabs it, then press jump again to leap off. Climbing a shaft means alternating walls, and a great deal of the level design assumes you are comfortable doing it at speed.

Collect the red and blue scrolls for sub-weapons and spirit power. Hold up and press attack to use whatever art you have equipped - the Windmill Throwing Star is the one to keep, since it returns to you like a boomerang and costs relatively little. Press Enter to cycle between what you are carrying.

Learn where enemies respawn. Ninja Gaiden regenerates an enemy the moment its spawn point scrolls back on screen, which means backing up to line up a jump can create the bird or jumping ninja that knocks you into a pit. Moving forward decisively is safer than being cautious, which is the opposite of most platformer instincts.

sections.heading: Cutscenes were the selling point
sections.body: Tecmo called them cinema displays, and they bookend each of the six acts with camera angles, framing and dialogue that look like storyboards. In 1989 that was close to unprecedented on the NES, and it is the direct ancestor of a lot of what console action games did in the following decade. The opening duel under the moon is still the image most people picture when the game is mentioned.

sections.heading: Act 6, and the reason people rage about this game
sections.body: The final act is where Ninja Gaiden's reputation comes from. Dying at any point during the three-part final boss sequence sends you back to the start of 6-1, not to a checkpoint, so a failed attempt costs you the entire act. Combined with aggressive knockback and pits, it produces the specific kind of difficulty that people remember decades later - not hard moments, but expensive ones.

sections.heading: Knockback is the real enemy
sections.body: Taking a hit while airborne sends Ryu backwards, and most deaths in this game are bottomless pits reached that way rather than health running out. The practical consequence is that positioning matters more than damage: jumping over a gap with an enemy on screen is a gamble, and clearing threats before you commit to a jump is nearly always worth the extra seconds.

sections.heading: Speed as the core appeal
sections.body: Beneath the difficulty, Ninja Gaiden is exhilarating because Ryu moves fast and responds instantly. There is no acceleration curve to fight, the sword swings the frame you press the button, and the wall jump lets a confident player cross a level in a continuous flow. Getting good at it feels less like memorising and more like learning to move, which is why it still holds up.

sections.heading: What the sub-weapons actually cost
sections.body: Spirit power is a shared pool, so every ninja art you throw is power you do not have for the boss at the end of the act. The Windmill Throwing Star is efficient because it returns; the Fire Wheel and Jump-and-Slash are expensive and situational. Arriving at a boss with a full bar and the star equipped turns several of the harder fights into short ones, so treating spirit power as a boss resource rather than a crowd-clearing tool is the better habit.

super-tennis.heroParagraph: Super Tennis is one of the SNES launch-window sports games that people still go back to, and its title screen credits Tokyo Shoseki alongside Nintendo with a 1991 copyright - a developer better known for schoolbooks than for one of the most respected tennis games ever made. It is simple to pick up and surprisingly deep once you notice how much the ball physics change between surfaces.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys and press Enter to serve. The four face buttons map to Z, X, A and S, and each produces a different shot - flat, topspin, lob and slice. Which one you press matters far more than where you are standing, because the ball's bounce and speed change completely with the spin you put on it.

Position before the ball arrives. The game gives you time to reach a shot only if you start moving as your opponent swings, not when the ball crosses the net. Watching their body rather than the ball is the single habit that separates players who rally comfortably from players who are always stretching.

Use the lob against anyone who rushes the net, and the slice to keep the ball low on grass. The computer opponents at higher difficulty close on the net aggressively, and a well-timed lob over their head is often a clean winner where a drive would simply be volleyed back past you.

sections.heading: Four surfaces that genuinely play differently
sections.body: Hard court, clay, grass and carpet are not cosmetic. Clay slows the ball and sits it up, rewarding patient baseline rallies; grass keeps it low and fast, which favours serve-and-volley; carpet is faster still. Choosing a surface that suits your style, or one that does not suit your opponent's, is a real strategic decision and it is why the game has aged as well as it has.

sections.heading: Singles, doubles and four players
sections.body: There are twenty selectable players with distinct attributes, and the game supports doubles - meaning with enough controllers it becomes a four-player game, which was a genuine rarity in 1991. Playing doubles changes the game substantially, because court coverage becomes about positioning relative to your partner rather than simply chasing the ball.

sections.heading: Tournament mode is the long game
sections.body: Beyond exhibition matches there is a full circuit to work through, with rankings and progressively better opposition. It is the mode the game is built around, and the difficulty ramp is well judged - early rounds let you settle into the shot system, and by the later stages you need to be varying spin deliberately rather than hitting everything flat.

sections.heading: Playing an SNES game on a keyboard
sections.body: The four face buttons land on Z, X, A and S here, with the shoulder buttons on Q and E and START on Enter. That puts all four shot types within reach of one hand while the other works the arrows, which suits tennis better than it suits most SNES genres. Every binding can be changed from the emulator's control settings if the defaults feel awkward.

sections.heading: Serving well is worth practising
sections.body: The serve has its own timing - a power meter you stop, and a direction you set before the toss - and it is the one shot in the game you control completely, with no opponent influencing it. A fast serve to the corner regularly wins the point outright against the AI and puts a human on the back foot immediately. Most players neglect it entirely and rally from a neutral position they did not need to accept.

super-bomberman.heroParagraph: Super Bomberman brought Hudson Soft's maze series to the SNES in 1993, and its title screen offers the three options that define it: Normal Game, Battle Mode and Password. The single-player campaign is perfectly good. Battle Mode is the reason the game is remembered - it is one of the purest multiplayer designs on the console, and it has ruined a great many friendships since.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys and drop a bomb with Z. Bombs explode in a cross shape after a few seconds, destroying soft blocks and anything standing in the blast - including you. The entire game is the tension between placing a bomb where it will do damage and being certain you have an escape route before you place it.

Blow up soft blocks to reveal power-ups. Fire extends your blast radius, extra bombs let you place more at once, and Speed makes you faster - though enough Speed pickups will make you genuinely hard to control, which is a real way to lose. The Remote Control lets you detonate on your own timing with X, and it is the strongest item in the game.

Think in lines, not squares. A bomb's blast travels along the row and column it sits in, so safety means standing behind a hard block or around a corner, never simply far away. The most common death in Bomberman is walking into a corridor that a bomb you had forgotten about is pointing straight down.

sections.heading: Battle Mode is the real game
sections.body: Up to four players fight in a single screen arena until one is left, and with the SNES Multitap that was a genuine four-player party game in 1993. Matches last under a minute, the skill curve is shallow enough that anyone can join and deep enough that good players dominate, and the losing players become spectators who can still lob bombs in from the edge in some rulesets.

sections.heading: Trapping, not chasing
sections.body: New players chase opponents around the maze. Experienced ones close off escape routes. Because the arena is a grid and blasts run in straight lines, the winning move is almost always to place a bomb that cuts off the corridor your opponent would retreat into, then place a second that covers where they actually are. Chasing tends to walk you into your own blast radius.

sections.heading: The single-player campaign
sections.body: Normal Game runs through themed worlds of rooms, each requiring you to destroy every enemy before a door opens, with a boss at the end of each set. It supports two-player co-op, which changes it considerably - friendly fire is on, so a careless partner is at least as dangerous as the enemies. Progress is kept with passwords from the title screen rather than a save battery.

sections.heading: Why the formula never needed changing
sections.body: Bomberman has barely altered since the 1980s because the core is close to perfect: one action, a hard timer on it, and a grid that makes every consequence legible at a glance. Nothing in a match is hidden from you, so every death is unambiguously your own error - which is exactly the quality that makes a multiplayer game worth replaying immediately.

sections.heading: The power-ups that can lose you a match
sections.body: Not every pickup helps. Too much Speed makes you overshoot the grid squares you meant to stop on, which in a game where safety is measured in single tiles is a reliable way to walk into your own blast. Some rulesets include genuinely bad items that force you to drop bombs constantly or reverse your controls. Grabbing everything on sight is a beginner habit; experienced players leave certain items on the floor deliberately.

factory-balls.heroParagraph: Factory Balls is a Bart Bonte game, made as an entry for the fourth JayIsGames game design competition on the theme of ball physics - and its own title screen says exactly that. The premise is deceptively plain: a box shows you the ball you are supposed to produce, a bin supplies blank white balls, and an arc of tools sits between them. Working out what order to use the tools in is the entire game.
instructions: Drag a ball out of the bin and drop it onto a tool to apply that tool. Paint pots colour the whole ball, and belts, caps and holders cover parts of it so the next coat of paint only reaches what is left exposed. Drop a ball back into the bin at any time to throw it away and start the level over - there is no penalty for doing so.

Read the box before you touch anything. The delivery box shows the target pattern, and the solution is always a sequence of masking and painting that produces exactly it. Working backwards from the finished design is far more reliable than experimenting forwards, because the last operation is usually the easiest one to identify.

Remember that covers must come off as well as go on. A belt that masked a stripe has to be removed before the ball can be delivered, and removing it after a second coat is often the step that produces the pattern you want. If a level looks impossible, the missing move is usually a removal rather than an addition.

sections.heading: A puzzle about order of operations
sections.body: Every level uses a small set of tools and the challenge is purely the sequence. Paint, then mask, then paint again gives a different result to masking first, and there is generally exactly one ordering that works. That makes Factory Balls a genuine logic puzzle rather than a dexterity test - nothing is timed, nothing moves, and the difficulty comes entirely from planning.

sections.heading: Fourteen levels that escalate quickly
sections.body: The game runs to fourteen levels, and the ramp is steep. The first few teach you one tool at a time; by the last third you are combining several masks in a specific order to produce patterns that are not obvious even once you know every tool. It is short enough to finish in a sitting and hard enough that the last levels are a real stopping point for most people.

sections.heading: Bart Bonte and the competition it came from
sections.body: Bonte is a Belgian developer known for minimal point-and-click puzzle games, and Factory Balls was his entry to the fourth Casual Gameplay Design Competition - a contest run by the site JayIsGames with a set theme. He noted at the time that he had deliberately made something other than his usual point-and-click. The game spawned a long series of sequels and remains one of the best-known browser puzzles of its era.
