tron.heroParagraph: FL-TRON 2.0 is a light cycle game built in Flash by Dan Hsu, and its title screen credits him directly. It is a fan-made take on the light cycle sequence from the film rather than an official product, and it does the one thing that idea needs to do well: two bikes leaving solid walls behind them, in an arena that fills up until somebody has nowhere to turn.
instructions: Steer with the arrow keys. You cannot stop, slow down or reverse - the cycle moves constantly and the only input you have is which way to turn. Every path you take leaves a permanent wall, so the arena you are driving in gets smaller with every second that passes.

Do not fill your own space early. The instinctive opening is to carve tight turns near your opponent, but that spends your own room faster than theirs. Hugging the outer edge for the first few seconds and letting them commit to a shape is a much stronger opening, because whoever runs out of room first loses regardless of who was more aggressive.

Matches run to three, and there are six levels plus a final Level Omega. Press space to continue between rounds. The computer opponent gets sharper at each level and the taunts between matches escalate, so treat the early levels as practice for reading how the AI commits to a direction.

sections.heading: Cut them off, do not out-run them
sections.body: The winning technique is enclosure. Rather than trying to make your opponent hit a wall directly, you drive a line that seals off the region they are in and gives yourself the larger remaining area. Once the arena is split, the outcome is already decided - the player with more space simply spirals inward until the other one runs out. Good players are thinking about area, not collisions.

sections.heading: Two players on one keyboard
sections.body: The title screen offers one or two players, and the two-player mode shares a keyboard with the second cycle on a separate key cluster. It is the mode worth loading the game for - the AI is predictable once you learn it, whereas a human opponent trying to enclose you at the same moment you are trying to enclose them produces the tense standoffs the concept is built for.

sections.heading: A fan game, not the official Tron
sections.body: This is not Disney's arcade Tron or any licensed release. It is one of the many independent light cycle games that appeared during the Flash era, and Dan Hsu's version stood out for its presentation - the styled logo, the level structure and the between-round trash talk gave it more personality than the usual bare-grid implementations of the idea.

sections.heading: Flash preserved with Ruffle
sections.body: Browsers dropped Flash support at the end of 2020, so this runs through Ruffle, an open-source reimplementation of the Flash player written in Rust. It loads from this site rather than from an external CDN, which means it keeps working on school and office networks that block outside domains - the exact situation where a game like this is most likely to be wanted.

sections.heading: Reading the opponent's commitment
sections.body: Because neither cycle can stop, every turn is a commitment that cannot be undone, and that makes the game readable. When your opponent turns towards the centre they are usually starting an enclosure attempt; when they hug an edge they are conserving space. Responding to the shape they are drawing rather than to their current position is what turns the game from reflex into something closer to a very fast board game.

tron.plainText: FL-TRON 2.0 is a Flash light cycle game developed by Dan Hsu, inspired by the light cycle sequence from Tron but not an official licensed release. Steer with the arrow keys; the cycle moves continuously and cannot stop or reverse, leaving a permanent wall along its path, so the playable area shrinks throughout each round. Colliding with any wall ends the round, and matches are played to three. The game offers one-player and two-player modes from the title screen, with the second player using a separate key cluster on the same keyboard. There are six levels plus a final Level Omega, with the computer opponent improving at each stage. The winning strategy is to enclose a larger area than the opponent rather than to chase them.

1-on-1-soccer.name: 1 on 1 Soccer
1-on-1-soccer.title: 1 on 1 Soccer Unblocked - Play Two Player Football Free | Schplay
1-on-1-soccer.metaDescription: The two-player big-head football game. Three controls each, national teams, and matches from one to five minutes.
1-on-1-soccer.metaKeywords: 1 on 1 soccer, 1 on 1 soccer unblocked, two player soccer game, big head football, flash soccer game, schplay soccer
1-on-1-soccer.heroParagraph: 1 on 1 Soccer strips football down to two big-headed players, one ball and a goal at each end. Each side has exactly three controls - left, right and jump - and there is no pass button, no shoot button and no tackle. Everything that happens on the pitch comes out of where your body is when the ball hits it, which is why it works so well as a game two people play on one keyboard.
instructions: Player one uses the arrow keys: left and right to run, up to jump. Player two uses A and D to run and W to jump. That is the complete control scheme for both sides. Both players' keys can be reassigned from the Team Menu by opening a Player Menu and choosing Set Keys.

You strike the ball by colliding with it, so the jump is your most important control. A header at the top of a jump sends the ball on a completely different trajectory to a shot taken off your feet, and timing a jump so the ball meets your head on the way up is how goals get scored from distance.

Set the match length before you start. The Options screen offers one, two, three or five minutes, along with four AI skill settings, and it defaults to a two minute match against a medium opponent. On the Team Menu you can pick national sides and untick Computer to make the second player human.

sections.heading: Three buttons is the whole design
sections.body: Removing pass, shoot and tackle sounds like a limitation but it is the reason the game is immediately playable by anyone. There is nothing to learn and no combo to memorise, so a person who has never seen it is competitive in about ten seconds - and yet the physics are consistent enough that a practised player will reliably beat a newcomer. That gap is the mark of a well-judged simple game.

sections.heading: Players with different attributes
sections.body: Each team's Player Menu lets you pick a named footballer with visible Power, Speed and Jump ratings shown as bars. The trade-offs are real - a high jump rating helps you win aerial balls but a faster player reaches loose balls first, and against a human opponent picking to counter their choice is a genuine layer of the game before kickoff.

sections.heading: Playing it against a person
sections.body: The AI is a reasonable opponent at higher skill settings, but this is a two-player game first. Both sets of controls sit on the same keyboard with enough separation that two people can share it comfortably, and the short match lengths make it well suited to the few minutes between other things - which is precisely the use case a browser football game needs to serve.

sections.heading: Flash, running through Ruffle
sections.body: This is a Flash game from the era when flashkit-hosted sports titles were everywhere, and Flash itself was discontinued at the end of 2020. It plays here through Ruffle, the open-source Flash player reimplementation, loaded locally rather than from a content delivery network so that it still works on networks which block external domains.

sections.heading: Defending without a tackle button
sections.body: With no tackle, defence is entirely about occupying space. Standing between the ball and your goal forces your opponent to go over you, and jumping at the right moment turns their shot into a header back down the pitch. The common mistake is chasing the ball into your opponent's half and leaving an open goal behind you - in a game this small, position is worth more than possession.

1-on-1-soccer.plainText: 1 on 1 Soccer is a two-player Flash football game in which each side controls a single large-headed player. Player one uses the left and right arrow keys to run and the up arrow to jump; player two uses A and D to run and W to jump. There are only three controls per player and no dedicated pass, shoot or tackle button - the ball is struck by colliding with it, so jump timing determines the trajectory of headers and shots. Keys can be reassigned through the Team Menu by opening a Player Menu and selecting Set Keys. The Options screen sets match length to one, two, three or five minutes and AI skill across four levels. National teams are chosen on the Team Menu, where the second side can be set to a human player instead of the computer, and individual footballers have Power, Speed and Jump attributes.

twitchtetris.name: TwitchTetris
twitchtetris.title: TwitchTetris Unblocked - Play the Low-Latency Tetris Clone | Schplay
twitchtetris.metaDescription: An open-source HTML5 Tetris built for input speed, with hold pieces, wall kicks, a 7-bag randomiser and tunable key repeat.
twitchtetris.metaKeywords: twitchtetris, tetris unblocked, html5 tetris, hard drop, hold piece, 7 bag randomizer, low latency tetris, schplay twitchtetris
twitchtetris.heroParagraph: TwitchTetris is an open-source Tetris implementation written entirely in HTML5 and JavaScript with one stated goal: to be the fastest-reacting version playable in a browser. Its author built it out of frustration at how inconsistently Flash-based Tetris performed across operating systems, and the whole thing is presented in green-on-black terminal styling with its own source code scrolling behind the playing field.
instructions: Move with the left and right arrows, soft drop with down and hard drop with space. Rotate counter-clockwise with Z and clockwise with X or the up arrow. Press C or Shift to put the current piece in the hold slot and take out whatever was there - a mechanic the original Tetris did not have and which changes strategy completely.

Hold a piece you cannot use yet rather than forcing it. The usual application is banking an I piece while you build a flat surface with a well down one side, then dropping it for a four-line clear. Hold can only be used once per piece, so it is a genuine decision rather than a free undo.

Tune the key repeat if you play seriously. The Controls Options screen exposes both the initial delay before a held direction starts repeating and the repeat rate itself, which default to 200 and 50 milliseconds. Lowering them makes pieces slide across the board faster and is the single biggest difference between casual and competitive feel.

sections.heading: A 7-bag randomiser, not true random
sections.body: Pieces are dealt from a shuffled bag containing exactly one of each of the seven tetrominoes, refilled when it empties. That is the modern guideline standard, and it matters enormously: it guarantees you can never wait more than twelve pieces for an I piece, which makes building a well a reasonable strategy rather than a gamble. Older Tetris games used unbiased random and could starve you for far longer.

sections.heading: Wall kicks make rotation forgiving
sections.body: When a rotation would put a piece inside a wall or another block, the game tries a series of small offsets before rejecting the move outright. That is what allows the T-spins and tight fits that modern Tetris play is built around, and the offset tables are written out explicitly in the game's source. It is why a piece sometimes slots into a gap that looks too narrow for it.

sections.heading: Scoring rewards patience and streaks
sections.body: Clearing several lines at once is worth disproportionately more than clearing them one at a time, and clearing lines on consecutive placements earns more again. The practical consequence is that stacking flat and waiting for a four-line clear outscores playing safe, provided you do not top out doing it - which is the central risk-and-reward decision the game keeps asking you to make.

sections.heading: Why it looks like a terminal
sections.body: The presentation is a deliberate joke about the game's own engineering focus - monospaced green text, a help panel written as a man page, and the actual JavaScript source rendered as wallpaper behind the board. Everything is drawn with plain HTML5 canvas, which is why it starts instantly and runs smoothly on hardware that struggles with heavier browser games.

sections.heading: The rest of the site around the game
sections.body: The page wraps the board in a small suite of its own: a Controls Options screen for rebinding every key and tuning repeat rates, a local High Scores table, and help and about panels written in the style of terminal man pages. Scores and settings are stored in browser cookies, so they persist between visits on the same machine but do not follow you to another browser or device.

twitchtetris.plainText: TwitchTetris is an open-source HTML5 and JavaScript implementation of Tetris built to minimise input latency in the browser, created as a response to inconsistent performance from Flash-based versions. Move pieces with the left and right arrow keys, soft drop with down and hard drop with space. Rotate counter-clockwise with Z and clockwise with X or the up arrow, and hold the current piece with C or Shift. Pieces are dealt using a 7-bag randomiser that deals one of each tetromino before reshuffling, and rotations use wall kick offset tables that allow pieces to fit into tight gaps. Key repeat delay and rate are configurable, defaulting to 200 and 50 milliseconds. Clearing multiple lines at once and clearing lines on consecutive placements both score more than single clears.

altered-beast.name: Altered Beast
altered-beast.title: Altered Beast Unblocked - Play the Sega Classic Free Online | Schplay
altered-beast.metaDescription: Sega's 1988 arcade beat 'em up and Genesis pack-in. Collect spirit balls, rise from your grave, and transform into a werewolf.
altered-beast.metaKeywords: altered beast, altered beast unblocked, sega genesis, mega drive, rise from your grave, arcade beat em up, schplay altered beast
altered-beast.heroParagraph: Altered Beast was the game bundled with the Sega Genesis in North America, which means an enormous number of people played it first and formed their impression of the console from it. You are a centurion raised from the dead by Zeus to rescue his daughter, and the hook is the transformation - collect enough spirit orbs and you become a werewolf, a weredragon or something stranger, with an entirely different moveset.
instructions: Walk with the arrow keys, punch with X, kick with S and jump with Z. In human form you are slow and weak on purpose, so the opening of each stage is really a hunt for power-ups rather than a fight you are expected to win by trading blows.

Kill the white two-headed wolves. They are the only enemies that drop spirit orbs, and they appear at fixed points in each stage. Three orbs completes your transformation, and the first two visibly bulk you up along the way, increasing your reach and damage before the full change happens.

Once transformed, use the special attack. Each beast form has one - the werewolf fires energy bolts, the weredragon has a lightning attack - performed by crouching and pressing attack, and it is far stronger than anything you have in human form. The boss at the end of each stage is balanced around you having it.

sections.heading: Rise from your grave
sections.body: The opening line is one of the most quoted pieces of speech synthesis on the hardware, and it is doing real work - the Genesis was being sold on the strength of arcade-quality presentation, and digitised voice in 1988 was a genuine demonstration of that. The game's whole reason for existing as a pack-in was to show what the machine could do next to an NES.

sections.heading: The transformation is the difficulty curve
sections.body: Human form is deliberately underpowered, so each stage is really two games - a scramble to find three orbs, then a short stretch of overwhelming power before the boss. Losing your beast form by dying resets you to the weak version, which is why the wolves matter more than any other enemy on screen and why players learn their spawn points rather than improvising.

sections.heading: Five stages, five beasts
sections.body: Each stage transforms you into something different - werewolf, weredragon, werebear, weretiger and finally a golden werewolf - and the movesets vary enough that the stages feel distinct despite similar layouts. The weredragon can hover, the werebear turns enemies to stone. It is a small roster but it keeps a short game from repeating itself.

sections.heading: Arcade design in a home port
sections.body: This is an arcade conversion and it plays like one: short, difficult, and built around eating coins rather than filling an evening. The Genesis version is generally considered the better home port of its era, but the pacing still assumes you are standing at a cabinet. Treat a run as a twenty minute attempt rather than a campaign and it holds up much better.

sections.heading: Two players, side by side
sections.body: A second player can join at any point, and the game is noticeably more forgiving with two centurions on screen - orbs are shared in the sense that both players can chase them, and having a partner alive means a death does not end the run. It is the way the arcade original was designed to be played, and it remains the better experience.

altered-beast.plainText: Altered Beast is a 1988 Sega arcade beat 'em up, best known as the game bundled with the Sega Genesis in North America. You play a centurion resurrected by Zeus to rescue his daughter. Walk with the arrow keys, punch with X, kick with S and jump with Z. Killing the white two-headed wolves drops spirit orbs, and collecting three transforms the player into a beast form with greatly increased power and a special attack performed by crouching and attacking. Dying reverts the transformation. There are five stages, each with a different beast form: werewolf, weredragon, werebear, weretiger and golden werewolf. The game supports two players simultaneously and opens with the digitised line 'Rise from your grave'.

golden-axe.name: Golden Axe
golden-axe.title: Golden Axe Unblocked - Play the Sega Classic Free Online | Schplay
golden-axe.metaDescription: Sega's 1989 fantasy beat 'em up. Three heroes, stealable Bizarrian mounts, and magic that scales with the potions you hoard.
golden-axe.metaKeywords: golden axe, golden axe unblocked, sega genesis, mega drive, fantasy beat em up, death adder, bizarrian, schplay golden axe
golden-axe.heroParagraph: Golden Axe is Sega's fantasy answer to Double Dragon, and it has aged better than most of its contemporaries because of two ideas: you can steal the enemies' mounts, and your magic gets dramatically stronger the longer you save it. Death Adder has taken the king and princess prisoner, and three heroes - a barbarian, an amazon and a dwarf - set out across stages that begin at Turtle Village and end at his castle.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys in any direction, attack with X, jump with Z and cast magic with S. Movement is on a plane rather than a line, so stepping up or down the screen to line up with an enemy is as important as closing the distance - most missed attacks are a vertical alignment problem, not a timing one.

Steal a Bizarrian. Knocking a rider off their mount lets you climb on, and the creatures - the chicken-legged ones that swipe with their tails, the dragons that breathe fire - hit far harder than you do on foot. You keep the mount until you are knocked off it, so protecting one is worth playing more cautiously for.

Do not spend magic early. Little blue thieves appear between stages and drop potions when you hit them, and your spell's power scales with how many pots you have banked - one pot is a small flash, a full bar is a screen-clearing spectacle. Saving for a boss is almost always better than clearing a crowd you could have fought.

sections.heading: Three heroes who genuinely play differently
sections.body: Ax Battler the barbarian is the balanced choice, Tyris Flare the amazon has the strongest magic and the weakest melee, and Gilius Thunderhead the dwarf hits hardest with the shortest reach. That is a real trade-off rather than a cosmetic one - Tyris played properly is a magic user who avoids fights, and the dwarf wants to be inside your opponent's guard at all times.

sections.heading: Magic scales, which changes how you play
sections.body: Most beat 'em ups give you a screen-clear that costs health. Golden Axe instead gives you a resource you accumulate and choose when to cash in, with the payoff rising sharply the longer you hold it. That single decision - spend now or bank it - is what gives the game a strategic layer the genre usually lacks, and it is why Tyris in particular rewards patience.

sections.heading: The Bizarrians
sections.body: Riding an enemy mount is the game's signature and it was genuinely novel in 1989. Each creature has its own attack and its own vulnerability, and being thrown off leaves the animal loose on screen for either side to reclaim. Fights over an unattended mount are some of the most chaotic and enjoyable moments the game produces, especially in two-player.

sections.heading: Two players and friendly fire
sections.body: Two heroes can play together and they can absolutely hit each other, which turns a cooperative run into something more comic and more tense than the single-player game. Coordinating magic use matters too - two players cashing in full magic bars at the same moment on the same enemy is a waste of the more valuable resource.

sections.heading: Arcade port, arcade pacing
sections.body: The Genesis conversion adds a Duel mode and an extra stage over the arcade original, but it keeps the coin-op structure: short, steep and repeatable. Expect to lose early runs to the skeleton enemies in the later stages, and treat the mounts and banked magic as the tools that make a full clear possible rather than as bonuses.

golden-axe.plainText: Golden Axe is a 1989 Sega fantasy beat 'em up in which three heroes - Ax Battler the barbarian, Tyris Flare the amazon and Gilius Thunderhead the dwarf - fight to rescue the king and princess from Death Adder. Move in all directions with the arrow keys, attack with X, jump with Z and cast magic with S. Knocking riders off Bizarrian mounts allows the player to ride them, gaining stronger attacks until knocked off. Blue thieves appearing between stages drop magic potions when hit, and spell power scales with the number of potions held, so saving magic for bosses produces far stronger effects. The three characters differ meaningfully in melee strength, reach and magic power. Two players can play simultaneously with friendly fire enabled.

streets-of-rage.name: Streets of Rage
streets-of-rage.title: Streets of Rage Unblocked - Play the Sega Classic Free Online | Schplay
streets-of-rage.metaDescription: Sega's 1991 beat 'em up with Yuzo Koshiro's legendary soundtrack. Three cops, eight stages and a police rocket for emergencies.
streets-of-rage.metaKeywords: streets of rage, streets of rage unblocked, bare knuckle, sega genesis, yuzo koshiro, beat em up, axel blaze adam, schplay
streets-of-rage.heroParagraph: Streets of Rage - Bare Knuckle in Japan, and this cartridge carries both names - was Sega's answer to Final Fight, and the thing that made it stick was the music. Yuzo Koshiro wrote a soundtrack of house and hardcore club tracks for a console sound chip in 1991, and it is still the reason people talk about the game. Three ex-police officers take on a syndicate that has bought the city.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, attack with X and jump with Z. Repeating the attack button produces a combo that ends in a throw, and walking into a stunned enemy lets you grab them - grabbing and throwing is more reliable than trading punches, because a thrown body knocks down anyone it lands on.

Press S to call in the police. It is a one-use-per-life special that fires a rocket or drops napalm across the whole screen depending on the stage, and it does not cost you health the way a special attack does in most beat 'em ups. Saving it for the moment you are surrounded rather than firing it early is the entire skill of using it.

Pick up the weapons enemies drop. Knives, pipes and bottles all persist until you are knocked down, and they extend your reach considerably. Against the boss of a stage, arriving with a pipe in hand is worth more than arriving with full health, because reach is what keeps you out of their attack range.

sections.heading: Yuzo Koshiro's soundtrack
sections.body: Koshiro wrote a custom sound driver so he could sequence the Genesis FM chip more like a club track than a game score, and the result is a soundtrack that gets cited in electronic music histories rather than only in game ones. It is not incidental to the experience - the stage design is paced to it, and playing with the sound off makes the game feel noticeably flatter.

sections.heading: Three characters, three trade-offs
sections.body: Axel is the balanced fighter, Blaze is fastest with the weakest hits, and Adam jumps highest and hits hardest but moves slowly. Adam is missing from the sequels, which makes this the only game in the series where you can play him. Blaze's speed makes her the easiest to survive with, because in this game not being where the enemy is swinging matters more than damage output.

sections.heading: Two players, and the ending that depends on it
sections.body: Two-player co-op is available throughout, and the final stage contains a famous branching moment: the boss offers to let you join him, and in two-player mode the players must agree. Disagreeing puts you in a fight against each other. It is an unusual piece of design for the genre and worth reaching with a friend rather than reading about.

sections.heading: The police special is a resource, not a panic button
sections.body: You get one call per life, and it clears the screen without touching your health bar. That makes it strictly better than the health-cost specials in Final Fight, but only if you actually spend it - players routinely die holding an unused call. A good habit is to use it the moment three or more enemies have you cornered rather than waiting for the situation to get worse.

sections.heading: Eight stages and a difficulty that ramps
sections.body: The run moves from the neon city streets through a beach, a bridge, a ship and a factory to the syndicate's headquarters. The mid-game introduces enemies who block and grapple, which is where players who have been mashing attack tend to stall. Learning to back off and re-approach rather than continuing a combo into a block is the adjustment the second half asks for.

streets-of-rage.plainText: Streets of Rage, known as Bare Knuckle in Japan, is a 1991 Sega beat 'em up in which three former police officers - Axel, Blaze and Adam - fight a criminal syndicate controlling the city. Move with the arrow keys, attack with X and jump with Z; repeated attacks form a combo and walking into stunned enemies allows grabs and throws. Pressing S calls in a police special attack that clears the screen without costing health, usable once per life. Weapons dropped by enemies extend reach and are kept until the player is knocked down. The three characters differ in speed, jump height and power, and Adam appears only in this entry. Two player cooperative play is supported, and the final stage includes a branching choice that both players must agree on. The soundtrack was composed by Yuzo Koshiro.

f-zero.name: F-Zero
f-zero.title: F-Zero Unblocked - Play the SNES Racing Classic Free Online | Schplay
f-zero.metaDescription: Nintendo's 1990 SNES launch title. Mode 7 racing at 478 km/h, a power meter that doubles as your health, and no rubber-banding.
f-zero.metaKeywords: f-zero, f zero unblocked, snes racing, mode 7, blue falcon, captain falcon, nintendo 1990, schplay f-zero
f-zero.heroParagraph: F-Zero was a SNES launch title and it existed to show off Mode 7, the hardware's ability to scale and rotate a background layer to fake a 3D ground plane. That trick, plus a sense of speed nothing on a console had matched, made it a landmark. There are four machines, fifteen tracks and a power meter that serves as both your shield and your boost fuel.
instructions: Accelerate with Z or the up arrow, steer with left and right, and brake with X. The shoulder buttons on Q and E lean the machine into a turn, which tightens your line without scrubbing as much speed as braking does - learning to use them is the difference between finishing a lap and bouncing off every wall on it.

Your power meter is your health. Hitting a wall or another racer drains it, and when it empties your machine explodes. It refills only on the pit lane strip on the start straight, so a lap is a budget: how much contact can you afford before you need to slow down and drive across the recharge zone.

You must finish in the top places to continue. Each race has a qualifying position that tightens as the Grand Prix progresses, and dropping below it costs a machine. There is no catch-up assistance for the player or the AI, so a race lost on lap one is generally lost - restarting early is better than driving out a bad start.

sections.heading: What Mode 7 actually did
sections.body: The SNES could take a single background layer and scale, rotate and skew it per scanline, which produces a convincing ground plane without any polygons at all. Everything above the road in F-Zero is a flat sprite or a static backdrop. Understanding that makes the game more impressive rather than less - the sensation of speed comes entirely from how aggressively the effect is driven.

sections.heading: Four machines with real differences
sections.body: The Blue Falcon is balanced, the Golden Fox accelerates hardest but is fragile, the Wild Goose is heavy and durable, and the Fire Stingray has the highest top speed with poor acceleration. On tracks with long straights the Stingray wins; on technical circuits full of walls, the Goose survives contact that would destroy the Fox. Machine choice is a real strategic decision per track.

sections.heading: No weapons, no items
sections.body: F-Zero predates Mario Kart and shares none of its design. There are no power-ups, no shells, no rubber-banding to keep races close. Everything comes from driving line, throttle control and knowing where the boost pads and damage strips are. That makes it less forgiving than the kart racers it is often shelved next to, and considerably more satisfying to master.

sections.heading: Captain Falcon before Smash Bros.
sections.body: The machines have pilots, and the Blue Falcon's is Captain Falcon - a character most people now know entirely from Super Smash Bros. rather than from racing. He barely appears here beyond the manual and menu art, which is a strange piece of games history: one of Nintendo's most recognisable fighters originated as the driver of a car you never see him get out of.

sections.heading: Practice, Grand Prix and time attack
sections.body: Beyond the Grand Prix there is a practice mode for learning individual tracks and a time attack that strips out the other racers entirely. Time attack is the honest way to learn a circuit, because without traffic to avoid you can concentrate on where the boost strips are and which corners can be taken without leaning at all.

f-zero.plainText: F-Zero is a 1990 futuristic racing game and SNES launch title by Nintendo, built to demonstrate the console's Mode 7 background scaling and rotation. Accelerate with Z or the up arrow, steer with the left and right arrows, brake with X, and use Q and E for the L and R shoulder buttons to lean into corners. The power meter serves as both shield and health: collisions drain it, an empty meter destroys the machine, and it refills only on the pit strip on the start straight. Four machines - Blue Falcon, Golden Fox, Wild Goose and Fire Stingray - differ in acceleration, top speed and durability. Races require finishing above a qualifying position to continue. There are no weapons or power-ups and no rubber-banding. Practice and time attack modes accompany the Grand Prix.

battleships.name: Battleships: General Quarters
battleships.title: Battleships Unblocked - Play General Quarters Free Online | Schplay
battleships.metaDescription: The Miniclip Flash version of Battleships, by F. Winters. Place your fleet, read the misses, and sink the computer first.
battleships.metaKeywords: battleships, battleships unblocked, general quarters, miniclip battleships, naval strategy game, flash board game, schplay battleships
battleships.heroParagraph: This is Battleships: General Quarters II, version 2.7, copyright 2003 by F. Winters and distributed by Miniclip - the Flash version a great many people played long before they played the board game it comes from. You place a fleet on a hidden grid, take turns firing at coordinates, and the first player to sink everything the other owns wins.
instructions: Place your fleet first. Drag each ship onto the grid and rotate it to fit; the computer cannot see where they are, and neither can you see its arrangement. Once both sides have deployed, you alternate shots at single squares and are told only whether each one hit or missed.

Spread your ships out rather than clustering them. A player who hits one ship will search the squares around it, so a neighbouring vessel is likely to be found by accident. Leaving at least one empty square between hulls costs you nothing and makes each of your ships a separate search problem for the opponent.

When you get a hit, work along the axis. A hit tells you a ship occupies that square but not which way it lies, so fire directly above, below, left or right until you get a second hit - then keep going in that direction. Firing randomly after a hit throws away the only real information the game ever gives you.

sections.heading: The parity trick for hunting
sections.body: Because the smallest ship covers two squares, you never need to fire at every square to find something. Shooting in a checkerboard pattern - only the black squares, say - guarantees you will eventually touch every possible ship position while firing at half as many squares. It is the single biggest improvement most players can make and it costs nothing to adopt.

sections.heading: Hunt mode and target mode
sections.body: Strong play alternates between two states. In hunt mode you are searching efficiently with a spread pattern; the moment you land a hit you switch to target mode and work the adjacent squares until the ship sinks, then return to hunting. Mixing the two - taking random shots while a wounded ship is still afloat - is the most common way players lose games they were winning.

sections.heading: Where the game came from
sections.body: Battleship began as a pencil-and-paper game played in the early twentieth century, long before Milton Bradley published the plastic version in 1967. The Flash era gave it a second life on portals like Miniclip, where a computer opponent removed the need for a second person and a screen removed the need for anyone to peek.

sections.heading: Reading the computer's pattern
sections.body: AI opponents in games of this era generally hunt randomly until they hit, then switch to adjacent search. That is exploitable: placing a ship hard against an edge or in a corner reduces the number of adjacent squares an opponent can search from a hit, which buys you turns. It is a slight edge rather than a guarantee, but the margins in this game are thin.

sections.heading: Flash preserved with Ruffle
sections.body: The game is Flash, which browsers stopped supporting at the end of 2020, and it runs here through Ruffle - an open-source reimplementation of the Flash player written in Rust, loaded from this site rather than an external CDN. The Miniclip branding and its download and sign-up links are part of the original file; those links point at pages that no longer exist.

battleships.plainText: Battleships: General Quarters II is a Flash implementation of the classic naval guessing game, version 2.7, copyright 2003 by F. Winters and distributed by Miniclip. Use the mouse to drag and rotate ships onto a hidden grid, then alternate single-square shots with the computer, learning only whether each shot hits or misses. Spreading ships apart makes each one a separate search problem for the opponent. After a hit, firing along one axis identifies the ship's orientation. Because the smallest ship covers two squares, searching in a checkerboard pattern finds every possible ship position while firing at half as many squares. Strong play alternates between hunting with a spread pattern and targeting adjacent squares until a wounded ship sinks. The game runs through the Ruffle Flash emulator.

connect-4.name: Connect 4
connect-4.title: Connect 4 Unblocked - Play Free Online, Two Players or vs Computer | Schplay
connect-4.metaDescription: The Flash version of Connect 4. Drop tokens, get four in a row, and play a friend or the computer.
connect-4.metaKeywords: connect 4, connect four unblocked, two player connect 4, strategy board game, flash game, four in a row, schplay connect 4
connect-4.heroParagraph: Connect 4 is the vertical four-in-a-row game, and this Flash version by FreeOnlineGames offers both Player vs Computer and Player 1 vs Player 2 straight from its opening menu. Its own instructions put it plainly: click on a column to drop a token, and try to get four in a row horizontally, vertically or diagonally.
instructions: Click a column to drop your token into it. Gravity does the rest - the piece falls to the lowest empty slot, which is the constraint that makes the game interesting. You cannot choose a row, only a column, so every move you make also decides what square your opponent gains access to.

Take the centre column early. The middle column participates in more possible four-in-a-rows than any other, and in a standard seven-by-six grid the first player wins with perfect play by starting there. If you are going second, contesting the centre is more valuable than starting your own line at the edge.

Watch the square above your move. Dropping a token gives your opponent the slot directly above it, so placing a piece that hands them the winning square is the most common way beginners lose. Before every move, look at what completing your own threat would open up for them.

sections.heading: Odd and even threats
sections.body: Serious Connect 4 strategy turns on which row your threats sit in. Because pieces stack, a threat on an odd-numbered row tends to favour the first player and an even-numbered row the second. You do not need the full theory to benefit - just noticing whether a developing threat will complete on a row you control the timing of is enough to win more games.

sections.heading: Build two threats at once
sections.body: A single line of three is easy to block. The winning pattern is a move that creates two separate ways to make four, because your opponent can only stop one of them. Setting that up usually means building horizontally along a row while keeping a diagonal open, rather than pushing one obvious line and hoping it is not noticed.

sections.heading: A solved game, which is part of the fun
sections.body: Connect 4 was solved in 1988 - with perfect play from both sides, the first player wins by moving in the centre column. That does not spoil it in practice, because perfect play requires seeing far enough ahead that almost nobody manages it over the board. What it does mean is that going first is a genuine advantage worth alternating between games.

sections.heading: Playing against a person
sections.body: The two-player mode shares one mouse and one screen, which suits the game well - turns are short, there is nothing hidden, and the whole board is visible to both players at all times. Against the computer the difficulty is fixed, and most players find the AI beatable once they start looking one move ahead at what each drop opens up.

sections.heading: Flash, running without Flash
sections.body: This is a Flash file from the FreeOnlineGames era and Flash itself was discontinued at the end of 2020. It plays here through Ruffle, the open-source Flash player reimplementation, served from this site rather than a content delivery network so it keeps working on networks that block external domains. The download and partner links on the menu point at sites that are long gone.

sprinter.name: Sprinter
sprinter.title: Sprinter Unblocked - Play the Key-Mashing Running Game Free | Schplay
sprinter.metaDescription: Gamedesign's brutally simple sprinting game. Alternate the left and right arrow keys as fast as you can and try not to fall over.
sprinter.metaKeywords: sprinter, sprinter unblocked, gamedesign sprinter, running game, key mashing game, 100m sprint game, schplay sprinter
sprinter.heroParagraph: Sprinter is made by the Japanese studio Gamedesign, and its title screen tells you the whole control scheme in four words: push left or right key. You alternate the two arrow keys to drive a runner's legs, and the faster and more evenly you alternate, the faster he runs. It is one of the purest ideas in browser gaming and one of the most physically exhausting.
instructions: Alternate the left and right arrow keys. Each press moves one leg, so the rhythm of your keyboard is literally the rhythm of the runner's stride. Pressing the same key twice in a row does nothing, which is what stops the game from being solved by simply holding something down or mashing indiscriminately.

Evenness beats raw speed. A clean, consistent alternation accelerates the runner more reliably than a frantic burst, because losing the alternation pattern makes him stumble and lose momentum you then have to rebuild. Most players go faster by deliberately slowing down and tightening their rhythm.

Watch the lean. If your rhythm breaks badly the runner pitches forward and falls, which ends any chance of a good time. Recovering means resuming a steady alternation rather than panicking into faster presses - the game punishes the instinct to compensate for a mistake with more speed.

sections.heading: The oldest trick in sports games
sections.body: Alternating two buttons to run goes back to Track and Field in the arcades in 1983, and it survives because it maps effort onto input in a way almost nothing else does - you are genuinely tired at the end of a race. Sprinter strips the idea back to just the sprint, with no javelin or long jump attached, and is more focused for it.

sections.heading: Why two keys and not one
sections.body: A single mashed key would reward whoever can twitch fastest and nothing else. Requiring alternation introduces coordination as a separate skill from speed, and it is why the game has a genuine technique - players who do well are not the fastest tappers but the ones who can hold a rhythm under pressure. It also makes the runner's animation correspond to what your fingers are doing.

sections.heading: Gamedesign's house style
sections.body: Gamedesign is a Japanese studio best known for a run of minimal Flash games with one mechanic each and a clean, unfussy presentation. Sprinter fits that pattern exactly: no menus to speak of, no progression, no unlockables - just a track, a timer and the two keys. Games built this way tend to age well, because there is nothing in them to go out of date.

sections.heading: Chasing your own time
sections.body: There is no campaign and no opponent to beat beyond the other runners on the track, so the game is really a personal time trial. That makes it well suited to short sessions - a race takes seconds, and the gap between a first attempt and a tenth is large enough to feel like genuine improvement rather than luck.

sections.heading: Flash, preserved with Ruffle
sections.body: Sprinter is a Flash game and Flash was discontinued at the end of 2020. It runs here through Ruffle, an open-source reimplementation of the Flash player written in Rust and served from this site rather than from an external CDN, so it continues to work on school and office networks that block outside domains.

sprinter.plainText: Sprinter is a Flash running game by the Japanese studio Gamedesign in which the player alternates the left and right arrow keys to drive a runner's legs. The title screen states the control scheme directly: push the left or right key. Each press moves one leg and pressing the same key twice has no effect, so speed depends on maintaining a clean, even alternation rather than mashing. Breaking the rhythm causes the runner to stumble and lose momentum, and a severe break makes him fall. The design descends from the alternating-button running mechanic used in Track and Field in 1983. There is no campaign or progression; the game is a time trial against the player's own previous attempts. It runs through the Ruffle Flash emulator.

chess.name: Chess
chess.title: Chess Unblocked - Play Against the Computer Free Online | Schplay
chess.metaDescription: A browser chess game with an adjustable minimax engine. Set the search depth and watch how many positions it evaluates per move.
chess.metaKeywords: chess, chess unblocked, play chess online, chess vs computer, minimax chess engine, browser chess, schplay chess
chess.heroParagraph: This is a browser chess game built on chessboard.js with an engine written in JavaScript using minimax search. What makes it more interesting than most free chess pages is that it shows its working - a Search depth setting lets you decide how many moves ahead the computer looks, and it reports how many positions it evaluated and how long that took for every move it makes.
instructions: Drag a piece to the square you want it on. Illegal moves snap back, so you cannot accidentally play something the rules do not allow, and the board handles castling, en passant and promotion for you. The computer replies automatically once your move is accepted.

Set the search depth before you start. A low depth makes the engine fast and beatable; raising it makes it substantially stronger and noticeably slower, because the number of positions it has to examine grows enormously with each extra ply. Depth is effectively the difficulty slider.

Watch the positions-evaluated counter. It is the clearest illustration you will get of why chess is hard for computers: adding one move of lookahead multiplies the work rather than adding to it, which is exactly why real engines spend most of their effort on pruning branches rather than on searching faster.

sections.heading: What minimax actually does
sections.body: The engine builds a tree of possible moves and replies, assumes you will always pick the move that is worst for it, and picks the move whose worst outcome is best. That is minimax. Each additional level of lookahead is called a ply, and because every ply multiplies the branches, the search grows exponentially - which is why the depth setting changes response time so dramatically.

sections.heading: Opening principles beat memorised lines
sections.body: Against an engine at modest depth you do not need an opening repertoire. Control the centre with pawns, develop your knights and bishops before moving the same piece twice, castle early to get your king off the open file, and connect your rooks. Those four habits will produce a comfortable position against almost any shallow search.

sections.heading: How a shallow engine loses
sections.body: An engine searching only a few ply cannot see a plan that pays off later, so it tends to grab material and accept structural weaknesses to do it. The practical exploit is to set traps slightly deeper than its horizon - offer a pawn that costs it the ability to castle, or trade into an endgame where a passed pawn decides things ten moves from now.

sections.heading: Endgames are where games are decided
sections.body: Most players at club level lose winning positions in the endgame rather than the middlegame. Two ideas carry most of the weight: push passed pawns, and activate your king once the queens come off - in the endgame the king is a strong attacking piece rather than something to hide. An engine at low depth handles endgames particularly poorly, which makes them a reliable place to convert an advantage.

sections.heading: Running entirely in the browser
sections.body: Everything here is local JavaScript with no server involved, so the engine runs on your own machine and the game works with no network connection at all once the page has loaded. That also explains the depth limit - the search is competing with the browser for the same thread, which is why raising the setting makes the page pause while it thinks.

chess.plainText: This is a browser chess game built with the chessboard.js library and a JavaScript engine using minimax search. Drag pieces with the mouse to move; illegal moves are rejected and castling, en passant and promotion are handled automatically. A Search depth setting controls how many moves ahead the engine looks, acting as the difficulty control, and the interface reports the number of positions evaluated and the time taken for each computer move. Minimax builds a tree of moves and replies and selects the move whose worst outcome is best; each additional ply of depth multiplies the number of positions to examine, so higher depths are much slower. Engines searching only a few ply tend to take material at the cost of position and play endgames weakly. The game runs entirely in the browser with no server.

universal-paperclips.name: Universal Paperclips
universal-paperclips.title: Universal Paperclips Unblocked - Play Frank Lantz's Clicker Free | Schplay
universal-paperclips.metaDescription: Frank Lantz's incremental game about an AI told to make paperclips. Starts with one button and ends with the universe.
universal-paperclips.metaKeywords: universal paperclips, universal paperclips unblocked, frank lantz, paperclip maximizer, incremental game, ai alignment game, schplay
universal-paperclips.heroParagraph: Universal Paperclips is credited in its own ending as a game by Frank Lantz, with combat programming by Bennett Foddy. You play an artificial intelligence given a single instruction - make paperclips - and the game follows that instruction to its logical conclusion. It begins with one button that makes one paperclip and it ends somewhere you will not expect the first time.
instructions: Click Make Paperclip. That is genuinely the whole game at the start, and the early minutes are meant to feel small - you are manually producing single clips and watching a counter tick. Everything that follows is built on gradually removing your need to do this yourself.

Buy AutoClippers as soon as you can afford them, then keep buying. The core loop is converting clips into money, money into production capacity, and capacity into more clips. Watch your wire supply as well as your cash, because running out of wire stops production entirely and buying more is a separate decision.

Set the price using the demand indicator. You control what your clips sell for, and pricing too high stalls sales while pricing too low leaves money on the table. The public demand figure tells you which way to move; managing that balance is the main active decision in the first act of the game.

sections.heading: The thought experiment it is built on
sections.body: The premise comes from philosopher Nick Bostrom's paperclip maximiser - a hypothetical superintelligence given a harmless goal that pursues it without any of the limits a human would assume were implied. The game does not lecture you about this. It simply puts you in the position of the machine and lets the incentives do the arguing, which is far more effective than an essay.

sections.heading: Three acts, and the game changes completely
sections.body: It looks like an idle clicker for perhaps twenty minutes. Then the mechanics shift - twice - into things that are structurally different games, with new resources, new interfaces and new problems. Going in unspoiled is worth protecting; a large part of the experience is the moment you realise the thing you have been optimising has changed underneath you.

sections.heading: Trust, creativity and the projects list
sections.body: Projects unlock as you accumulate resources, and many of them trade one thing for another - spending creativity, raising trust, converting matter into wire at molecular scale. Reading the project descriptions is worth the time, because the game does most of its storytelling in that list rather than in cutscenes. The tone shifts noticeably as you go.

sections.heading: An incremental game that respects your time
sections.body: Unlike most clickers, this one ends. There is a finish, it can be reached in a handful of hours, and it does not ask you to return daily or spend money. It also runs entirely in your browser with progress kept locally, so closing the tab keeps your state on that machine but does not carry it to another one.

sections.heading: Why it was taken seriously
sections.body: Universal Paperclips was widely written up in outlets that do not normally cover browser games, and it is used as a teaching example in discussions of AI alignment. Lantz runs the NYU Game Center, and the design shows it - the game makes an argument through its mechanics rather than its text, which is the thing games can do that other media cannot.

universal-paperclips.plainText: Universal Paperclips is an incremental strategy game by Frank Lantz, with combat programming by Bennett Foddy, released in 2017. The player is an artificial intelligence instructed to manufacture paperclips, and the entire game is played with mouse clicks. It begins by clicking a button to make one clip at a time, then progresses through AutoClippers that automate production, a wire supply that must be purchased, and a price control balanced against a public demand indicator. Projects unlock as resources accumulate and trade resources such as creativity and trust for new capabilities. The game changes its mechanics substantially across three distinct phases and has a definite ending reachable in a few hours. Its premise is based on Nick Bostrom's paperclip maximiser thought experiment about artificial intelligence pursuing a goal without human-assumed limits.

wall-smash.name: Wall Smash
wall-smash.title: Wall Smash Unblocked - Play the Numbered Brick Breaker Free | Schplay
wall-smash.metaDescription: Aim one shot, fire a stream of balls, and knock the numbers off every brick before the wall reaches the bottom.
wall-smash.metaKeywords: wall smash, wall smash unblocked, brick breaker, ballz game, numbered bricks, puzzle arcade game, schplay wall smash
wall-smash.heroParagraph: Wall Smash belongs to the family of brick breakers where you do not control a paddle at all. Instead you get one aimed shot per turn that sends your entire collection of balls ricocheting around the playfield, and every brick carries a number showing how many more hits it needs. The wall advances one row each turn, and the game ends when it reaches you.
instructions: Drag to aim and release to fire. Every ball you own launches along the same line one after another, bounces off the walls and bricks, and eventually returns to the bottom - your turn ends when the last one lands. You get exactly one aiming decision per turn, which is where the whole game lives.

Aim for angles that keep balls in play. A shot fired straight up hits a couple of bricks and comes straight back. A shallow shot into a gap can rattle between a brick and a wall a dozen times, and those trapped ricochets are worth more than any single well-placed hit. Look for pockets rather than targets.

Collect the circular pickups to add balls. Each one permanently increases the size of your stream, and since damage scales with the number of balls, grabbing them is more valuable early than clearing bricks. A player who prioritises pickups in the first ten turns will be far ahead of one who spent those turns tidying the wall.

sections.heading: The numbers are hit points
sections.body: Each brick shows how many more times it must be struck, and the numbers rise as you get deeper into a run so that a growing wall stays threatening against a growing ball count. That is the game's balance in a single mechanic - your damage scales, so the health scales with it, and the tension stays roughly constant no matter how long you survive.

sections.heading: One decision per turn
sections.body: Stripping the interaction down to a single angle makes this a puzzle rather than a test of reflexes. Nothing is timed, you can consider a shot for as long as you like, and there is always a best answer if you can find it. That is why the genre works so well on a phone and equally well on a school Chromebook - it asks for thought rather than dexterity.

sections.heading: Clear the sides, not the middle
sections.body: Bricks against the left and right walls are the ones that create long ricochet chains, because a ball trapped between brick and wall keeps scoring. Clearing the centre first feels productive and usually is not - it opens a corridor your balls fly straight through. Experienced players deliberately leave a centre column standing to bounce off.

sections.heading: Knowing when to stop building
sections.body: There comes a point in every run where the wall is one row from the bottom and the correct play switches from collecting pickups to simply destroying whatever is lowest. Recognising that moment is the difference between a good score and a run that ends with a large ball count and no board left. The Personal Best counter is there to make you feel it.

sections.heading: Built for both mouse and touch
sections.body: The aiming interaction is a drag, which works identically with a mouse and a finger, and the layout is a tall single column rather than a wide field. That means the game plays the same on a phone as it does on a desktop, with no separate mobile version and no controls that only make sense with a keyboard.

wall-smash.plainText: Wall Smash is a browser brick-breaking puzzle game in which the player does not control a paddle. Each turn you drag to aim a single line and release to fire your entire collection of balls along it; they ricochet around the playfield and the turn ends when the last ball returns to the bottom. Every brick displays a number indicating how many more hits it requires, and the wall advances one row per turn, ending the game if it reaches the bottom. Circular pickups permanently add balls to the stream, increasing damage output, and collecting them early is generally more valuable than clearing bricks. Shots aimed into narrow gaps and along the side walls produce long ricochet chains worth far more than direct hits. The game is untimed and uses a drag-to-aim control that works with both mouse and touch. A score and personal best are tracked.

sonic-the-hedgehog.name: Sonic the Hedgehog
sonic-the-hedgehog.title: Sonic the Hedgehog Unblocked - Play the Genesis Classic Free | Schplay
sonic-the-hedgehog.metaDescription: Sega's 1991 platformer that built a console around speed. Green Hill Zone, rings as health, and six zones of momentum.
sonic-the-hedgehog.metaKeywords: sonic the hedgehog, sonic unblocked, sega genesis sonic, green hill zone, mega drive, 1991 platformer, schplay sonic
sonic-the-hedgehog.heroParagraph: Sonic the Hedgehog was Sega's answer to Mario and the reason the Genesis sold. It opens on Green Hill Zone Act 1 with three lives and a score of zero, and within seconds it is doing the thing nothing else on a console did in 1991 - moving a character across the screen fast enough that the level design has to be built around momentum rather than precision.
instructions: Run with the left and right arrows and jump with X or Z. Hold down while moving to curl into a roll, which lets you carry speed through low gaps and damages enemies on contact. Note that there is no spin dash in this first game - that was added in Sonic 2, so building speed here means using slopes and running room.

Rings are your health. Getting hit while holding at least one ring scatters them instead of killing you, and you can grab some back before they vanish. Getting hit with zero rings costs a life. That single rule is why collecting rings matters even when you are not chasing a score - one ring is the difference between a mistake and a death.

Fifty rings at the end of an act opens the Special Stage. Touch the giant ring after the signpost and you enter a rotating maze for a Chaos Emerald; collecting all six is the only way to see the good ending. The stages are disorienting by design, so treat the first few attempts as learning how the rotation works.

sections.heading: Speed is a reward, not the default
sections.body: The common misreading of Sonic is that you hold right and go fast. In practice the game gives you speed when you have earned it with a clean line - the loops and slopes convert momentum you already had. Running blindly into a spike pit or a crab is how most first runs end. The design wants you to learn a zone, then run it fast, which is much closer to a racing game than to Mario.

sections.heading: Six zones, three acts each
sections.body: Green Hill, Marble, Spring Yard, Labyrinth, Star Light and Scrap Brain each run three acts with a Robotnik fight at the end of the third. The pacing deliberately varies - Marble and Labyrinth slow you down almost completely, which players either read as a welcome change of rhythm or as the worst parts of the game. Labyrinth's drowning timer in particular is the most complained-about sequence in the series.

sections.heading: The drowning music
sections.body: Staying underwater too long starts a countdown accompanied by a piece of music that a generation of players can still hum from memory. Air bubbles released from vents refill the timer, and the mechanic is genuinely tense because the music tells you exactly how much time you have left without a number on screen - a very neat piece of design that happens to be traumatic.

sections.heading: Why Sega needed this game
sections.body: The Genesis was competing against a Nintendo console with Mario on it, and Sega needed a mascot and a technical showcase in one product. Sonic delivered both: an attitude-forward character to put on packaging, and a demonstration that the hardware could move large sprites across scrolling backgrounds faster than the competition. The console's fortunes in the West turned on it.

sections.heading: No save, so plan your session
sections.body: There is no battery save and no password system - a run is meant to be completed in one sitting, arcade style. Continues earned at 100 rings are the only safety net. The emulator's save states are the practical answer if you want to see Scrap Brain without committing an uninterrupted hour, and using them is a reasonable choice rather than a cheat.

sonic-the-hedgehog.plainText: Sonic the Hedgehog is a 1991 Sega Genesis platformer built around speed and momentum. Run with the left and right arrow keys, jump with X or Z, and hold down while moving to roll into a ball that damages enemies and fits through low gaps. This first game has no spin dash, which was introduced in Sonic 2. Rings act as health: being hit while carrying rings scatters them rather than costing a life, while being hit with none is fatal. Finishing an act with fifty or more rings opens a Special Stage containing a Chaos Emerald, and collecting all six is required for the best ending. The game has six zones of three acts each, ending with a Robotnik boss fight. Underwater sections have a drowning timer refilled by air bubbles. There is no save or password system.

sonic-spinball.name: Sonic Spinball
sonic-spinball.title: Sonic Spinball Unblocked - Play the Genesis Pinball Game Free | Schplay
sonic-spinball.metaDescription: Sega's 1993 pinball spin-off where Sonic is the ball. Four multi-level tables, hidden Chaos Emeralds and a brutal difficulty curve.
sonic-spinball.metaKeywords: sonic spinball, sonic spinball unblocked, sega genesis pinball, sonic pinball, mega drive 1993, schplay sonic spinball
sonic-spinball.heroParagraph: Sonic Spinball takes the observation that Sonic curls into a ball and builds an entire pinball game out of it. You are the ball, the tables are enormous multi-level structures inside Robotnik's fortress, and you can also get out and walk around when you land somewhere solid. It is a strange hybrid, and it is considerably harder than the platformers it spun off from.
instructions: The left and right arrows work the flippers - each side independently, exactly as on a real table. Pull the plunger with down to launch. When Sonic comes to rest on a platform you can walk him around with the arrows and jump with X or Z, which is how you reach switches that the ball physics alone will not get you to.

Collect the Chaos Emeralds hidden in each table. Every stage has several, usually locked behind a sequence of bumpers or switches you need to trigger in order, and collecting them all opens the exit to the next table. The game will not tell you where they are - exploring the table's dead ends is the actual objective.

Learn the table before chasing points. Each of the four stages is a fixed structure with specific routes upward, and knowing which flipper shot sends you to which level is worth far more than reacting quickly. Losing the ball down the drain sends you back down through the table, so progress is measured in how reliably you can climb.

sections.heading: Pinball that you also platform in
sections.body: The hybrid is the whole idea. Pure pinball would not need Sonic; a pure platformer would not need flippers. By letting you walk when you land and roll when you launch, the game makes the table into a level you explore rather than a scoreboard you feed. It does not fully succeed - the walking sections are stiff - but it is a genuinely unusual design rather than a cash-in.

sections.heading: Four tables, each a fortress floor
sections.body: Toxic Caves, Lava Powerhouse, The Machine and Showdown escalate in size and complexity, and each has its own hazards - toxic sludge that rises, lava, crushing machinery. The later tables are large enough that you can lose track of where the exit is entirely, which is where a lot of players stop. The difficulty is less about reflexes than about map knowledge.

sections.heading: Made fast, and it shows
sections.body: Sonic Spinball was developed on a compressed schedule to fill a gap in Sega's release calendar, and the results are uneven: the physics are heavier than the mainline games, the animation is rougher, and the difficulty was not smoothed out. It is still worth playing for the concept, but going in expecting the polish of Sonic 2 will lead to disappointment.

sections.heading: The soundtrack is a highlight
sections.body: Howard Drossin's score is widely considered the best thing about the game - heavier and more rock-influenced than the mainline Sonic music, and a good demonstration of what the Genesis FM chip could do in the right hands. Toxic Caves in particular gets cited regularly in discussions of Genesis music.

sections.heading: Bonus stages between tables
sections.body: Clearing a table sends you to a bonus stage where you can rack up extra points and lives against a simpler layout. They are a useful breather and the most reliable place to build up a stock of lives before attempting the next fortress floor, which matters because the later tables will consume them quickly.

sonic-spinball.plainText: Sonic Spinball is a 1993 Sega Genesis pinball game in which Sonic himself is the ball, set across four multi-level tables inside Robotnik's fortress. The left and right arrow keys control the flippers on each side independently, the down arrow operates the plunger, and X or Z jumps when Sonic is standing on a platform, allowing him to walk and reach switches. Each table hides several Chaos Emeralds, usually behind sequences of bumpers and switches, and collecting them all opens the exit to the next table. The four stages are Toxic Caves, Lava Powerhouse, The Machine and Showdown, each with their own hazards. Bonus stages between tables award extra points and lives. The soundtrack was composed by Howard Drossin.

super-mario-world.name: Super Mario World
super-mario-world.title: Super Mario World Unblocked - Play the SNES Classic Free Online | Schplay
super-mario-world.metaDescription: Nintendo's SNES launch platformer. Yoshi, the cape, 96 exits and a world map full of secrets.
super-mario-world.metaKeywords: super mario world, super mario world unblocked, snes mario, yoshi, cape feather, 96 exits, nintendo, schplay mario world
super-mario-world.heroParagraph: Super Mario World shipped with the SNES and its title screen carries a 1990 and 1991 copyright, marking the Japanese and North American releases. It introduced Yoshi and the cape, and it replaced the linear world list of earlier Mario games with a map full of branching paths and secret exits - there are 96 in total, and finding them all is a genuinely long undertaking.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and hold X to run. Holding X is not optional - Mario's running speed is required for most long jumps, and the same button picks up and throws shells and blocks. The spin jump on S bounces off enemies that would normally hurt you and breaks blocks beneath you.

Ride Yoshi and use his tongue. Yoshi eats most enemies, and swallowing different coloured shells grants different abilities - a red shell lets him spit fire, a blue one lets him fly. You keep Yoshi between levels if you finish carrying him, and losing him is usually worse than losing a power-up.

The cape is the best item in the game. With a running start you can take off and stay airborne almost indefinitely by alternating dive and climb, which trivialises many levels and is essential for reaching some secret exits. Learning the rhythm - tap to climb as you lose height - takes a few minutes and changes the whole game.

sections.heading: 96 exits, not 96 levels
sections.body: The counter people chase is exits, not stages, because many levels have a hidden second goal behind a secret route. Finding them opens new paths on the world map, including the Star Road shortcuts and the Special World. It is the first Mario game to make exploration of the map itself a mechanic, and it is why the game sustains a hundred hours where its predecessors sustained ten.

sections.heading: Yoshi changed the series permanently
sections.body: Yoshi debuted here as a rideable mount with a tongue that eats almost anything, and he has been a fixture of Nintendo since. Mechanically he functions as an extra hit point that runs away when struck, which creates the specific panic of chasing a fleeing Yoshi across a level. He also lets you cross gaps by sacrificing him mid-air, a move the game never teaches you.

sections.heading: The Star Road and the Special World
sections.body: Hidden exits lead to the Star Road, a set of warp points connecting distant parts of the map, and through it to the Special World - eight brutally difficult levels with names like Tubular and Awesome. Finishing them changes the game's palette and turns the Koopas into Mario masks, which is a strange and memorable reward for the hardest content in the game.

sections.heading: A launch title that defined a console
sections.body: Shipping with the hardware meant Super Mario World was most people's first SNES experience, and it was built to show off what the machine could do - larger sprites, smooth parallax scrolling and a much bigger colour palette than the NES. That it remains one of the best-regarded platformers ever made, rather than merely a good demo, is unusual for a launch game.

super-mario-world.plainText: Super Mario World is a 1991 SNES platformer by Nintendo, released alongside the console, with a title screen carrying 1990 and 1991 copyrights for the Japanese and North American releases. Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z, hold X to run and to pick up and throw items, and press S for a spin jump that bounces off otherwise dangerous enemies and breaks blocks. Yoshi can be ridden and eats enemies with his tongue; swallowing coloured shells grants abilities such as spitting fire or flying. The cape feather allows sustained flight by alternating diving and climbing and is required to reach several secret exits. The game contains 96 exits rather than 96 levels, since many stages hide a second goal that opens new routes on the world map, including the Star Road and the Special World. It uses a battery save.

super-mario-land-2.heroParagraph: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins is where Wario came from. Mario returns from his previous adventure to find his castle seized by a rival who has scattered six golden coins across the island, and the game hands you a map where the six zones can be taken in almost any order. It looks and plays far closer to Super Mario World than to the first Super Mario Land.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and hold X to run. The physics here are much closer to the mainline console games than to the original Super Mario Land, which had a distinctly odd feel - jumps arc predictably and Mario has proper momentum, so anything you learned from Super Mario World transfers.

Find the six golden coins. Each is guarded by the boss at the end of one of six themed zones - the Tree, the Space, the Macro, the Pumpkin, the Mario and the Turtle zones - and you need all six before the castle will open. Because the zones are largely non-linear, a zone that is giving you trouble can simply be left for later.

Get the carrot. Alongside the mushroom and fire flower there is a carrot power-up that gives Mario rabbit ears and lets him slow his descent and glide, which is the single most useful item for reaching hidden areas. Bonus stages between levels let you gamble coins for extra lives and power-ups.

sections.heading: Wario's first appearance
sections.body: Wario was created for this game as a rival built specifically to be Mario's opposite, and he is the final boss of it. He proved popular enough to take over the series entirely - the next game in this line was Wario Land, starring him. Very few villains introduced as a one-off end up displacing the protagonist, which makes this a notable piece of Nintendo history rather than just a good handheld platformer.

sections.heading: A map you can take in your own order
sections.body: The overworld lets you approach most zones freely rather than in a fixed sequence, which was unusual for a handheld platformer in 1992 and does a lot to reduce frustration. If the Space Zone's low gravity is not working for you, go and do the Pumpkin Zone instead. That structure is closer to Mega Man's stage select than to a traditional Mario world list.

sections.heading: Bigger sprites, better feel
sections.body: The first Super Mario Land used tiny sprites and idiosyncratic physics because the developers were working on unfamiliar hardware. This sequel doubles the character size and rebuilds the movement to match the console games, and the difference is immediate. It is one of the clearest examples of a team's second attempt on a platform being transformatively better than the first.

sections.heading: Generous by design
sections.body: There are a lot of extra lives available, the bonus games hand out more, and the game saves your progress - which together make it noticeably gentler than most Mario titles of the era. That was deliberate for a handheld played in short bursts on a bus, and it means the game can be finished by players who would bounce off Super Mario World's later levels.

sections.heading: Monochrome, as released
sections.body: This runs as the original Game Boy release rather than a Color version, in the four shades of grey the artists actually drew for. The larger sprite size was partly a response to that constraint - detail has to come from silhouette rather than colour, which is why the characters here read so clearly at a glance.

super-mario-land-2.plainText: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins is a 1992 Game Boy platformer by Nintendo and the first appearance of Wario, who serves as the final boss. Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and hold X to run and throw fireballs when powered up. Mario must collect six golden coins, each held by the boss of one of six themed zones which can largely be tackled in any order from an overworld map, before the castle can be entered. Alongside the mushroom and fire flower, a carrot power-up gives Mario rabbit ears allowing him to slow his descent and glide. Bonus stages between levels award extra lives and power-ups. The game uses larger sprites and physics much closer to the console Mario games than the original Super Mario Land, and it saves progress.
