kirbys-dream-land-2.heroParagraph: Kirby's Dream Land 2 is the handheld sequel that brought copy abilities to the Game Boy and added something the console games did not have: three animal friends who change how each power works. Swallow an enemy to take its ability, then ride a hamster, an owl or a fish, and the same ability behaves completely differently. It turns seven powers into a much larger set.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z and inhale with X. Pressing down while a swallowed enemy is in your mouth copies its ability instead of spitting it out - that is the central mechanic and the thing missing from the first Dream Land. You can drop an ability at any time to pick up a different one.

Find and ride the animal friends. Rick the hamster gives you grip on ice and slopes, Kine the fish swims properly against currents, and Coo the owl flies steadily through wind that would blow Kirby around. Each also modifies whatever ability you are carrying, so a spark power on Coo is a different weapon to a spark power on foot.

Collect the Rainbow Drops to see the true ending. They are hidden one per world behind puzzles that usually require a specific ability and a specific animal friend together, which is the game's real challenge. Finishing without them gives you a shorter, unsatisfying conclusion, so exploring properly is worth the time.

sections.heading: Abilities times animals
sections.body: There are seven copy abilities and three animal friends, and almost every combination produces a distinct attack - burning while riding Kine is not the same as burning on foot. That multiplication is how a Game Boy game gets a movelist much larger than its memory should allow, and it is the reason this entry is remembered fondly rather than as a smaller Kirby's Adventure.

sections.heading: The animal friends solve terrain
sections.body: Each friend is really a movement solution to a specific hazard: Rick for slippery ground, Kine for strong currents, Coo for wind. Levels are built with those hazards in mind, so part of the puzzle is noticing which friend a section wants and going back for them. Losing a friend to a hit is a genuine setback rather than a minor inconvenience.

sections.heading: Dark Matter, and a series arc beginning
sections.body: The true final boss is Dark Matter, an entity possessing King Dedede rather than Dedede himself, and it is the start of a story thread that continues through Dream Land 3 and Kirby 64. For a series usually treated as self-contained and cheerful, this trilogy has a surprisingly consistent through-line, and it starts here.

sections.heading: How it sits against the first game
sections.body: Kirby's Dream Land was deliberately built as an easy entry point with no copy abilities at all. This sequel keeps the accessible surface - unlimited flight, plentiful health - while putting the real challenge in optional collection. That two-layer approach became the standard Kirby design and it works particularly well here, because the Rainbow Drop puzzles are genuinely difficult.

sections.heading: Monochrome with Super Game Boy support
sections.body: The cartridge is Super Game Boy enhanced, meaning it offered a colour palette and border when played through that accessory on a SNES. Running as a plain Game Boy title here, it displays in the original four-shade greyscale - which is how most people played it, and how the sprite work was designed to read.

kirbys-dream-land-2.plainText: Kirby's Dream Land 2 is a 1995 Game Boy platformer by HAL Laboratory and the first handheld Kirby game with copy abilities. Move with the arrow keys, jump with Z, inhale with X and press down while holding an enemy to copy its ability rather than spitting it out. Kirby can float indefinitely by gulping air. Three animal friends can be ridden: Rick the hamster grips ice and slopes, Kine the fish swims against currents and Coo the owl flies steadily through wind, and each modifies the behaviour of whichever copy ability Kirby is carrying. Hidden Rainbow Drops, one per world, usually require a specific combination of ability and animal friend, and collecting them all is required for the true ending against the final boss Dark Matter, who is possessing King Dedede.

donkey-kong-land.metaDescription: Rare's 1995 Game Boy platformer. Pre-rendered ape sprites squeezed onto four shades of grey, with all-new levels.
donkey-kong-land.metaKeywords: donkey kong land, donkey kong game boy, rare 1995, diddy kong, dk land, handheld platformer, schplay donkey kong land
donkey-kong-land.heroParagraph: Donkey Kong Land is Rare taking the pre-rendered 3D look of Donkey Kong Country and forcing it onto a Game Boy screen with four shades of grey. It should not work, and the fact that it does is the most interesting thing about it. This is not a port - the levels are entirely new, built for a smaller screen and a machine with a fraction of the power.
instructions: Run with the arrow keys, jump with Z and hold X to run and roll. Rolling off the end of a platform and jumping mid-roll extends your jump distance considerably, which is the technique the level design assumes you know - several gaps simply cannot be crossed without it.

Swap between Donkey and Diddy with V. Donkey is heavier and can defeat larger enemies with a ground slap, while Diddy is faster and jumps further. Losing one leaves you playing as the other alone, and finding a DK barrel restores your partner - so a barrel is effectively an extra life.

Watch the screen size, not the level. The Game Boy's small viewport is the real difficulty here: enemies and pits appear with much less warning than they would on a television, so the safe approach is to move deliberately and let the screen scroll ahead of you rather than running blind.

sections.heading: How the graphics work at all
sections.body: The Country games rendered 3D models and converted them to sprites, which gave them a distinctive pre-rendered look. Doing that with four shades of grey on a screen a fraction of the size meant reducing each character to a readable silhouette with just enough shading to suggest volume. The result is dense and occasionally hard to read, but as a technical exercise it is remarkable.

sections.heading: New levels, not a port
sections.body: Rare built original stages rather than shrinking the console game's, which is why Donkey Kong Land has its own identity. Some sections are noticeably harder than anything in Country, partly because the smaller screen removes reaction time. Treat it as a third game in the series rather than as a portable version of the first.

sections.heading: Barrels, and the animal buddies
sections.body: Barrels are throwable weapons, containers for your missing partner and, in blast form, level transport. Rambi the rhino and Expresso the ostrich return as rideable animal buddies with their own movement rules. Learning which barrels are worth carrying to the next screen instead of throwing immediately is a real part of playing well.

sections.heading: A password system
sections.body: Progress is kept with passwords rather than a battery save, so write yours down before closing the tab. It is worth noting that the emulator's own save states work alongside this and are considerably more convenient - the password system was designed for a machine you turned off rather than a browser tab you might close accidentally.

sections.heading: Part of a Game Boy trilogy
sections.body: Donkey Kong Land was followed by two sequels that loosely paralleled Donkey Kong Country 2 and 3, forming a handheld trilogy of their own. This first entry is the roughest of the three and the most impressive technically, since it established that the Country look could be done on the hardware at all.

donkey-kong-land.plainText: Donkey Kong Land is a 1995 Game Boy platformer developed by Rare, adapting the pre-rendered sprite style of Donkey Kong Country to the Game Boy's four-shade greyscale display with entirely new levels rather than ported ones. Run with the arrow keys, jump with Z, and hold X to run, roll and pick up barrels; jumping out of a roll extends jump distance and is required for several gaps. Press V to swap between Donkey Kong and Diddy Kong, who differ in weight, speed and jump distance, and DK barrels restore a lost partner. Barrels serve as weapons, containers and transport, and the animal buddies Rambi the rhino and Expresso the ostrich can be ridden. Progress is saved using passwords rather than a battery. Two sequels followed on the same hardware.

super-mario-kart.metaDescription: Nintendo's 1992 SNES original that invented the kart racer. Eight drivers, twenty tracks, power slides and a split screen throughout.
super-mario-kart.metaKeywords: super mario kart, super mario kart unblocked, snes mario kart, mode 7 racing, power slide, battle mode, schplay mario kart
super-mario-kart.heroParagraph: Super Mario Kart invented an entire genre, and its title screen carries a 1992 Nintendo copyright. Eight drivers, twenty tracks and a set of items designed to punish whoever is winning - every kart racer since has been built from these parts. It is also noticeably harder and more technical than its descendants, because power sliding here is a skill rather than an assist.
instructions: Accelerate with Z, steer with the arrows and use items with X. The shoulder buttons on Q and E make your kart hop, and holding one while turning starts a power slide. Mastering the slide is not optional - the AI drivers use it constantly, and taking corners without it will lose you several seconds a lap.

Coins are speed. Collecting coins scattered on the track raises your top speed, and getting hit costs you some. That mechanic disappeared from later Mario Kart games for decades, and it means the racing line here is not just the fastest path but the one that picks up coins without leaving the tarmac.

The screen is always split. Even in single player the bottom half shows a map or a rival, because the game was built around two-player racing on one television. That halves your forward visibility compared to a modern kart game, so learning tracks matters more than reacting to what appears.

sections.heading: Mode 7 again, this time with two players
sections.body: Like F-Zero, Super Mario Kart uses the SNES's Mode 7 background scaling to fake a 3D track. Doing it in split screen for two players simultaneously was the harder trick, and it is the reason the viewport is arranged the way it is. Everything on the track - karts, items, obstacles - is a flat sprite drawn over that rotating plane.

sections.heading: Battle Mode was the point for many players
sections.body: Four arenas, two players, three balloons each and a pile of shells. Battle Mode has no laps and no finish line, and for a great many households it was played far more than the Grand Prix. It is the clearest demonstration that Mario Kart was designed as a multiplayer game with a single-player mode attached rather than the reverse.

sections.heading: The AI cheats, and knowing that helps
sections.body: Computer drivers in this game have rubber-banded speed and infinite character-specific items - Bowser throws endless fireballs, Toad drops endless mushrooms - regardless of item boxes. Understanding that the AI is not playing by your rules changes how you race: building a lead is less valuable than staying clean, because the field will catch up regardless.

sections.heading: Eight drivers with real stat differences
sections.body: The roster splits into lightweights who accelerate quickly and get pushed around, and heavyweights with higher top speeds that shove others off the road. Because the tracks are narrow and lined with hazards, weight class matters more here than in later entries - a collision that a heavy driver shrugs off will send a light one into the sand.

sections.heading: Where the series went next
sections.body: Everything that followed - Mario Kart 64's four-player split, the blue shell, anti-gravity - is a variation on what this game established: a racing game where skill and chaos are deliberately balanced against each other so that a less skilled player can still win a race. That design choice is why the series outsold nearly every other racing franchise.

super-mario-kart.plainText: Super Mario Kart is a 1992 SNES racing game by Nintendo and the first kart racer, using Mode 7 background scaling to render its tracks. Accelerate with Z, steer with the arrow keys, use items with X, and press the shoulder buttons on Q or E to hop, holding one while turning to power slide. Power sliding is essential for competitive lap times. Coins collected on the track increase top speed and are lost when hit. The screen is split horizontally at all times, including in single player, because the game was designed around two-player racing. Eight drivers are divided into lightweight and heavyweight classes with different acceleration, top speed and collision behaviour. Computer opponents use rubber-banded speed and unlimited character-specific items. A four-arena Battle Mode for two players uses balloons instead of laps.

warios-woods.heroParagraph: Wario's Woods inverts the falling-block puzzle. Instead of steering pieces down from above, you play Toad standing inside the well, picking up monsters and bombs and physically carrying them into position while more rain down on you. It is the only puzzle game of its era where you are a character in the playfield rather than a cursor above it.
instructions: Walk Toad with the arrow keys, pick up and put down stacks with Z, and kick a stack sideways with X. Toad can carry a whole column of pieces at once and climb the walls, so moving material around the well is a physical task with travel time rather than an instant placement.

Match monsters with a bomb. Lining up three or more identical monsters in a row - horizontally, vertically or diagonally - does nothing on its own; you must complete the line with a bomb of the same colour to detonate it. That extra requirement is what separates this from every other match-three of the period.

Clear the whole screen to advance. The objective in each round is to remove every monster, not to survive indefinitely, and Birdo drops more material as you work. Chaining detonations so one clears into the next produces the large combos the scoring rewards, and it is the only way through the later rounds at speed.

sections.heading: A puzzle game with a body
sections.body: Giving the player a character with walking speed, jump height and climbing ability turns every placement into a small movement problem. You cannot simply decide where a piece goes; you have to get Toad there, carry it, and not be crushed on the way. It makes the game more frantic than Tetris and considerably more physical, which is exactly what makes it distinct.

sections.heading: Bombs are the whole economy
sections.body: Because a line only clears when a matching bomb completes it, bombs are the scarce resource and everything else is arrangement. Good play means building lines that are ready and waiting for the bomb colour you expect, rather than reacting to what falls. Wasting a bomb on a two-monster line is the most common beginner error.

sections.heading: The last licensed NES game in North America
sections.body: Wario's Woods holds an odd distinction: the NES version was the final officially licensed release for that console in North America, arriving in 1994 when the SNES had long since taken over. This is the SNES version, which has more elaborate presentation, an animated Birdo dropping pieces and a two-player versus mode the NES version handles differently.

sections.heading: Toad as a protagonist
sections.body: Toad almost never headlines a game, and here he is the only playable character in the main mode - Wario is the antagonist and Birdo assists. It is a strange piece of casting that makes more sense once you see the mechanics: the game needs a small, fast character who can carry things and climb, and none of the usual leads fit that description.

sections.heading: Versus mode
sections.body: Two players can compete side by side, with clears on one screen sending trouble to the other in the way the genre demands. It is less famous than Tetris or Puyo Puyo head to head, but the carrying mechanic makes for a very different kind of pressure - you can see your opponent physically scrambling, which is oddly more stressful than watching a stack rise.

warios-woods.plainText: Wario's Woods is a 1994 SNES puzzle game by Nintendo in which the player controls Toad inside the playfield rather than directing falling pieces from above. Lining up three or more identical monsters horizontally, vertically or diagonally does not clear them - the line must be completed with a bomb of the same colour to detonate. mario-paint.heroParagraph: Mario Paint is not really a game - it is a drawing program, an animation tool and a music sequencer that Nintendo shipped in 1992 with a mouse in the box. Its title screen carries a 1992 copyright and a hand cursor that responds to yours. Decades later it is still the reason people know what a Mario Paint Composer is, because the music tool outlived everything else about it.
instructions: Use your mouse for everything. Mario Paint was designed for the SNES Mouse peripheral, and the emulator maps your ordinary mouse onto it, so the pointer works exactly as intended. There is no keyboard alternative - this is one of the few cartridges that is genuinely unplayable with a gamepad.

Explore the title screen before you start. Almost every letter and object on it responds to being clicked with an animation or a sound, which was Nintendo's way of teaching you that the mouse was the whole interface. It remains one of the most charming introductions to a piece of software anyone has written.

Open the music composer. The stave lets you place notes as Mario characters and objects, each a different instrument, across three octaves with adjustable tempo. It is limited compared to real sequencing software, and that limitation is exactly why people have spent thirty years recreating complex songs inside it.

sections.heading: What is actually in it
sections.body: There are four main tools: a paint program with stamps and a fill bucket, a stamp editor for drawing your own, a frame-by-frame animation tool, and the music composer. There is also a fly-swatting minigame, which is the only conventionally game-like thing on the cartridge and which people played far more than the developers can have expected.

sections.heading: The music tool that would not die
sections.body: Mario Paint's composer has had a long afterlife. Fan-made recreations run in browsers, there are conventions of arrangers who transcribe entire scores into it, and the instrument sounds are recognisable to people who have never touched the original cartridge. Very little software from 1992 has that kind of continuing cultural presence.

sections.heading: Nothing saves without hardware
sections.body: The original cartridge saved your work to battery-backed memory, and losing that was a genuine hazard. In an emulator the save behaviour depends on the browser's storage, so treat anything you make as temporary unless you use the emulator's own save state feature deliberately. It is worth knowing before you spend an hour on a drawing.

sections.heading: Why a mouse was included at all
sections.body: Nintendo bundled the SNES Mouse specifically for this cartridge, and very few other games supported it well - Mario Paint was both the reason to buy the peripheral and almost the only reason. That makes it an unusual artefact: a piece of creative software sold as a game, on a console, to an audience that mostly had no other use for the hardware it shipped with.

sections.heading: The fly swatting minigame
sections.body: Hidden behind an icon on the main screen is Gnat Attack, in which you swat flies with the cursor across three increasingly frantic stages. It exists to give you a reason to practise with the mouse, and it is genuinely difficult in the later waves - enough that it has its own small following independent of the rest of the cartridge.

bloons-tower-defence.heroParagraph: This is the original Bloons Tower Defense from Ninja Kiwi - the game that turned a simple dart-popping browser toy into one of the longest-running tower defence series there is. You start a new game with 650 money and 40 lives, and balloons follow a fixed path across the screen while you build towers beside it to pop them before they reach the end.
instructions: Click a tower in the Build Towers panel and place it next to the path. Five types are available - dart tower, tack shooter, ice tower, bomb tower and super monkey - each with a different range, rate of fire and cost. Towers only attack what passes within their radius, so placement matters more than raw quantity.

Learn the bloon hierarchy. Red bloons are the weakest; blue move faster and contain a red inside; green contain a blue; yellow are faster still; and black bloons are small, slower than yellows, and contain two yellows each. Popping a layer reveals what is inside it, so a wave of blacks is far more work than the count suggests.

Upgrade rather than sprawl. The dart tower's piercing upgrade lets each dart pop up to two bloons instead of one, which effectively doubles that tower's output for far less than a second tower costs. Concentrating upgrades on well-placed towers beats scattering cheap ones around the map.

sections.heading: The ice tower's trade-off
sections.body: The ice tower freezes nearby bloons, which sounds strictly good until you read the detail: frozen bloons are immune to darts and tacks, and only bombs will destroy them. Placing ice next to your dart towers can therefore make your defence worse rather than better. It is the most interesting decision in the game and the one new players most reliably get wrong.

sections.heading: Placement beats purchase
sections.body: The strongest positions are on the inside of tight corners and next to sections where the path doubles back, because a tower there covers two stretches of track at once. A cheap tower in a corner often out-performs an expensive one on a straight. Before buying anything, look at the path shape and find the spots where a single circle of range overlaps the most track.

sections.heading: Where the series went
sections.body: Ninja Kiwi built this out of an earlier Flash game called Bloons, in which you simply threw darts at balloon arrangements. The tower defence version arrived in 2007 and the series has run through six numbered sequels and a large mobile business since, adding monkey specialisations, heroes and towers far beyond these five. The core loop has barely changed.

sections.heading: Money in, lives out
sections.body: Every bloon that reaches the end costs you lives, and every one you pop pays money. That makes the difficulty curve self-correcting in an unusual way: a leak is not just damage, it is lost income that would have funded the towers you need for the next round. Early rounds are where a run is won, because that is where compounding starts.

sections.heading: Flash, running through Ruffle
sections.body: Bloons TD is a Flash game and Flash was discontinued at the end of 2020. It runs here through Ruffle, an open-source Flash player reimplementation written in Rust and served from this site rather than an external CDN, so it works on networks that block outside domains. link-to-the-past.metaDescription: Nintendo's 1991 SNES masterpiece. Two overlapping worlds, the Master Sword, and the template every Zelda since has followed.

link-to-the-past.heroParagraph: A Link to the Past is the game that fixed the Zelda formula in place. Its top-down exploration, its dungeon-item-boss loop and its overworld full of things you cannot reach yet are all still the shape of the series more than thirty years later. It also introduced the idea the game is best known for - a second world laid over the first, where every location has a warped counterpart.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, swing your sword with X and use whatever item you have equipped with Z. The A key is the action button - it lifts pots, throws them, talks to people and, once you have the Pegasus Boots, makes Link run. Press Enter to open the inventory and swap the item on Z.

Cut everything. Bushes, pots and grass hide rupees, hearts and bombs, and the game expects you to be constantly harvesting them - your supply of arrows and bombs comes almost entirely from destroying scenery rather than from shops. It also hides staircases and switches under objects you would otherwise walk past.

Every dungeon gives you the item that beats it. Find the big chest, take what is in it, and the boss at the end will be vulnerable to exactly that. If a boss looks impossible, the answer is nearly always the item you just picked up rather than better reflexes - and that item usually also opens a part of the overworld you could not reach before.

sections.heading: Two worlds stacked on top of each other
sections.body: Partway in, the Dark World opens - a corrupted mirror of the overworld where the geography matches but the terrain does not. A cliff in one world is a bridge in the other, so reaching an unreachable spot means crossing over, walking somewhere, and crossing back. It is a genuinely elegant puzzle structure and it turns the map into two maps that have to be solved together.

sections.heading: The Master Sword sequence
sections.body: The first act builds to pulling the Master Sword from its pedestal in the Lost Woods, which requires three pendants from three dungeons. It is one of the most-copied story beats in games, and the moment it happens the tone of the whole game changes - what looked like a rescue mission becomes something much larger. Everything before it is effectively a long prologue.

sections.heading: Bottles are the best items in the game
sections.body: There are four bottles hidden around the world and they are easy to miss. Each can hold a fairy that revives you automatically on death, or a potion that refills health and magic. Carrying four fairies is effectively four extra lives, and it is the single biggest difference between struggling in the late dungeons and walking through them.

sections.heading: The battery save, and what that meant
sections.body: Three save slots on the cartridge let you stop and come back, which sounds unremarkable now and was a significant design freedom in 1991 - it is why the game could be this large. In the emulator that save lives in your browser rather than on a chip, so the emulator's own save states are worth using alongside it for anything you would be upset to lose.

sections.heading: Why people still start here
sections.body: For a lot of players this is the recommended entry point to the series - it is more readable than the NES original, less demanding than the 3D games, and short enough to finish. The pacing is unusually good: every twenty minutes something opens up, and the game almost never leaves you without a clear next thing to try.

link-to-the-past.plainText: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past is a 1991 SNES action adventure by Nintendo that established the template for the series. Move with the arrow keys, swing the sword with X, use the equipped item with Z, and use A as the action button for lifting, throwing, talking and running with the Pegasus Boots; Enter opens the inventory. Cutting bushes, grass and pots yields rupees, hearts, arrows and bombs and reveals hidden passages. Each dungeon contains an item in its big chest that is used to defeat that dungeon's boss and opens new areas of the overworld. Partway through, the Dark World opens as a mirrored version of the map where terrain differs, requiring the player to travel between worlds to reach otherwise inaccessible locations. Four hidden bottles can store fairies that automatically revive Link. The game uses a battery save with three slots.

metal-gear-solid.name: Metal Gear Solid: Ghost Babel
metal-gear-solid.title: Metal Gear Solid Ghost Babel Unblocked - Play the Game Boy Classic | Schplay
metal-gear-solid.metaDescription: Konami's 2000 handheld Metal Gear, widely rated one of the best Game Boy Color games ever made. Top-down stealth done properly.
metal-gear-solid.metaKeywords: metal gear solid, ghost babel, metal gear game boy, konami 2000, stealth game, solid snake, schplay metal gear
metal-gear-solid.heroParagraph: Released in the West as Metal Gear Solid and known in Japan as Ghost Babel, this is a handheld Metal Gear built from scratch for the Game Boy Color rather than a port of the PlayStation game. It is regularly named among the best titles on the system, and it works because it went back to the top-down stealth of the MSX originals instead of trying to shrink a 3D game onto a two-inch screen.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, attack with X and use your equipped item with Z. Press Enter to open the menu where weapons and items are equipped separately - you always have one of each active, and switching quickly between them is most of the moment-to-moment play.

Watch the guards' vision cones and stay out of them. Getting spotted triggers an alert that brings reinforcements, and the correct response to an alert is almost always to break line of sight and hide until it times out rather than to fight. Flattening against a wall lets you peer around corners without stepping into view.

Use the Codec constantly. Calling your support team gives hints about the area you are in, the boss you are stuck on and the equipment you should be carrying. The game hides a great deal of its guidance behind optional conversations, and players who never call tend to conclude it is more obtuse than it is.

sections.heading: Top-down stealth, deliberately
sections.body: Rather than emulate the PlayStation game's camera, Ghost Babel returns to the overhead view of Metal Gear and Metal Gear 2 on the MSX2. That choice is why it works - stealth needs you to see the guard patrols you are avoiding, and a small screen with a fixed overhead view communicates that far better than a cramped 3D camera could.

sections.heading: A story that is not quite canon
sections.body: Ghost Babel is set in an alternate continuity branching after the first Metal Gear, which is why the Japanese title is different from the Western one. Kojima supervised rather than directed it. That freedom let the writers tell a self-contained story with its own cast and ending rather than fitting into an increasingly complicated timeline.

sections.heading: Thirteen levels and a lot of extra modes
sections.body: The main campaign runs thirteen stages, but the cartridge also carries a large VR training mode with over a hundred missions covering sneaking, weapons and puzzle scenarios. That bulk is unusual for a handheld game of the period and it is why the cartridge has a reputation for value as well as quality.

sections.heading: Boss fights on a small screen
sections.body: The bosses are the standout sequences - each is a pattern puzzle fought in a confined arena with a specific weapon or tactic as the answer. Because the viewport is small, the designers had to make every tell readable at a glance, and the result is a set of fights that are legible and fair in a way a lot of larger stealth games are not.

sections.heading: Colour, and the hardware it needs
sections.body: This is a Game Boy Color title rather than an original monochrome Game Boy game, so it runs in full colour and uses the extra processing the hardware offered. The emulator here runs it on the Game Boy core, which handles Color cartridges, so what you see is the palette the artists actually worked with.

metal-gear-solid.plainText: Metal Gear Solid: Ghost Babel is a 2000 Game Boy Color stealth action game by Konami, released in the West as Metal Gear Solid. It uses a top-down view following the MSX Metal Gear games rather than adapting the PlayStation title's 3D camera. Move with the arrow keys, attack with X, use the equipped item with Z, open the menu with Enter and access the Codec with V. Weapons and items are equipped separately. Guards have vision cones and being spotted triggers an alert that summons reinforcements; breaking line of sight and hiding ends the alert. Pressing against walls allows peering around corners. Codec conversations provide hints about areas, bosses and equipment. The campaign runs thirteen stages and the cartridge includes a VR training mode with over a hundred missions. The story is set in an alternate continuity branching after the first Metal Gear.

the-legend-of-zelda.name: The Legend of Zelda
the-legend-of-zelda.title: The Legend of Zelda Unblocked - Play the NES Original Free Online | Schplay
the-legend-of-zelda.metaDescription: Nintendo's 1986 original, running as the Classic NES Series GBA release. Eight dungeons, no map markers, and a world that never tells you where to go.
the-legend-of-zelda.metaKeywords: legend of zelda, zelda nes unblocked, classic nes series, hyrule, triforce, nintendo 1986, schplay zelda
the-legend-of-zelda.heroParagraph: The Legend of Zelda is where open-world design starts. Ganon has stolen the Triforce of Power, Zelda has broken the Triforce of Wisdom into eight pieces, and the game drops you into Hyrule with a sword and no instructions whatsoever. This cartridge is the Classic NES Series release for Game Boy Advance, which is the original game with a save feature attached.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys, swing your sword with Z and use your selected item with X. Press Enter to open the subscreen and choose which item sits on X - you can only have one active at a time, so switching between the bow, the boomerang and the candle is a constant part of play.

Burn bushes and bomb walls. A great many entrances in Hyrule are hidden behind scenery, and the game never marks them. The candle sets bushes alight and bombs open cracked walls; if you are stuck, the answer is usually a suspicious-looking rock face or a lone bush in an odd place.

Your sword only fires beams at full health. At full hearts Link throws his sword as a projectile, and losing a single heart takes that away - which means health is offensive capability, not just survival. Fairies and potions matter more than they look, and the blue candle, the raft and the ladder open large parts of the map.

sections.heading: A world with no guidance at all
sections.body: There is no quest marker, no map objective and no character telling you where dungeon three is. The game expects you to explore, take notes and share findings with friends - which is exactly what happened in 1986 and is the reason Nintendo shipped it with a fold-out map. Playing it now, the honest advice is to accept that wandering is the intended activity rather than a failure state.

sections.heading: Eight dungeons and a second quest
sections.body: Nine labyrinths hold the Triforce pieces and Ganon, each with its own map, compass and item. Finish the game and a Second Quest unlocks with entirely rearranged dungeons and harder enemies - effectively a whole extra game hidden inside the cartridge, which was an extraordinary amount of content for the hardware.

sections.heading: Why this is the GBA version
sections.body: This is a Classic NES Series cartridge, the line Nintendo released for Game Boy Advance in the early 2000s. The game itself is unchanged, but the GBA release adds a save feature and displays at the GBA's slightly different aspect. It is the original in every way that matters, with the convenience of not needing to write down a password.

sections.heading: The first battery save in a console game
sections.body: The NES cartridge shipped with a battery-backed save chip, which was close to unheard of and is a large part of why a game this long could exist on the hardware at all. Everything about the design - the size of Hyrule, the number of dungeons - depends on being able to stop and come back, and that is a technical decision shaping a creative one.

sections.heading: It's dangerous to go alone
sections.body: The old man in the first cave hands you a sword with a line that has outlived nearly every other piece of writing on the console. It is also a genuine piece of design: the game puts a cave directly in front of your starting position so that the first thing you learn is that caves contain useful things, which is the lesson the entire rest of Hyrule depends on.

the-legend-of-zelda.plainText: The Legend of Zelda is Nintendo's 1986 action adventure and an early open-world design, presented here as the Classic NES Series release for Game Boy Advance, which adds a save feature to the unchanged original. Move with the arrow keys, swing the sword with Z, use the selected item with X, and press Enter to open the subscreen and change which item is equipped. The game provides no quest markers or directions. Many entrances are hidden and must be revealed by burning bushes with the candle or bombing cracked walls. Link's sword fires a projectile beam only at full health. Nine labyrinths contain the eight Triforce pieces and Ganon, each holding a map, compass and item. Completing the game unlocks a Second Quest with rearranged dungeons. The original NES cartridge used a battery save.

bomberman.name: Bomberman
bomberman.title: Bomberman Unblocked - Play the NES Original Free Online | Schplay
bomberman.metaDescription: Hudson Soft's 1987 original, running as the Classic NES Series GBA release. Fifty stages, one exit each, and a robot trying to become human.
bomberman.metaKeywords: bomberman, bomberman nes unblocked, hudson soft 1987, classic nes series, maze bombing game, schplay bomberman
bomberman.heroParagraph: This is the Bomberman that started it all - Hudson Soft's 1987 NES release, here as the Classic NES Series cartridge for Game Boy Advance. Unlike the multiplayer battles the series became famous for, the original is a single-player game about a robot working through fifty stages of a maze, blowing up walls to find the exit hidden underneath one of them.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys and drop a bomb with X. Bombs detonate in a cross after a short delay and destroy soft blocks, enemies and you without discrimination. Every stage is a grid of indestructible pillars and destructible blocks, and you are looking for the door concealed beneath one of the blocks.

Clear all the enemies before you take the exit. Reaching the door without killing everything does not complete the stage, so the objective is really two objectives: find the exit and clear the field. Blowing up the door itself with a bomb spawns extra enemies, so be careful where you place things once you have found it.

Collect the power-ups hidden under blocks. Fire extends your blast, extra bombs let you place more at once, and the remote control lets you detonate on your own timing with Z instead of waiting for the fuse. There are also hazardous items in some versions, so grabbing everything without thinking is not always correct.

sections.heading: Before it was a party game
sections.body: The multiplayer Battle Mode that defines Bomberman for most people came later. This original is a solo maze game with a time limit per stage, closer in feel to a puzzle arcade title than to the four-player chaos of the SNES entries. Playing it makes clear how much the series changed while keeping identical mechanics.

sections.heading: The robot who wants to be human
sections.body: The original game's premise is that Bomberman is a robot labouring in an underground bomb factory who has been told that escaping to the surface will turn him human. It connects to Hudson's earlier game Lode Runner - reaching the surface turns him into that game's protagonist, which is a piece of shared-universe writing nobody expected from a maze game.

sections.heading: Fifty stages and a strict timer
sections.body: Each stage has a countdown, and running it down spawns extra enemies rather than simply ending the level, which punishes cautious play. The practical approach is to bomb efficiently in straight lines from safe positions rather than clearing the field neatly - you rarely have time to be tidy.

sections.heading: Why the Classic NES Series version
sections.body: Nintendo's Classic NES Series reissued a set of NES games on Game Boy Advance cartridges in the early 2000s, unchanged apart from the addition of saving and the GBA's screen dimensions. It is the original game rather than a remake, which matters for a title whose appeal is entirely in its 1987 design.

sections.heading: Thinking in lines
sections.body: As in every Bomberman since, blasts travel along the row and column a bomb sits in, so safety is a matter of standing behind a hard pillar or around a corner rather than merely far away. The single most common death in this game is walking back into a corridor that a bomb you had forgotten about is pointing straight down.

bomberman.plainText: Bomberman is Hudson Soft's original 1987 NES maze action game, presented here as the Classic NES Series release for Game Boy Advance. Move with the arrow keys and drop bombs with X; bombs explode in a cross pattern after a delay and destroy soft blocks, enemies and the player. Each of the fifty stages hides an exit door beneath one of the destructible blocks, and the stage is only completed by clearing all enemies as well as finding the door. Bombing the exit door spawns additional enemies. Power-ups hidden under blocks include Fire for a larger blast, extra bombs and a remote control allowing manual detonation. Each stage has a countdown timer, and running it out spawns more enemies. Unlike later entries the original has no multiplayer battle mode.

castlevania.name: Castlevania
castlevania.title: Castlevania Unblocked - Play the NES Classic Free Online | Schplay
castlevania.metaDescription: Konami's 1986 original, running as the Classic NES Series GBA release. Six stages, a whip, and jumps you cannot take back.
castlevania.metaKeywords: castlevania, castlevania nes unblocked, konami 1986, simon belmont, dracula, classic nes series, schplay castlevania
castlevania.heroParagraph: Castlevania's title screen carries a 1986 and 1987 Konami copyright, and this is the Classic NES Series cartridge for Game Boy Advance with a stage-continue feature added. Simon Belmont walks into Dracula's castle with a whip and six stages between him and the count. Its reputation rests on one design decision that people still argue about: you cannot steer in mid-air.
instructions: Walk with the arrow keys, jump with Z and crack the whip with X. Once you leave the ground your trajectory is fixed - no mid-air adjustment at all - so every jump has to be correct before you make it. That is not a bug or a limitation of the era; it is the constraint the whole game is balanced around.

Collect hearts and use sub-weapons. Hearts are not health, they are ammunition for the throwing weapons you find in candles - the axe, the holy water, the cross, the dagger and the stopwatch. Hold up while attacking to use whichever you are carrying, and note that picking up a new one replaces the old one.

Holy water is the answer to most bosses. It burns on the ground where it lands and locks enemies in a damage loop, and combined with the double or triple shot upgrade it trivialises several fights that are otherwise very hard. If a boss is stopping you, going back for holy water is more effective than practising the fight.

sections.heading: The stiff jump is the game
sections.body: Modern platformers let you correct a jump mid-flight. Castlevania does not, and that turns every gap and every staircase into a commitment. It makes the game feel heavy and deliberate rather than floaty, and it means enemies placed to knock you off ledges - particularly the Medusa heads - are a genuine threat rather than an annoyance. Learning the game means learning to look before you leap, literally.

sections.heading: Knockback into pits
sections.body: Taking a hit sends Simon backwards, and most deaths in the game are falls caused by damage rather than by running out of health. The consequence is that clearing enemies before committing to a jump is nearly always worth the extra seconds, and that a full health bar does not mean you are safe on a narrow ledge.

sections.heading: Six stages and a run of famous bosses
sections.body: The castle runs through six blocks ending in the Grim Reaper and then Dracula himself, with the Phantom Bat, Medusa, the Mummies and Frankenstein's Monster along the way. Death on stage five is widely considered harder than Dracula, and arriving at that fight without holy water is the point most runs end.

sections.heading: Music that outlived the console
sections.body: Vampire Killer, Stalker and Wicked Child are among the best-known pieces of NES music ever written, and Konami's sound team pushed the hardware hard to get them. The soundtrack has been rearranged in nearly every subsequent Castlevania game, which is unusual persistence for a set of tunes composed for two pulse channels and a triangle wave.

sections.heading: The Classic NES Series reissue
sections.body: This cartridge is Nintendo's Game Boy Advance reissue of the NES original, which adds the ability to continue from a stage rather than restarting the game. The title screen shows that option directly. Everything else is the 1986 game unchanged, including its difficulty.

castlevania.plainText: Castlevania is Konami's 1986 NES action platformer, presented here as the Classic NES Series release for Game Boy Advance which adds a stage continue feature. Simon Belmont walks with the arrow keys, jumps with Z and attacks with a whip using X; holding up while attacking uses the carried sub-weapon. Jump trajectory cannot be altered once airborne, so jumps must be committed to in advance. Hearts collected in the level are ammunition for sub-weapons rather than health, and sub-weapons - the axe, holy water, cross, dagger and stopwatch - replace each other when picked up. Holy water burns on the ground and locks enemies in a damage loop, making it highly effective against bosses. Being hit knocks Simon backwards, causing most deaths by falling. The castle has six stages ending with the Grim Reaper and Dracula.

frost-bite.name: Frost Bite
frost-bite.title: Frost Bite Unblocked - Play the Nitrome Puzzle Platformer Free | Schplay
frost-bite.metaDescription: Nitrome's 2008 icy puzzle platformer, in their signature pixel art. Freeze, climb and dig your way through a level map.
frost-bite.metaKeywords: frost bite, frost bite nitrome, nitrome games unblocked, pixel art platformer, ice puzzle game, schplay frost bite
frost-bite.heroParagraph: Frost Bite is a Nitrome game - its title screen carries the studio's 2008 copyright - and it looks exactly like one. Nitrome built a reputation in the Flash era on dense, colourful pixel art and one clever mechanic per game, and this is their icy entry: a puzzle platformer set in a frozen landscape, played across a level map you unlock as you go.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys and jump with up. The level map is navigated with the mouse - you select which stage to play from it, and completed stages unlock the ones beyond them, so progress is visible as a route across the map rather than a level counter.

Read the ice before you step on it. Nitrome's puzzle games are built around a single interaction you have to work out rather than be told, and in a game about frozen ground the questions are always about what holds your weight, what melts, and what you can climb once it is frozen solid.

Treat each stage as a puzzle with one intended solution. These are not games you brute-force with reflexes - if a section seems to demand a jump you cannot make, the route is almost certainly somewhere else. Dying is cheap and restarting is quick, so experimenting is the correct way to play.

sections.heading: Who Nitrome are
sections.body: Nitrome is a small British studio that made a long run of browser games through the Flash era, all sharing a distinctive chunky pixel style and a habit of building each game around a single unusual mechanic. They were one of the few Flash studios with a recognisable house style, and their games hold up better than most of the era precisely because the art was never trying to be realistic.

sections.heading: A level map, not a level list
sections.body: Rather than a linear sequence, Frost Bite presents a map with routes between stages, and the map itself communicates progress and structure. It is a small thing but it changes how a session feels - you can see where you have been and what is still locked, which gives a browser game a sense of scale it would not otherwise have.

sections.heading: Built when Flash games had scores
sections.body: The title screen carries Scores, Help and Credits alongside Play, which was standard for a portal game in 2008 - high score tables were how these games kept people coming back before achievements existed. The scores here are local rather than online, since the servers that once backed them are long gone.

sections.heading: Preserved rather than lost
sections.body: An enormous amount of Flash-era work vanished when browsers dropped the plugin at the end of 2020, and studios like Nitrome are among the most-missed. This copy runs through Ruffle, an open-source reimplementation of the Flash player written in Rust, served locally rather than from a CDN so it works on networks that block outside domains.

sections.heading: Short sessions by design
sections.body: Flash puzzle platformers were built for the specific situation of someone with ten spare minutes and a browser, and Frost Bite is paced accordingly - stages are short, restarts are instant, and the map lets you stop and resume without losing much. That makes it particularly well suited to being played the way it is being played here.

frost-bite.plainText: Frost Bite is a puzzle platformer by the British studio Nitrome, released in 2008 as a Flash game, with the studio's characteristic pixel art style. Move with the arrow keys and jump with the up arrow; the level map is navigated with the mouse and completing stages unlocks further ones along routes across the map. The game is built around a single ice-based mechanic that the player is expected to work out rather than be told, and each stage has an intended solution rather than being a test of reflexes. The title screen offers Play, Scores, Help and Credits, with score tables kept locally. The game runs through the Ruffle Flash emulator, served locally rather than from a content delivery network.

btd-2.title: Bloons Tower Defense 2 Unblocked - Play Free Online | Schplay
btd-2.metaDescription: Ninja Kiwi's sequel adds monkey glue, new tracks and round-by-round control. Pop the bloons before they escape.
btd-2.metaKeywords: bloons tower defense 2, btd2 unblocked, ninja kiwi, monkey glue, dart monkey, tower defence, schplay btd2
btd-2.heroParagraph: Bloons Tower Defense 2 is Ninja Kiwi's follow-up to the game that made the series, and it expands in the directions the first one needed. There are more tracks, more towers, and - crucially - you press Start Round yourself, which means you decide when the pressure arrives rather than waiting for a timer to decide for you.
instructions: Click a tower and place it next to the track, then press Start Round when you are ready. That last part is the important change from the first game: rounds do not begin until you say so, which turns every gap between waves into a planning phase rather than a scramble.

Try monkey glue. It slows bloons that pass through it, and the game is specific about the limit - each blob can slow twenty bloons before it wears out. That makes it a consumable area effect rather than a permanent tower, and it is most valuable placed just before a cluster of damage rather than spread thinly.

Keep upgrading the Dart Monkey. It remains the backbone of any defence because it is cheap enough to place several and its upgrades multiply what each dart does. Spreading money across many different tower types looks more interesting and generally performs worse than concentrating on a few well-placed, well-upgraded ones.

sections.heading: Starting rounds yourself changes the game
sections.body: In the first Bloons TD the waves came at you on a schedule. Here you trigger each one, which means a careful player can bank money, plan placements and enter every round exactly as prepared as they can be. It also introduces a genuine decision - rushing rounds produces more income sooner, at the cost of facing them with a weaker defence.

sections.heading: Reading the round hints
sections.body: The game tells you what is coming before each round, in the same conversational tone as the first game - warnings about waves of blacks, or a note that the next level has no yellows in it. Reading them is worth the two seconds: knowing a wave is mostly black bloons tells you to prioritise bombs, since blacks are immune to some other damage types.

sections.heading: Placement still beats spending
sections.body: The strongest towers sit on the inside of tight corners and where the track doubles back, so a single range circle covers two stretches at once. In a game where money is the limiting factor throughout, getting twice the coverage from one purchase compounds through the whole run. Look at the shape of the track before buying anything.

sections.heading: Where the series went from here
sections.body: Ninja Kiwi kept iterating - by Bloons TD 6 there are monkey specialisation paths, heroes, and a large mobile business built on the same core loop. What is striking playing the early entries is how little the fundamental idea needed to change: bloons follow a path, you build things beside it, and layers pop into more layers.

sections.heading: Flash, running through Ruffle
sections.body: This is a Flash game and Flash was discontinued at the end of 2020. It plays here through Ruffle, the open-source Flash player reimplementation written in Rust and served from this site rather than from a CDN, so it works on networks that block external domains. Links to Ninja Kiwi's own site from the menus point at pages that have long since changed.

btd-2.plainText: Bloons Tower Defense 2 is Ninja Kiwi's Flash sequel to the original Bloons Tower Defense, adding more tracks and towers and letting the player start each round manually rather than on a timer. Use the mouse to select and place towers beside the track and to buy upgrades, then press Start Round to begin the next wave. Monkey glue slows bloons that pass through it, with each blob able to slow twenty bloons before wearing out. The Dart Monkey remains the most cost-effective tower, particularly when upgraded. The game provides a written hint before each round describing what is coming. Towers placed on tight corners and where the track doubles back cover more of the route with a single range circle. The game runs through the Ruffle Flash emulator.

deal-or-no-deal.name: Deal or No Deal
deal-or-no-deal.title: Deal or No Deal Unblocked - Play the Game Show Free Online | Schplay
deal-or-no-deal.metaDescription: The Flash version of the TV game show. Twenty-six cases, one million dollars, and a banker who knows more than you do.
deal-or-no-deal.metaKeywords: deal or no deal, deal or no deal unblocked, game show game, 26 cases, banker offer, flash game, schplay deal or no deal
deal-or-no-deal.heroParagraph: Deal or No Deal turns a television format into a game about expected value and nerve. You pick one of twenty-six numbered cases to keep, then open the others one at a time, eliminating amounts from the board. Between rounds the banker offers to buy your case, and the whole game is the question of whether that offer is better than what you are holding.
instructions: Click a case to keep as your own - the game opens by asking you to pick the one you think holds the million. Every case you open afterwards reveals an amount that is removed from the board, and the two columns on either side track what is still in play, from one cent up to a million dollars.

Watch the board, not the cases. There is nothing to learn about which numbered case holds what - the numbers are meaningless. The only real information is which amounts remain unopened, because that is what determines both your odds and what the banker will offer.

Understand what the banker is doing. The offer is calculated from the remaining amounts and is deliberately below the true average, especially early on. As the board empties the offers get closer to fair value, which is why holding out through the first few rounds is usually correct and why the interesting decisions come late.

sections.heading: Expected value versus the offer
sections.body: The mathematically neutral value of your case is the average of every amount still on the board. If four cases remain holding one dollar, a thousand, ten thousand and a million, that average is a little over a quarter of a million. An offer meaningfully below that is the banker buying your risk cheaply - and an offer above it, which does occasionally happen late, is worth taking every time.

sections.heading: Why people take bad deals anyway
sections.body: The format works because expected value is not the same as what a person should do. A guaranteed large sum is worth more to most people than a coin flip with the same average, and the show is built on that gap. Playing it as a browser game with no real money makes the mathematically correct play much easier - which is itself a good demonstration of why the televised version is tense.

sections.heading: The board is the whole interface
sections.body: Two columns list every amount from a penny to a million, and each opened case strikes one off. Because both the low and high sides matter, a good round is one that removes small amounts and a bad one removes the top prizes. The visible asymmetry of that is what creates the drama, and the interface is designed so you can read your position instantly.

sections.heading: Twenty-six cases and six to go
sections.body: The opening round asks you to open several cases before the first offer, and the counter in the corner tracks how many are left before the banker calls. Later rounds require fewer openings each, so the pace accelerates - the early game is a formality and the last few decisions carry almost all the weight.

deal-or-no-deal.plainText: Deal or No Deal is a Flash adaptation of the television game show. The player selects one of twenty-six numbered cases to keep, then opens the remaining cases one at a time, removing the revealed amounts from a board that runs from one cent to one million dollars. Between rounds a banker offers to buy the player's case, and the player chooses to accept or continue. Case numbers carry no information; the only meaningful data is which amounts remain unopened, since these determine both the odds and the size of the offer. The banker's offers are calculated below the average of the remaining amounts, moving closer to that average as fewer cases remain. Early rounds require several cases to be opened before each offer, with fewer required in later rounds. The game runs through the Ruffle Flash emulator.

stack.heroParagraph: Stack is a one-button game rendered in clean isometric blocks, and its own on-screen instruction is the whole manual: click, or press the spacebar, to place the block. A slab slides back and forth above your tower and you drop it. Whatever overhangs the block beneath is sliced off and falls away, so every imperfect placement makes the next one harder.
instructions: Click or press space to drop the moving block. It will land where it is at that instant, and any part of it that extends past the block below is cut off permanently. The tower gets narrower with every miss, which means early sloppiness compounds into an impossible target twenty blocks later.

Aim for perfect placements. Landing a block exactly on the one below removes no width at all, and consecutive perfect drops start growing your tower back - which is the only way to recover from a bad start. Chasing perfects rather than merely surviving is what separates a score of ten from a score of fifty.

Ignore the speed and watch the edge. The block's travel speeds up as you climb, and the instinct is to react faster. The better approach is to fix your eye on the near edge of the block below and press when the moving edge aligns with it, which is a much smaller judgement than trying to track the whole slab.

sections.heading: Why one button works
sections.body: With a single input there is nothing to learn and nothing to configure - the whole skill is timing, and everyone starts equal. That design is why the genre exploded on phones and why it works just as well in a browser tab: no instructions, no controls to remember, and a run that ends fast enough to make one more attempt irresistible.

sections.heading: The perfect-drop mechanic
sections.body: Slicing on every drop would make runs strictly finite and short. Rewarding exact placements with width recovery gives skilled players a way to sustain a run indefinitely in principle, and it converts the game from a survival timer into something with an actual ceiling worth chasing. It also makes the colour bands, which shift as you climb, a readable measure of how far you have come.

sections.heading: Isometric rendering with no 3D
sections.body: The tower is drawn in an isometric projection - parallel lines rather than true perspective - which is why it reads as three dimensional while remaining cheap to render and perfectly crisp. It is the same trick used by decades of strategy games, and it makes the alignment judgement the game depends on much easier to read than a perspective camera would.

sections.heading: Built for both mouse and touch
sections.body: Because the only input is a single tap, click or key press, the game is identical on a phone and a desktop with no separate mobile version. The keyboard alternative is a small courtesy that matters here - on a laptop, pressing space is noticeably more precise than clicking a trackpad.

sections.heading: Score, and what a good run looks like
sections.body: The counter at the top is simply blocks placed. A first attempt usually ends in single figures, twenty is a comfortable score, and past forty the block is moving fast enough that most drops are near-misses being rescued by earlier perfects. There is no end state beyond your own tower running out of width.

stack.plainText: Stack is a one-button arcade game in which an isometric block slides back and forth above a tower and the player clicks or presses the spacebar to drop it. Any part of the dropped block that overhangs the block beneath is cut away permanently, making the tower narrower with each imperfect placement. Landing a block exactly on the one below is a perfect placement that removes no width, and consecutive perfect drops increase the tower's width again, allowing recovery. The block's travel speed increases as the tower grows. The score is the number of blocks successfully placed, and a run ends when a drop misses the tower entirely. The game uses a single input and plays identically with a mouse, a keyboard or a touchscreen.

javascript-breakout.heroParagraph: Breakout is the game Atari built in 1976 from an idea by Nolan Bushnell and Steve Bristow, prototyped in hardware by Steve Wozniak, and it is the direct ancestor of every brick-breaker since. This is a JavaScript recreation that runs in the browser with no plugin: a paddle, a ball, and rows of bricks that have to be removed one bounce at a time.
instructions: Move the paddle with the mouse or the left and right arrow keys, and press space to launch. The ball's angle off the paddle depends on where it hits - striking it near the edge sends the ball off sharply, while the centre returns it steeply. That is the only aiming control you have, and it is the whole skill of the game.

Work the ball into the gap behind the wall. The classic technique is to break a channel up one side so the ball gets trapped between the bricks and the ceiling, where it clears rows on its own while you wait. It is far more efficient than picking bricks off from below and it is the strategy the original arcade cabinet was designed to reward.

Expect the ball to speed up. Breakout traditionally accelerates after a set number of hits and again when you reach the higher rows, and the paddle often shrinks partway through. Anticipating where the ball will be, rather than chasing where it is, is the adjustment the later stages demand.

sections.heading: Where it came from
sections.body: Atari commissioned Breakout as a single-player answer to Pong, and Steve Wozniak designed the original circuit with a famously small number of chips while Steve Jobs handled the contract. It shipped in 1976, and a few years later the same basic idea - a paddle, a ball and a wall - had spawned an entire genre. Very few games have that direct a line of descent.

sections.heading: The angle off the paddle is everything
sections.body: Because the paddle imparts angle based on contact point, a good player is not simply returning the ball but aiming it. Deliberately catching the ball near the paddle edge to steer it toward a specific column is how you carve the channel up the side, and it turns a reaction game into something closer to a very fast game of snooker.

sections.heading: Why the genre never died
sections.body: Brick breakers persisted through Arkanoid's power-ups, DX-Ball's shareware era, and the modern ball-count variants where you fire dozens of balls at numbered bricks. The core keeps working because it is legible instantly and has a skill ceiling well above where most players stop - the same reason Tetris and Pong are still around.

sections.heading: Running as plain JavaScript
sections.body: This version needs no Flash, no plugin and no download - it is HTML5 canvas and JavaScript, which is why it starts instantly and works on any modern browser including on a phone. Recreating Breakout is a common exercise for people learning game programming, which is why open-source versions like this one are plentiful and often carry a permissive licence.

sections.heading: Keyboard or mouse
sections.body: Mouse control gives you the finest positioning and is what most players prefer, but the arrow keys are more predictable on a trackpad where a small hand movement can send the paddle across the screen. Both are supported here, and switching between them mid-game is fine - the paddle simply follows whichever you last used.

contra-iii.name: Contra III: The Alien Wars
contra-iii.title: Contra III: The Alien Wars Unblocked - Play the SNES Classic Free | Schplay
contra-iii.metaDescription: Konami 1992 on the SNES - carry two weapons at once and lock your aim mid-run.
contra-iii.metaKeywords: contra iii, the alien wars, contra 3 unblocked, snes contra, konami 1992, run and gun, schplay contra
contra-iii.heroParagraph: Contra III: The Alien Wars is the entry that took the series onto the SNES and used every bit of the extra hardware to do it. The title screen credits it to Konami in 1992, and it is still the benchmark the rest of the series is measured against - relentless, precise, and built around a handful of ideas that no earlier Contra had room for.
instructions: Move and aim with the arrow keys, fire with S and jump with X. The big change from earlier Contra games is that you carry two weapons at once and swap between them with Z, so a power-up never has to be a painful choice. Press A to set off a smart bomb, which clears the screen and is meant to be spent rather than hoarded.

Learn the shoulder buttons. Holding Q or E locks your aim in the direction you are currently facing while letting you keep running - which is the only way to back away from something while still shooting at it. Almost every hard section in the game becomes manageable once you stop trying to solve it with movement alone.

You die in one hit, so treat positioning as the whole game. Learn where enemies enter the screen, stay near the middle where you have room to dodge in either direction, and remember that the Spread gun is forgiving but the Laser does far more damage to bosses. Two players can share the screen, which halves the pressure on each of you but doubles the chaos.

sections.heading: Two weapons, no regrets
sections.body: Every Contra before this one made power-ups a gamble: pick up the wrong gun and you were stuck with it. Contra III gives you two slots and a swap button, which quietly changes how you play. You can hold a Spread for crowds and a Laser for bosses and switch at the moment it matters, and you can grab an unknown power-up without fear because your good weapon is still parked in the other slot. It also means dying costs you less, since you only lose what you were holding rather than everything you had built up.

sections.heading: The overhead stages
sections.body: Two of the six stages drop the side view entirely and put you above the action, rotating the whole floor around you as you turn. This is the SNES Mode 7 effect used as a design idea rather than a showpiece: you have to find and destroy a set of targets scattered across a rotating arena while the camera keeps reorienting under your feet. Players tend to either love these stages or find them disorienting, and they are the part of the game most obviously built to show off what the new hardware could do that the NES could not.

sections.heading: Difficulty as the point
sections.body: Contra III is hard on purpose and honest about it. Enemies fire patterns rather than random shots, bosses telegraph every attack, and a death almost always traces back to a decision you can identify and change. That is the difference between this and a game that is merely unfair - repetition genuinely makes you better at it. The Easy setting shortens the game rather than simply weakening enemies, so players who want to see all six stages should start on Normal even if the first attempts are short.

sections.heading: Where it sits in the series
sections.body: Contra and Super C established the formula on the NES; Contra III refined it with better hardware and is generally regarded as the peak of the 2D run-and-gun era, alongside Konami's own later Hard Corps on the Genesis. It was also released outside Japan under different names - Super Probotector in Europe, where the human commandos were replaced with robots to satisfy stricter content rules of the time. This is the North American release, so you play as Bill and Lance rather than their robot stand-ins.

contra-iii.plainText: Contra III: The Alien Wars is a run-and-gun action game developed and published by Konami for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, copyright 1992 as shown on its title screen. The player controls Bill Rizer or Lance Bean fighting an alien invasion across six stages. Unlike earlier Contra games, the player can carry two weapons simultaneously and switch between them, and can use smart bombs that clear the screen. The shoulder buttons lock the player's aim direction while allowing continued movement. Two of the stages use an overhead perspective with a rotating floor rendered using the SNES Mode 7 graphics mode. The player dies from a single hit. The game supports two-player simultaneous cooperative play. It was released in Europe as Super Probotector: Alien Rebels with robot protagonists. The game is widely regarded as one of the best entries in the Contra series and a high point of the 16-bit run-and-gun genre.

donkey-kong.name: Donkey Kong
donkey-kong.title: Donkey Kong Unblocked - Play the Original Arcade Classic Free | Schplay
donkey-kong.metaDescription: The 1981 arcade game that introduced Mario - climb the girders, dodge the barrels and rescue Pauline.
donkey-kong.metaKeywords: donkey kong, donkey kong unblocked, classic nes series, arcade 1981, mario jumpman, nintendo, schplay arcade
donkey-kong.heroParagraph: Donkey Kong is the game that started almost everything. Released to arcades by Nintendo in 1981, it introduced the character who would become Mario, gave Shigeru Miyamoto his first hit, and effectively invented the platform game - a genre built on jumping over things rather than shooting them. This is the Classic NES Series re-release, the version Nintendo issued for the Game Boy Advance.
instructions: Run with the left and right arrow keys, climb ladders with up and down, and jump with Z. That is the entire control scheme, which is part of why the game has aged so well - there is nothing to learn beyond the timing.

Jump barrels at the last possible moment. Jumping early is the most common mistake: the barrel keeps rolling while you are in the air and catches you on the way down. Wait until it is almost on you, then jump. You can also jump over a barrel as it rolls down a ladder you are climbing past, which is worth points but is far riskier than simply avoiding it.

Grab the hammer when a screen gets crowded, but watch the clock. The hammer smashes barrels and fireballs for big points, and while you hold it you cannot climb ladders or jump - so taking it at the wrong moment traps you on a girder until it runs out. The bonus timer at the top drains steadily and is your real opponent on later boards.

sections.heading: The stage the NES version left out
sections.body: The arcade original had four stages: the sloped girders, the cement factory with its conveyor belts and pie trays, the elevators, and the rivets. The NES port - which is what this Classic NES Series cartridge reproduces - dropped the cement factory entirely, most likely to fit the game into the cartridge memory available in 1983. Players who grew up with the console version and later found the arcade one are usually surprised to discover a whole stage they had never seen. The three remaining boards then repeat at increasing speed rather than cycling through four.

sections.heading: Mario before he was Mario
sections.body: The character you control was originally called Jumpman, and the plot placed him as the owner of an ape who had escaped with his girlfriend Pauline. He picked up the name Mario later, and Pauline was largely replaced by Princess Peach as the series moved on - though she returned decades afterwards in Donkey Kong games and in Super Mario Odyssey. Donkey Kong himself went from villain to hero over the same period, which makes this one of the few games where you can watch an entire franchise's cast being invented in real time.

sections.heading: Why it still holds up
sections.body: Donkey Kong is short, has no story to sit through and no systems to learn, and every failure is instantly legible - you jumped too early, or you climbed into a fireball. That combination is rare and is why the game survives as something people actually play rather than merely respect. The scoring is deep enough to sustain competitive play, and the world-record chase around it has been documented in films and is still contested by a small group of players today.

sections.heading: The kill screen
sections.body: The arcade version famously breaks at level 22 - a counter overflow gives the player far too little bonus time to finish the board, killing them regardless of skill and capping the maximum achievable score. It is one of the most-discussed bugs in gaming, partly because it put a hard ceiling on a world record that would otherwise be open-ended. Console ports behave differently, so this version is not the one to hunt that particular ceiling on.

donkey-kong.plainText: Donkey Kong is an arcade platform game developed and published by Nintendo in 1981, designed by Shigeru Miyamoto. The player controls a carpenter originally named Jumpman, later renamed Mario, who must climb a construction site to rescue Pauline from a large ape. The player runs, climbs ladders and jumps over rolling barrels and fireballs, and can pick up a hammer to destroy obstacles temporarily at the cost of being unable to jump or climb. The arcade version contains four stages: girders, cement factory, elevators and rivets. The Nintendo Entertainment System port omits the cement factory stage. The arcade game contains a well-known counter overflow at level 22 that makes the stage impossible to complete, known as the kill screen. Donkey Kong is credited with popularising the platform genre and introducing the Mario character. This version is the Classic NES Series re-release for Game Boy Advance.
