dr-mario.heroParagraph: Dr. Mario is Nintendo's answer to the falling-block puzzle game, and its title screen still reads copyright 1990 Nintendo. Instead of clearing lines you are clearing a bottle: coloured viruses sit in it, you drop two-tone capsules on top of them, and lining up four of a colour makes that run vanish. Clear every virus and you move to the next level.
instructions: Move the falling capsule left and right with the arrow keys, speed its descent with down, and rotate it with Z or X. Each capsule has two halves that can be different colours, so rotation is how you decide which colour lands where - and a vertical capsule that only half-matches will split, with the unmatched half dropping down on its own.

Four in a row clears, and the four can be any mix of capsule halves and viruses in any straight line, horizontal or vertical. This is the key difference from Tetris: you are not filling rows, you are building colour runs, and the viruses already in the bottle count towards them. Aim your capsules at viruses rather than at empty space.

Keep the bottle low and leave yourself a column. The game ends when the neck of the bottle is blocked, so junk that piles up in the middle is far more dangerous than junk at the edges. Setting up chains - where one clear drops halves that immediately complete another run - is the main source of big scores and the fastest way out of a bad board.

sections.heading: Not a Tetris clone
sections.body: The two games are usually shelved together and they work almost nothing alike. Tetris is about geometry: you are packing shapes to eliminate complete rows, and colour is decoration. Dr. Mario is about colour matching against fixed targets, and shape barely matters - every piece is the same two-cell capsule. The result is that Tetris rewards spatial planning while Dr. Mario rewards reading the board for the run you can close next, which is a genuinely different skill. Plenty of players are good at one and hopeless at the other.

sections.heading: The virus level dial
sections.body: Before you start you choose a virus level from 0 to 20 and a speed setting. The virus level controls how many viruses are seeded into the bottle and how deep they sit, and it changes the game far more than the speed does. Low levels are a gentle colour-matching exercise; level 15 and above buries viruses under each other so that reaching the bottom row requires planned chains rather than opportunistic matches. Most players settle somewhere around 10 to 15 as the point where it stops being trivial and has not yet become punishing.

sections.heading: The half-capsule rule
sections.body: The single mechanic that separates competent players from good ones is what happens to leftovers. When a clear removes one half of a capsule, the other half becomes a free-floating single cell and falls until it lands on something. Skilled play uses this deliberately: you set up a clear knowing exactly where the orphaned halves will drop, so that they complete a second run on landing. Chains built this way clear far more of the bottle than any single match can, and they are the difference between surviving level 18 and not.

sections.heading: A soundtrack people remember
sections.body: Dr. Mario shipped with two selectable music tracks, Fever and Chill, composed by Hirokazu Tanaka. Fever in particular has outlived the game itself - it has been rearranged for later Nintendo titles and is one of the more recognisable pieces of music from the NES library. It is a small thing, but the ability to pick your track was unusual at the time and the game is much better for having a genuinely good one.

dr-mario.plainText: Dr. Mario is a puzzle video game developed and published by Nintendo, copyright 1990 as shown on its title screen. The level is cleared when all viruses are destroyed, and the game ends if the bottle fills to the neck. Capsules can be moved horizontally, dropped faster and rotated. When a match removes one half of a capsule the remaining half falls independently, which allows chain reactions. The player selects a virus level from 0 to 20 and a falling speed before starting. metroid.heroParagraph: Metroid is where an entire genre begins. Its opening text still reads, in the game's own spelling, an emergency order to defeat the Metroid of the planet Zebeth and destroy the Mother Brain - and then it drops you into a dark maze with no map, no directions and a gun that cannot yet reach most of the places you need to go.
instructions: Run with the arrow keys, jump with Z and fire with X. Hold up to aim your beam upward, and press down to curl into the Morph Ball, which is how you get through the low horizontal gaps that make up half the map. Press V to switch to missiles once you have found them, and Enter to check your status.

Shoot everything and jump at every ceiling. Metroid hides passages behind blocks that look identical to solid wall, and the game will not hint at them. If an area seems to be a dead end, it usually is not - fire at the floor, the ceiling and both walls before you accept it. This sounds tedious and is genuinely how the game is meant to be played.

Upgrades are the map. Every item you find opens somewhere you have already been and could not pass: the Morph Ball opens tunnels, the Bombs open floors, the High Jump and Ice Beam open vertical shafts. When you are stuck, go back to a place that looked impossible earlier rather than pushing further into somewhere new. Freezing enemies with the Ice Beam also turns them into platforms, which is required in several places.

sections.heading: The game that named a genre
sections.body: The word metroidvania exists because of this game and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. The idea Metroid contributed is the one in the name of the design: a single connected world rather than discrete levels, gated not by keys or locked doors but by your own abilities, so that progress feels like understanding the map better rather than being granted permission to continue. Nearly every modern game described as an exploration platformer - Hollow Knight, Ori, Axiom Verge - is working from the template that starts here.

sections.heading: No map, by design
sections.body: Metroid shipped without an in-game map, and modern players usually find this the hardest thing to adjust to. It was not an oversight so much as an assumption about how people played in 1986 - drawing your own map on paper was a normal part of playing adventure games at the time, and the game's sprawling, near-symmetrical corridors are built to make that act meaningful. If you would rather not, a printed map is not cheating; later games in the series added one precisely because the design works better with it.

sections.heading: Samus Aran
sections.body: Metroid ends by revealing that the armoured bounty hunter you have been playing is a woman, a twist that was genuinely unusual for 1986 and is the reason Samus Aran became one of the few widely recognised female protagonists of the era. The reveal is tied to how quickly you finish - beating the game faster shows more of it, which was the game's way of rewarding replay before achievements existed. Samus went on to headline one of Nintendo's three longest-running franchises.

sections.heading: Passwords instead of saves
sections.body: The Japanese original was released on the Famicom Disk System, which could save your progress to disk. The cartridge version sold elsewhere had no such hardware, so Nintendo replaced saving with a password system - a long string of characters shown when you die that restores your items and position. This is also the origin of the game's most famous piece of folklore: entering JUSTIN BAILEY as a password produces a valid, partially-equipped game state with Samus out of her armour, a result of the password format rather than a deliberate Easter egg.

metroid.plainText: Metroid is an action-adventure game developed by Nintendo Research and Development 1 and published by Nintendo, originally released for the Famicom Disk System in 1986 and for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1987. The player controls bounty hunter Samus Aran exploring the underground world of the planet Zebeth to destroy the Mother Brain and the Metroid organisms. The game world is a single interconnected map explored non-linearly, in which progress is gated by power-ups such as the Morph Ball, Bombs, High Jump Boots, Varia Suit and Ice Beam. ice-climber.metaDescription: Nintendo's 1985 vertical climber. Smash through the ice above you, dodge the topis, and catch the condor at the summit.
ice-climber.metaKeywords: ice climber, ice climber unblocked, popo nana, nes 1985, nintendo classic, condor, schplay retro
ice-climber.heroParagraph: Ice Climber sends Popo and Nana up thirty-two mountains by having them smash the floor above their own heads. It is a Nintendo game from 1985 with a genuinely odd central idea - you make progress by destroying the ceiling and then jumping through the hole you just made - and a reputation, entirely earned, for jump physics that take some getting used to.
instructions: Walk with the left and right arrows, jump with Z and swing your hammer with X. To climb, stand under a block of ice, swing upward to break it, and jump through the gap. Your hammer only breaks the block directly overhead, so lining yourself up matters more than timing does.

Get used to the jump. You have almost no air control compared to later Nintendo platformers, so a jump is largely committed the moment you leave the ground - aim before you press rather than trying to steer mid-flight. You also take damage from landing on a topi or a seal rather than bouncing off it, which is the opposite of what Mario has trained most players to expect.

Every eighth mountain ends in a bonus stage where a condor flies overhead. Jumping and grabbing it is worth a large score bonus, and missing it costs you nothing but the points - so it is always worth the attempt. Watch its flight path for a moment before committing rather than jumping the instant it appears.

sections.heading: Breaking the ceiling to climb
sections.body: Most platform games ask you to find the route someone else laid out. Ice Climber asks you to make one. The blocks above you are the level, and your hammer is the tool that turns them into a staircase - which means two players climbing the same mountain are constantly changing the terrain under each other. It is a small inversion of a familiar idea and it gives the game a texture nothing else on the NES really has. It also means a mountain can be made harder by careless smashing, since a hole in the wrong place can strand you.

sections.heading: Topis, seals and the nudge
sections.body: The recurring enemies are the topis, small creatures that push blocks of ice sideways to repair the holes you have made, and the seals, which simply block your path. Neither is difficult on its own; the difficulty is that they act while you are mid-climb and you cannot adjust once you are airborne. In the original Japanese release the enemy was a seal, changed to a yeti-like creature outside Japan - one of the more curious localisation decisions of the era.

sections.heading: A second life through Smash Bros.
sections.body: Ice Climber would probably be a footnote if the Ice Climbers had not been added as a playable character in Super Smash Bros. Melee in 2001. Popo and Nana appear as a pair - you control one and the other follows - which turned a fifteen-year-old NES curiosity into a character a whole generation recognised before ever playing the original. It is one of the clearest examples of Smash Bros. functioning as Nintendo's own museum.

sections.heading: Two players, mixed blessing
sections.body: The two-player mode is simultaneous rather than alternating, which was still relatively uncommon in 1985. It is also, famously, a good way to fall out with someone: since both climbers share one screen, the player who climbs faster drags the camera upward and can scroll the slower one off the bottom, killing them. Whether this is a flaw or the best thing about the mode depends entirely on who you are playing with.

Sessions are short by nature - a single mountain takes a minute or two - which makes it a reasonable thing to pick up for a few minutes at a time.

ice-climber.plainText: Ice Climber is a platform game developed and published by Nintendo, released for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1985. The player controls Popo or Nana, the Ice Climbers, ascending thirty-two vertical mountain stages by using a mallet to break the ice blocks forming the floor above them and jumping through the resulting gaps. Enemies include topis, which push ice blocks to repair broken floors, and seals that obstruct movement. The player character has limited mid-air control. Every eighth stage concludes with a bonus stage in which the player can jump to catch a condor for additional points. The game supports two-player simultaneous play on a shared screen, in which a player who falls below the bottom edge loses a life. The Ice Climbers were later added as a playable character in Super Smash Bros. Melee. This version is the Classic NES Series re-release for Game Boy Advance.

links-awakening-dx.metaDescription: The 1998 colour re-release of Nintendo's Game Boy Zelda. Washed up on Koholint Island, wake the Wind Fish to escape - if you really want to.
links-awakening-dx.metaKeywords: links awakening dx, zelda game boy color, koholint island, wind fish, links awakening unblocked, schplay zelda
links-awakening-dx.heroParagraph: Link's Awakening opens with Link shipwrecked and unconscious on a beach that belongs to no kingdom he knows. There is no Zelda, no Ganon and no Triforce - just an island called Koholint, a sleeping whale-like creature called the Wind Fish, and the growing suspicion that something about the place is not what it appears. This is the DX release, which added colour and a whole extra dungeon.
instructions: Move with the arrow keys and use your two equipped items with Z and X. Unlike later Zelda games nothing is permanently bound to a button - even the sword and shield occupy item slots - so you will be opening the inventory with Enter constantly to swap things around. That friction is the one genuinely dated part of the design.

Talk to everyone, twice. Koholint is small and densely written, and the villagers give real directions rather than filler - often the only pointer you will get toward the next dungeon. Several characters change what they say after story events, so circling back through the village after a dungeon is usually worth the couple of minutes.

Each dungeon gives you the item that unlocks the next stretch of the island. If you are stuck on the overworld, the answer is nearly always something you just found - Roc's Feather to jump a gap, the Power Bracelet to shift a rock, the Flippers to cross water. Trading is also a real questline here: a long chain of villagers each swap one item for another, and it ends in something you need.

sections.heading: A Zelda with no Hyrule
sections.body: Link's Awakening started as an unofficial after-hours project and it shows in the best possible way. Freed from the series' usual furniture, it fills Koholint with things that would fit nowhere else - Goombas and Piranha Plants from Mario appear as enemies, a side-scrolling section runs through several caves, and a Kirby lookalike shows up as a mini-boss. It is the strangest game in the series and, for a lot of players, the one they remember most clearly.

sections.heading: What the DX version added
sections.body: The original was a 1993 Game Boy game in four shades of grey. The 1998 DX release for Game Boy Color added full colour, a photographer who appears throughout the island and builds an album of your journey, and an entirely new Color Dungeon that rewards you with a permanent boost to either your attack or your defence. It also runs on the original Game Boy, in black and white, which was a common courtesy at the time. This is the DX version, so the extra dungeon and the photo album are both here.

sections.heading: The ending people still argue about
sections.body: The game tells you fairly early that waking the Wind Fish is how you leave the island, and then spends the rest of its length making you care about a place you have been told will not survive your success. It is a genuinely unusual thing for a 1993 handheld game to attempt, and it is the reason Link's Awakening gets discussed in terms usually reserved for much later games. The 2019 Switch remake reproduced the ending intact, which suggests Nintendo knew exactly what it had.

sections.heading: Small island, dense design
sections.body: Koholint fits on a handful of screens and yet holds eight dungeons plus the Color Dungeon, a trading sequence that spans the whole map, and a set of secret seashells scattered in places you will only reach with later items. The density is deliberate: because the map is small you learn it properly, so when a new item lets you cross a gap you have walked past twenty times, you know immediately where to go. Very few open worlds since have managed that particular feeling.

Link's Awakening is a long game by handheld standards, so be aware that progress does not carry between sessions here; it is better approached as something to dip into than to try to finish in one run.

links-awakening-dx.plainText: The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening DX is an action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Color, released in 1998 as an enhanced version of the 1993 Game Boy title Link's Awakening. Link is shipwrecked on Koholint Island and must collect eight Instruments of the Sirens to wake the Wind Fish and leave. The game is played from a top-down perspective with items assigned to two configurable buttons, including the sword and shield. It contains eight main dungeons, a trading sequence spanning the island, and secret seashells. The DX version adds colour graphics, a photographer character with a photo album, and an additional Color Dungeon granting a permanent attack or defence upgrade. The game is notable for excluding the usual Zelda setting, characters and Triforce, for including cameo enemies from the Mario series, and for its ending. A remake was released for Nintendo Switch in 2019.

ecco-the-dolphin.metaDescription: Sega's 1992 underwater adventure. Swim, sing and watch your air as you search the ocean for a pod that vanished into the sky.
ecco-the-dolphin.metaKeywords: ecco the dolphin, ecco unblocked, sega genesis, underwater game, dolphin game, 1992 sega, schplay retro
ecco-the-dolphin.heroParagraph: Ecco the Dolphin is a 1992 Genesis game about a dolphin whose entire pod is lifted out of the sea by a waterspout, leaving him alone in an empty ocean. It is beautiful, strange, unusually quiet, and much harder than its cover suggests - and it is the only game of its era where your most-used ability is singing.
instructions: Swim in any direction with the arrow keys, hold Z to accelerate and press X to charge into something. S is your sonar, and you will use it constantly: a short pulse maps the geometry around you and reveals passages, while aiming it at other sea creatures is how you talk to them and get told where to go next.

Watch the air meter. Ecco is a mammal and drowns, so the bar at the top of the screen is a constant background clock - surface to refill it, and plan any long underwater passage around where the next air pocket is. Running out is the most common way to die in the early game, and the level design is quite deliberately built to make you nervous about it.

Learn what to charge and what to avoid. Ecco's attack requires speed, so you must build up momentum before hitting something - tapping the button next to an enemy does nothing. Many hazards, particularly jellyfish and the spiky creatures, cannot be attacked at all and simply have to be swum around. Glyphs block your path until you sing at them, and some need a key glyph found elsewhere in the level.

sections.heading: Sonar as the core mechanic
sections.body: Most action games give you a weapon and build everything around it. Ecco gives you a voice. Sonar maps the terrain, opens the glyph barriers that gate each level, and is how every conversation in the game happens - whales, other dolphins and the odd stranger all respond to being sung at. It makes exploration feel genuinely different from swimming through a level with a map, because the world only reveals itself in the pulses you send out. That one design decision is why the game is still discussed thirty years on.

sections.heading: Much harder than it looks
sections.body: The art and the subject matter suggest something gentle, and the game is not. Ecco is fragile, the air meter never stops draining, the levels are large mazes with easy-to-miss exits, and several later stages are genuinely brutal - the Welcome to the Machine section in particular has a long-standing reputation as one of the hardest sequences on the Genesis. Going in expecting a relaxing swim is the single most common reason people bounce off it.

sections.heading: A story that goes somewhere unexpected
sections.body: What begins as a search for a missing pod becomes, over the course of the game, something involving time travel, an ancient undersea civilisation and an alien species that farms the ocean. Designer Ed Annunziata drew on fringe ideas about dolphin intelligence and lost civilisations that were circulating at the time, and the result is a game whose plot escalates in a direction essentially no player predicts from the first level. It is worth experiencing unspoiled.

sections.heading: The name
sections.body: The dolphin is named for the echo in echolocation, and the game's Japanese release used a spelling reflecting that. The five-dot pattern on Ecco's head is a recurring motif, and the common claim that the game is named after oceanographer Jacques Cousteau or the Eco movement is not accurate - though the game's environmental sympathies are real enough, and were unusual for a mainstream console release in 1992.

ecco-the-dolphin.plainText: Ecco the Dolphin is an action-adventure game developed by Novotrade International and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis in 1992, created by Ed Annunziata. The player controls a bottlenose dolphin named Ecco searching for his pod after it is removed from the ocean by a waterspout. Ecco swims freely in all directions, must periodically surface for air as tracked by an on-screen meter, and attacks by building speed and charging. The sonar ability maps the surrounding terrain, communicates with other sea creatures and activates glyph barriers that gate progress through levels. The story involves time travel, the lost city of Atlantis and an alien species harvesting the ocean. The game is known for its difficulty, particularly the level Welcome to the Machine, and for its distinctive underwater art. Ecco is named for echolocation. The game uses a password system to record progress between levels.

gunstar-heroes.name: Gunstar Heroes
gunstar-heroes.title: Gunstar Heroes Unblocked - Play Treasure's Genesis Classic Free | Schplay
gunstar-heroes.metaDescription: Treasure 1993 Genesis debut - combine two weapons into one and fight bosses that keep coming apart.
gunstar-heroes.metaKeywords: gunstar heroes, gunstar heroes unblocked, treasure, sega genesis, run and gun, 1993, schplay retro
gunstar-heroes.heroParagraph: Gunstar Heroes was the first game Treasure ever released, and it arrived in 1993 looking like a studio showing off everything it could do at once. It opens with Red and Blue sprinting after a hovercraft shouting that they have to stop him, and it barely slows down after that - a run-and-gun built around a weapon system that lets you fuse your guns together.
instructions: Run and aim with the arrow keys, fire with S, jump with X and grab enemies with Z. Before the first stage the game asks you to choose Fixed or Free shot: Fixed locks you in place while firing so you can aim precisely, and Free lets you run and shoot at once. Free is easier to pick up; Fixed is what most experienced players end up using.

Combine your weapons. You carry two of four base guns - Force, Lightning, Chaser and Flame - and holding both together produces a different weapon entirely rather than just switching. Chaser plus Lightning gives homing lightning; Flame plus Chaser gives tracking fire. Experimenting with pairs is most of the game's depth, and some combinations are dramatically stronger than the guns they are made from.

Do not forget you can grab. Melee is unusually good here - you can seize most ordinary enemies and throw them, slide into them, or drive them into the ground, and doing so costs no ammo and often clears a crowd faster than shooting. Players who treat this purely as a shooter miss roughly half of the moveset.

sections.heading: The weapon combination system
sections.body: Four base weapons, held two at a time, and the ability to merge whichever pair you are carrying gives a set of distinct combined weapons rather than a simple upgrade ladder. What makes it work is that the combinations are not just stronger versions - they behave differently enough to change how you approach a stage. Chaser combined with Lightning produces a homing beam that trivialises some bosses and is nearly useless against others, so the choice you make at a weapon pickup is a real decision rather than a reflex to grab the newest thing.

sections.heading: Bosses that come apart
sections.body: Treasure built its reputation on boss design and this is where it starts. Gunstar Heroes' bosses are large multi-part constructions that lose pieces as you damage them and change behaviour as they do, so a fight has visible phases you can read off the boss itself rather than off a health bar. Seven Force, a robot that transforms through a series of animal shapes mid-fight, is the one everyone remembers, and the studio reused the idea in later games including Alien Soldier and Radiant Silvergun.

sections.heading: Treasure's debut
sections.body: Treasure was formed by former Konami staff who wanted to make original games rather than licensed sequels, and Gunstar Heroes was their first release. It is unusually confident for a first game - the sprite counts, scaling effects and sheer amount happening on screen were pushing the Genesis harder than most of its library, and it established the house style the studio kept for a decade. If you like this, Alien Soldier and Dynamite Headdy are the obvious next stops on the same hardware.

sections.heading: The dice maze
sections.body: Partway through the game sits a board-game stage where you roll a die and move around a grid of squares, each triggering a fight, a shop or a trap. It has essentially nothing to do with the rest of the game and is the sort of thing that gets cut from most projects. Its survival here is a fair summary of Gunstar Heroes as a whole: the game is full of ideas that a more disciplined studio would have removed, and it is much more memorable for keeping them.

Gunstar Heroes supports two players simultaneously on the original hardware; here it is best approached as a single-player game, and it is short enough that a full run is realistic in one sitting.

gunstar-heroes.plainText: Gunstar Heroes is a run-and-gun action game developed by Treasure and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis in 1993. It was Treasure's first released game. The player controls Red or Blue, members of the Gunstar family, fighting to prevent the resurrection of a destructive entity. The player carries two of four base weapons - Force, Lightning, Chaser and Flame - and can combine the two held weapons to produce distinct combined weapons with different behaviour. The player can also grab, throw and slide into enemies. Before starting, the player chooses between Fixed shot, which prevents movement while firing, and Free shot, which allows movement while firing. Bosses are large multi-part constructions that change behaviour as components are destroyed, including Seven Force, which transforms between several forms. The game includes a board-game stage in which the player rolls a die to move between squares. The game supports two-player simultaneous cooperative play.

ranger-x.title: Ranger X Unblocked - Play the Sega Genesis Mech Shooter Free | Schplay

ranger-x.metaKeywords: ranger x, ranger x unblocked, sega genesis mech, gau entertainment, 1993 genesis, run and gun, schplay retro
ranger-x.heroParagraph: Ranger X is one of the Genesis library's better-kept secrets - a 1993 mech action game with some of the most impressive visual work on the system and a set of mechanics nothing else quite copied. You pilot a hovering mech accompanied by a separate support unit, and your weapons run on a meter that recharges from sunlight.
instructions: Move and aim with the arrow keys, fire your main weapon with S, and hold X to thrust - your mech hovers rather than jumps, so vertical position is something you hold rather than something you commit to. Z fires the sub-weapon, which is the heavier of the two and draws much more from your energy meter.

Watch the energy bar and let it refill. Your weapons drain a meter that recharges over time, and it charges faster in daylight than in the darker indoor stages - so firing constantly is not viable. The rhythm of the game is short bursts of fire followed by deliberate pauses, which is unusual for a run-and-gun and is the main thing new players get wrong.

Use the support unit. A second machine follows you around and fires independently, and you can position it relative to yourself - parking it above or behind you to cover an angle you cannot. Treating it as scenery wastes a significant part of your firepower, particularly in the boss fights where its covering fire can hold one threat off while you deal with another.

sections.heading: An energy meter instead of ammunition
sections.body: Most run-and-gun games give you infinite shots and make difficulty a question of aim and position. Ranger X instead gives you a shared energy pool that every weapon draws from and that refills on its own, faster in sunlit areas than in dark ones. The effect is to make restraint a skill: you learn to hold fire through the parts of a stage you can dodge, so that you arrive at the next real threat with a full bar. Very few games of this era asked for that kind of discipline, and it gives Ranger X a distinct pace.

sections.heading: The mech and its partner
sections.body: You control two machines at once - the walking mech you pilot and a support unit that follows you and fires on its own. You can direct where the partner sits relative to you, which turns it into a movable gun emplacement rather than a pet. In some configurations the two combine into a single vehicle for faster movement. It is a genuinely clever piece of design that gives the player something to manage during fights beyond their own position, and it is the main reason Ranger X still gets recommended.

sections.heading: Pushing the Genesis
sections.body: Ranger X is frequently cited as one of the best-looking games on the Sega Genesis. It uses layered parallax scrolling, careful palette work and a lot of animated background detail to get an impression of depth out of hardware that was usually outmatched by the SNES on colour. The attract sequence alone - silhouetted mountains under a dark sky, with the staff roll printed over it - is more atmospheric than most Genesis title screens managed, and it credits Y. Hiraiwa as music composer and N. Iwadare as sound operator.

sections.heading: A game that got overlooked
sections.body: Released in 1993 by Gau Entertainment and published by Sega, Ranger X landed in an extremely crowded year and never found the audience its quality warranted. It has no franchise behind it, no sequel and no famous mascot, which is most of the explanation - it is simply a very good game that arrived without anything to make people notice it. That makes it one of the more rewarding things to find in the Genesis catalogue now, when the obvious titles have all been played.

The game opens with a lengthy attract sequence and staff roll - press Start to skip past it and reach the title screen if you would rather get straight into a stage.

ranger-x.plainText: Ranger X is a run-and-gun action game developed by Gau Entertainment and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis in 1993. The player pilots a hovering mech accompanied by a separate support unit that fires independently and can be positioned relative to the player, and which can combine with the main mech into a single vehicle. Weapons draw from a shared energy meter that recharges over time, recharging faster in sunlit areas than in dark ones, requiring the player to manage firing rather than shoot continuously. The mech hovers using a thrust control rather than jumping. The game is frequently cited for its graphics, using layered parallax scrolling and detailed animated backgrounds considered among the best on the Sega Genesis. Its attract sequence credits Y. Hiraiwa as music composer and N. Iwadare as sound operator. The game received little commercial attention on release and has no sequels.

particle-clicker.metaKeywords: particle clicker, cern game, physics idle game, particle clicker unblocked, incremental game, webfest, schplay
particle-clicker.heroParagraph: Particle Clicker puts you in charge of a particle physics laboratory. You click a detector to collect data, spend that data on research, convert research into reputation, and use reputation to attract funding and staff who then collect data for you. It was built at CERN during a hackathon in 2014, and the discoveries you unlock along the way are real ones.
instructions: Click the detector in the middle of the screen to collect data. Every click produces a small amount, and at the start that is your only income - so the opening few minutes are genuinely just clicking while you accumulate enough to buy the first useful thing.

Spend data on research from the left panel, and reputation on staff from the right. Research unlocks upgrades and converts into reputation; reputation lets you hire people who generate data without you clicking. The whole game is a loop between those two panels, and the point at which hired staff out-earn your clicking is the point it becomes an idle game rather than a clicking one.

Do not neglect upgrades. The Upgrades panel multiplies what everything else produces, and it is easy to pour everything into hiring more people while ignoring the multipliers that would make the people you already have worth several times as much. As a rule, buy an upgrade whenever you can afford one without stalling your next hire.

sections.heading: Built at CERN
sections.body: Particle Clicker was made during CERN Webfest, a summer hackathon where students working at the laboratory spend a weekend building things that communicate science to the public. That origin explains the game's unusual shape: it is a genuine incremental game rather than a quiz with a score attached, but the progression is mapped onto how a real physics collaboration actually works - you need data, and to get data you need instruments, and to get instruments you need a reputation that attracts funding.

sections.heading: The discoveries are real
sections.body: Each research item you unlock corresponds to an actual result in particle physics, with a short description you can read once you have bought it. Working through them takes you roughly along the history of the field, from early detector work up to the Higgs boson. It is a light touch - nobody is going to learn physics from a clicker game - but the descriptions are accurate and it is a much better use of the genre than the usual cookies or paperclips.

sections.heading: How the incremental loop works
sections.body: The genre convention is that manual input gets you started and automation takes over. Here the two currencies keep that from being a single straight line: data comes from clicking and from staff, reputation comes from completing research, and staff cost reputation rather than data. So a run has a rhythm - click up enough data to fund research, cash the research into reputation, spend reputation on people who then click for you - rather than one number climbing forever. It also means you can stall by over-investing in one side.

sections.heading: It keeps running while you are away
sections.body: Once you have staff, the laboratory produces data whether or not the tab is open, and the game saves your progress to your browser's local storage. That makes it a reasonable thing to leave in a background tab and check on occasionally rather than something to sit and grind at. Because the save lives in your own browser, clearing site data will reset it, and progress will not follow you to a different computer.

That means it loads and runs on restricted networks where the original version would silently fail, and it makes no requests to any outside domain while you play. The game is open source under the terms in its own licence file.

An upgrades panel provides multipliers to production. The research items correspond to real discoveries in particle physics and include accurate descriptions, progressing roughly through the history of the field.
